"Lucy's Treats sells three different boxes of raisins:

Which box of raisins is the best deal?" :question/worked-solution "The best deal is the box with the lowest unit price. So, we need to compute the unit prices for all three boxes. To compute the unit price, we divide the price by the total number of ounces.   

- Dividing the total cost by the number of ounces in box $A,$ we get

$$
2.28÷12=0.19\,.
$$

So, the unit price of box $A$ is $$0.19.$

- Dividing the total cost by the number of ounces in box $B,$ we get

$$
5.44÷32=0.17\,.
$$

So, the unit price of box $B$ is $$0.17.$

- Dividing the total cost by the number of ounces in box $C,$ we get

$$
3.52÷22=0.16\,.
$$

So, the unit price of box $C$ is $$0.16.$

From the above, we see that box $C$ has the lowest unit price of $$0.16/\text{oz}.$ Therefore, box $C$ offers the best deal." :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields 3}\left[(2x-1)^3(x-2)^9\right].$" :question/worked-solution "Here, we apply the product rule and the power rule to get

$$
\eqalign{
\lim_\limits{x\rightarrow 3}\left[(2x-1)^3(x-2)^9\right]   &= \lim_\limits{x\rightarrow 3}(2x-1)^3\cdot  \lim_\limits{x\rightarrow 3}(x-2)^9\[3pt]
                                                                                    &= \left(\lim_\limits{x\rightarrow 3}(2x-1)\right)^3\cdot  \left(\lim_\limits{x\rightarrow 3}(x-2)\right)^9\[3pt]
                                                                                    &= (2\cdot 3 -1)^3\cdot (3-2)^9\[3pt]
                                                                                    &= 5^3 \cdot 1^9\[3pt]
                                                                                    & = 125.
}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186054513 :question/problem "The figure below shows the graph of $f(x).$ Determine $\lim_\limits{x\rightarrow 2} \left(\dfrac{2-7x}{xf(x)+2}\right)^3.$

![](images/50/5059a2cee34ad8547bf1af6239ab4a8356e715cd920707cf5f33d2de105a5c1d.png)" :question/worked-solution "From the graph, we find $\lim_\limits{x\rightarrow 2} f(x)=3.$ Therefore, using the power rule, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 2}{(\frac{2-7x}{xf(x)+2})}^{3} & ={({lim}_{x\to 2}\frac{2-7x}{xf(x)+2})}^{3} \\  & ={(\frac{2-7(2)}{(2\cdot 3)+2})}^{3} \\  & ={(\frac{-12}{8})}^{3} \\  & ={(\frac{-3}{2})}^{3} \\  & =-\frac{27}{8}.\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186054604 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-156d5c20-d8d9-52c6-bf0a-a41e2c4bb6cd"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186054518 :question/problem "Find $\lim_\limits{x \to 1} \dfrac{\sqrt{x+8}}{x-2}.$" :question/worked-solution "Applying the quotient rule, we get

$$
\lim_\limits{x\rightarrow 1} \dfrac{\sqrt{x+8}}{x-2}
=\dfrac{\lim_\limits{x\rightarrow 1} \sqrt{x+8}}{\lim_\limits{x\rightarrow 1}(x-2)}.
$$

We calculate the limits of the numerator and denominator, separately.

Applying the root rule in the numerator, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 1}\sqrt{x+8} & =\sqrt{{lim}_{x\to 1}(x+8)} \\  & =\sqrt{1+8} \\  & =\sqrt{9} \\  & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

For the denominator, we have
 

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 1}(x-2) & =1-2 \\  & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Consequently,

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{\sqrt{x+8}}{x-2} & =\frac{3}{(-1)} \\  & =-3\,.\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186054605 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-522ad648-b326-5d90-9d3d-5351c0a03cfc"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186054519 :question/worked-solution "According to the power rule and the quotient rules,

 

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to -2}{(\frac{f(x)}{{x}^{2}-1})}^{2/3} & ={(\frac{{lim}_{x\to -2}f(x)}{{lim}_{x\to -2}({x}^{2}-1)})}^{2/3}.\end{aligned}
$$

We find from the graph that the limit of the numerator is

$$
\lim_\limits{x\rightarrow -2} f(x)=1.
$$

 We also calculate the limit of the denominator as
 

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to -2}({x}^{2}-1) & =(-2)^{2}-1=3.\end{aligned}
$$

 So we get
 

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to -2}{(\frac{f(x)}{{x}^{2}-1})}^{2/3} & ={(\frac{{lim}_{x\to -2}f(x)}{{lim}_{x\to -2}({x}^{2}-1)})}^{2/3} \\  & ={(\frac{1}{3})}^{2/3} \\  & =\sqrt[3]{\frac{1}{9}}.\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186233993 :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-8f764e06-5d80-555d-8746-1b05ecbf0c86"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 3}\frac{\sqrt[3]{10x-3}}{{x}^{2}-3}.$" :question/worked-solution "Applying the quotient rule, we get

$$
{lim}_{x\to 3}\frac{\sqrt[3]{10x-3}}{{x}^{2}-3}=\frac{{lim}_{x\to 3}(\sqrt[3]{10x-3})}{{lim}_{x\to 3}({x}^{2}-3)}
$$

We calculate the limits of the numerator and denominator, separately.

Applying the root rule in the numerator, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 3}(\sqrt[3]{10x-3}) & =\sqrt[3]{10(3)-3} \\  & =\sqrt[3]{30-3} \\  & =\sqrt[3]{27} \\  & =3\,.\end{aligned}
$$

For the denominator, we have
 

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 3}({x}^{2}-3) & =(3)^{2}-3 \\  & =6\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Consequently,

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 3}\frac{\sqrt[3]{10x-3}}{{x}^{2}-3} & =\frac{3}{6} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\,.\end{aligned}

More precisely, if $n$ is any positive integer and $\lim_\limits{x\rightarrow a}f(x)=L,$ then

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to a}(f(x))^{n}={({lim}_{x\to a}f(x))}^{n}={L}^{n}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

For example, with the power rule, we can evaluate a limit like 

$$
\lim_\limits{x\rightarrow 2}(3x-4)^{8}
$$

 by evaluating the limit of the expression within parentheses and then taking the power of the result.

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 2}(3x-4)^{8} & ={({lim}_{x\to 2}(3x-4))}^{8} \\  & =(3\cdot 2-4)^{8} \\  & ={2}^{8} \\  & =256\,.\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186055955 :tutorial/content "The **root rule** states that the limit of a root is the root of the limit (provided that the root exists).

More precisely, if $n$ is any positive integer and $\lim_\limits{x\rightarrow a}f(x)=L,$ then

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to a}\sqrt[n]{f(x)}=\sqrt[n]{{lim}_{x\to a}f(x)}=\sqrt[n]{L}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

For example, with the root rule, we can evaluate a limit like 

$$
\lim_\limits{x\rightarrow 2}\sqrt{3x-2}
$$

 by evaluating the limit of the expression within the root and then taking the root of the result:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 2}\sqrt{3x-2} & =\sqrt{{lim}_{x\to 2}(3x-2)} \\  & =\sqrt{3\cdot 2-2} \\  & =\sqrt{4} \\  & =2\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186055956 :tutorial/content "If we combine the power rule and the root rule, then we get the following useful generalization: if $\lim_\limits{x\rightarrow a}f(x)=L,$ then for any fraction $p/q,$ we have

$$
\lim_\limits{x\rightarrow a}\left(f(x)\right)^{p/q} =  \left(\lim_\limits{x\rightarrow a} f(x)\right)^{p/q} = L^{p/q}
$$

provided that $L^{p/q}$ exists.

For example, we can evaluate a limit like 

$$
\lim_\limits{y\rightarrow 64} y^{-1/6}
$$

 by evaluating the limit of $y$ and then exponentiating the result to the fractional exponent:

 

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{y\to 64}{y}^{-1/6} & ={({lim}_{y\to 64}y)}^{-1/6} \\  & =(64)^{-1/6} \\  & ={({2}^{6})}^{-1/6} \\  & ={2}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186054899 :activity/expected-seconds 900.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]} [:db/retract 17592186051350 :answer-field/choices 17592186051351] [:db/retract 17592186051350 :answer-field/choices 17592186051352] [:db/retract 17592186051362 :answer-field/choices 17592186051363] [:db/retract 17592186051362 :answer-field/choices 17592186051364] [:db/retract 17592186051362 :answer-field/choices 17592186051365] [:db/retract 17592186051362 :answer-field/choices 17592186051366] [:db/retract 17592186051362 :answer-field/choices 17592186051367] {:db/id 17592186054848 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-bf7a3bf9-7841-5c39-8953-649f06640b22"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186054425 :question/problem "List the elements of the following set: 

$$
A = \big\{a, c,3, \{c,3 \}, \emptyset, \{\emptyset\}\big\}
$$" :question/worked-solution "The elements of the set $A$ are as follows:

$$
a, \quad c, \quad 3, \quad \{c,3\}, \quad \emptyset, \quad \{\emptyset\}
$$

**Watch Out!**

- The elements $c,3,$ and $\{c,3\}$ are three separate entities. The first two are the elements $c$ and $3,$ and the third is a set *containing* these two elements.

- The elements $\emptyset$ and $\{ \emptyset \}$ are also separate entities. The first one is the empty set (i.e., the set containing no elements), while the second is a set that contains the empty set." :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186054849 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-68a9ef69-1a68-5a42-bd02-0ed93671db30" "question-f2f32264-6492-5e60-8c09-298d7626357d"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186054426 :question/problem "Which of the following is **not** a set?

I. $\{ 2, 4, 6 \}$

II. $\{ \{ 2 \}, \{ 4, 6 \} \}$

III. $2, 4, 6$

IV. $\emptyset$" :question/worked-solution "A set is a collection of elements listed between two braces (curly brackets). However, note that the null set (the set that does not contain any elements) can be written as either $\{\}$ or $\emptyset.$

- $\{ 2, 4, 6 \}$ is a set. The elements are $2,$ $4,$ and $6,$ and they are listed between two braces.

- $\{ \{ 2 \}, \{ 4, 6 \} \}$ is a set. The elements are $\{ 2 \}$ and $\{ 4, 6 \},$ and are listed between the two outermost braces.

- $2, 4, 6$ is *not* a set. The numbers $2,$ $4,$ and $6$ are *not* listed between two braces.

- $\emptyset$ is the empty set. Therefore, it is a set.

In conclusion, only III is not a set." :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186054850 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-6ae10c4a-b478-5b9e-9599-7eb7b75dca9d" "question-6b96bbb9-30d0-511e-a26c-5b394ffc1b3c" "question-f10fdf14-c3b0-5ff7-a1e1-67a02a7a3852"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186054427 :question/problem "Write the following statement using element notation:

$\qquad$ $1$ and $2$ are elements of a set $S,$ but $3,$ $4,$ and $5$ are not." :question/worked-solution "If $a$ is an element of $S,$ we write $a \in S.$ Otherwise, if $a$ is *not* an element of $S,$ we write $a \notin S.$

- Since $1$ and $2$ are elements of $S,$ we write $1,2 \in S.$

- Since $3,$ $4,$ and $5$ are *not* elements of $S,$ we write $3,4,5 \notin S.$

All together, we have the following statement:

$$
1,2 \in S\quad \textrm{and}\quad 3,4,5 \notin S
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186054851 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-101cf0dd-9e7d-5358-b3ec-977545014b49" "question-76066cd5-d606-50ce-8894-909f30c9f6a3"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186054428 :question/problem "Express the following sets using an ellipsis:

- The set $X$ of all positive integers greater than or equal to $10$

- The set $Y$ of integers less than zero

- The set $A$ of all natural numbers greater than $5$ and less than $5\, 005$" :question/worked-solution "Remember that an ellipsis means "and so on up to" if it's followed by a specific element, or "and so on" if not.

- To express the set $X,$ we start with the first positive integer greater than or equal to $10,$ which is $10.$ The next integer is $11,$ the one after that is $12,$ and so on, which we denote with an ellipsis:

$$
X = \{10, 11, 12, \ldots \}
$$

- To express the set $Y,$ we start with the first integer less than zero, which is $-1.$ The next integer less than zero is $-2,$ the one after that is $-3,$ and so on, which we denote with an ellipsis:

$$
Y = \{ -1, -2, -3, \ldots \}
$$

However, note that it is conventional to write a set of numbers from least to greatest, just like is shown on the number line. Writing the elements of $Y$ from least to greatest, we have

$$
Y = \{ \ldots , -3, -2, -1\}.
$$

- To express the set $A,$ we start with the first positive integer greater than $5,$ which is $6.$ The next integer is $7,$ the one after that is $8,$ and so on up to $5\, 004$ (the largest integer less than $5\, 005$). So, we have

$$
A = \{6, 7, 8, \ldots , 5004\}.
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186054970 :question/problem "Which of the following is an element of the set $C=\{\{a\},\,b,\,\{c\},\,d,\,\{e\}\}?$" :question/worked-solution "The elements of our set are as follows:

$$
\{a\},\,b,\,\{c\},\,d,\,\{e\}
$$

Among the given options, the only element that belongs to the set is $\{e\}.$

**Watch out!** Note that $e$ is *not* an element of our set. Our set contains an element $\{e\}$ that is a set itself." :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186051350 :answer-field/correct "answer-5e87d1b9-c21c-5e07-8bcb-e7801cafe650" :answer-field/choices ["answer-dbed2e9b-2062-58e1-bbcb-34bffd5958e8" "answer-5e87d1b9-c21c-5e07-8bcb-e7801cafe650"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-dbed2e9b-2062-58e1-bbcb-34bffd5958e8" :answer/id #uuid "dbed2e9b-2062-58e1-bbcb-34bffd5958e8" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\{d\}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-5e87d1b9-c21c-5e07-8bcb-e7801cafe650" :answer/id #uuid "5e87d1b9-c21c-5e07-8bcb-e7801cafe650" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\{e\}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-bf7a3bf9-7841-5c39-8953-649f06640b22" :question/id #uuid "bf7a3bf9-7841-5c39-8953-649f06640b22" :question/math-academy-id "q-181262" :question/problem "Which of the following is an element of the set $A=\{♢,\,10,\,a,\,◻\}?$" :question/worked-solution "The elements of our set are as follows:

Usually, the elements of a set have some property in common. For example, a set could be a class at school where the students are the members of the set. The common property is that all the students are members of the class.

To write a set, we list the elements between two braces (curly brackets). Commas are used to separate the elements.

So, for example, the set of the primary colors would be written as

$$
S =\{ \text{yellow}, \: \text{red}, \: \text{blue} \}.
$$

The elements of this set are $\text{yellow},$ $\text{red},$ and $\text{blue}.$

A set that does not contain any elements is known as the **null set** or **empty set** and is written as either

$$
\emptyset \quad  \text{or} \quad \{\}.
$$

Note the following:

- *A set may contain other sets as elements.* For instance, the set

$$
T = \{1, \: 2, \: 3, \: 4, \: \{5, 6\}\}
$$

contains the set $\{5, 6\}$ as an element. However, it does *not* contain the elements $5$ and $6$.

- *Order doesn't matter.* The order in which the elements are listed is irrelevant. For instance, the following sets represent the same thing:

$$
A = \{1, \: 2, \: 3 \} = \{2, \: 3, \: 1\}
$$

It's usually easier to understand a set if the elements are listed in some order.

- *Duplicates don't matter.* Having multiple copies of an element does not affect the structure of a set. For example, the following sets represent the same thing:

$$
B = \{m, \: n, \: p, \: q\} = \{m, \: m, \: m, \: n, \: n, \: p, \: p, \: p, \: q\}
$$

When writing a set, we should try to organize it so that each element is listed once only." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186056037 :tutorial/content "By convention, sets are denoted by uppercase letters, while lowercase letters refer to elements of the set.  

There is a special notation, $\in,$ for expressing elements of sets. For example, if $a$ is an element of a set $A,$ we write

$$
a \in A.
$$

For example, for the set $S,$ given by

$$
S = \{ \text{yellow}, \text{red}, \text{blue} \},
$$

we can write 

$$
\text{yellow}\in S.
$$

Similarly, if $a$ is *not* an element of $A,$ then we write

$$
a \notin A.
$$

For example, 

$$
\text{green} \notin S.
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186056038 :tutorial/content "When a set contains only a few elements, we can write them all explicitly. 

For example, the set $A$ containing all positive even integers less than $20$ could be written as follows:

$$
A = \{2, \: 4, \: 6, \: 8, \: 10, \: 12, \: 14, \: 16, \: 18\}
$$

However, when a set contains many elements, we can save ourselves the pain of writing out all its elements using an ellipsis, "$\ldots$". 

For example:

- The set $B$ containing all positive even integers less than $200$ can be written as

$$
B = \{2, \: 4, \: 6, \: \ldots, \: 198\}.
$$

:question/problem "A meteorologist measured two particular features, ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2},$ at various locations throughout California. The collected data was stored in a standardized observation matrix, where each row contains both features for a particular location. 
The first and second principal components of the data are approximately

$$
{v}_{1}≈[\begin{aligned}0.667 \\ 0.745\end{aligned}],\,{v}_{2}≈[\begin{aligned}-0.745 \\ 0.667\end{aligned}].
$$

By combining the two measured features linearly, the meteorologist wants to construct a single feature that preserves the maximum amount of variance of the collected data. Which of the following could be the best candidate for the new feature?" :question/worked-solution "Recall the direction in which the data varies the most (the direction where we have the maximum variance) corresponds to the *first principal component* of the data.

![](images/f7/f7c823606bbbe77326819df5d487b5e0019dd7439b46124547f71681b9484f6d.png)

 

Let  

$$
V=[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ {v}_{1} & {v}_{2} \\ | & |\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0.667 & -0.745 \\ 0.745 & 0.667\end{aligned}]
$$

be the matrix of principal components. 

Then, applying the change of variables $Y=XV,$ we can convert our observation matrix $X$ into a new matrix $Y$ of (linearly) transformed observations such that

- the covariance matrix of $Y$ is diagonal (meaning that the new features ${y}_{1}$ and ${y}_{2}$ are uncorrelated), and

- the features ${y}_{1}$ and ${y}_{2}$ are arranged in order of decreasing variance (meaning that most of the variance is concentrated in ${y}_{1}$).

Applying our change of variables to a single observation $x=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}{y}_{1} & {y}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]V \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & {x}_{2}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0.667 & -0.745 \\ 0.745 & 0.667\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0.667{x}_{1}+0.745{x}_{2} & -0.745{x}_{1}+0.667{x}_{2}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

As a result, we have that ${y}_{1}=0.667{x}_{1}+0.745{x}_{2}$ will contain most of the variance of the data. 

Therefore, the best candidate for the new single feature is

$$
{y}_{1}=0.667{x}_{1}+0.745{x}_{2}.
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-8c4e8c66-d4aa-5c56-a392-1d26ce6b88cb"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "7eb658cd-5383-5f28-8b76-9d708b2f6422" :question/math-academy-id "q-344079" :question/problem "A physicist measured two particular features, ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2},$ for each oscillation produced when a mass hanging on a spring is displaced and then released. The collected data was stored in a standardized observation matrix, where each row contains both features for a particular oscillation. 
The first and second principal components of the data are approximately

$$
{v}_{1}≈[\begin{aligned}0.456 \\ 0.890\end{aligned}],\,{v}_{2}≈[\begin{aligned}0.890 \\ -0.456\end{aligned}].
$$

By combining the two measured features linearly, the physicist wants to construct a single feature that preserves the maximum amount of variance of the collected data. Which of the following could be the best candidate for the new feature?" :question/worked-solution "Recall the direction in which the data varies the most (the direction where we have the maximum variance) corresponds to the *first principal component* of the data.

![](images/f0/f0f0623703d1a3767a7c3efd275e977c6933465faeb761991f00da705bac4a2c.png)

 

Let  

$$
V=[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ {v}_{1} & {v}_{2} \\ | & |\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0.456 & 0.890 \\ 0.890 & -0.456\end{aligned}]
$$

be the matrix of principal components. 

Then, applying the change of variables $Y=XV,$ we can convert our observation matrix $X$ into a new matrix $Y$ of (linearly) transformed observations such that

- the covariance matrix of $Y$ is diagonal (meaning that the new features ${y}_{1}$ and ${y}_{2}$ are uncorrelated), and

- the features ${y}_{1}$ and ${y}_{2}$ are arranged in order of decreasing variance (meaning that most of the variance is concentrated in ${y}_{1}$).

Applying our change of variables to a single observation $x=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}{y}_{1} & {y}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]V \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & {x}_{2}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0.456 & 0.890 \\ 0.890 & -0.456\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0.456{x}_{1}+0.890{x}_{2} & 0.890{x}_{1}-0.456{x}_{2}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

As a result, we have that ${y}_{1}=0.456{x}_{1}+0.890{x}_{2}$ will contain most of the variance of the data. 

Therefore, the best candidate for the new single feature is

$$
{y}_{1}=0.456{x}_{1}+0.890{x}_{2}.
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-e68ffcc9-1fd2-5b21-96cd-20a43203877f"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id Our goal is to understand the relationship between these features and property values.

Problems involving multi-dimensional data analysis, such as this one, pose several challenges:

- Multi-dimensional data is often difficult to analyze.

- Visualization can be virtually impossible.

- Storing multi-dimensional data on a computer can require substantial hardware resources.

We can overcome these challenges using **dimensionality reduction.** Dimensionality reduction works by compressing data into a smaller number of variables while (ideally) preserving as much information as possible.

To demonstrate the basic idea behind dimensionality reduction, consider the following data set for the variables $x$ and $y{:}$

![](images/8a/8a8d724370467974845492c885ee680473c48f983a28680613740305c353e701.png)

Notice that the data does not vary much in the $y$-direction. Therefore, we can transform the data set by projecting all points onto the $x$-axis. This process removes the variation in $y$ with almost no loss of overall information, as shown below:

![](images/3f/3f9acbf44838ebe6099b250bb60d88dcae970158d7db86230f597ecbf62c5d43.png)

Multi-dimensional data typically exhibit characteristics suitable for dimensionality reduction:

- Many variables are often correlated. In our house prices example, the number of bedrooms and bathrooms likely correlate. This means that one variable can often be expressed in terms of another. Or, we can find a new variable that describes the variation in both original variables.

- Ultimately, we can aim to reduce the higher-dimensional structure of the data to a more fundamental, lower-dimensional structure containing only uncorrelated variables.

By reducing the dimensionality of the data, we can work with a compact representation that retains only the most critical variables and discards the rest. This simplifies analysis and visualization." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186185304 :tutorial/content "In the previous section, we saw that dimensionality reduction compresses data into fewer, uncorrelated variables. **Principal Component Analysis (PCA)** is a widely used technique for achieving this.

Suppose we have a sample of $n$ observations, each with $m$ features. We organize this data into an $n \times m$ **observation matrix** $X,$ where each row is an observation and each column is a feature.

For example, if we had $n=3$ observations of $m=2$ features, our observation matrix might look like this:
![](images/ac/ac2f4b137b2c63734a7ce5f03f42c099b12aa62bb74a4345a948d512bc378c0e.svg)
Before applying PCA, we must standardize the data. This is because PCA is sensitive to the scale of features. For instance, measuring a feature in meters versus centimeters would lead to different results. We standardize by giving each column a mean of $0$ and a standard deviation of $1.$

For our example, the first column has mean $2$ and standard deviation $1,$ while the second column has mean $20$ and standard deviation $10.$ Our standardized observation matrix $X$ is:
![](images/dc/dcb9c2bda09dbc8417c65d4345467a5eb2b580c61b77679c5273909d59cc6727.svg)
Next, we'll use this standardized data to analyze the relationships between the features." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186185309 :tutorial/content "Now that our data matrix $X$ is standardized, we examine the relationships between its features using the **sample covariance matrix**, $C.$ For standardized data, this is calculated as:

$$
C=\dfrac{1}{n-1} X^T X
$$

Using our standardized matrix from the previous slide, where $n=3$:

$$
\begin{aligned}C & =\frac{1}{3-1}[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-1 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}2 & 2 \\ 2 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The diagonal entries of $C$ are the variances of the features, and the off-diagonal entries are the covariances between pairs of features." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186185308 :tutorial/content "Let's look again at the covariance matrix we just calculated:
![](images/e5/e5359936cd43c32f4c937effa775f6d65527dbd1e14882b25ecef7b31afd7515.svg)
Notice that the matrix $C$ is symmetric. In fact, the sample covariance matrix is *always* a real symmetric matrix.

Recall from linear algebra that any real symmetric matrix is **orthogonally diagonalizable**. This means we can find an orthogonal matrix $V$ and a diagonal matrix $D$ such that

$$
V^T C V = D
$$

The entries of the diagonal matrix $D$ are the eigenvalues of $C,$ and the columns of the matrix $V$ are the corresponding orthonormal eigenvectors.

Next, we shall see how to use the matrix $V$ to find uncorrelated features for our data." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186185307 :tutorial/content "Recall that our goal is to find new features that are uncorrelated — equivalently, features whose covariance matrix is diagonal. In the previous section, we found an orthogonal matrix $V$ such that $V^T\!CV$ is diagonal. This motivates defining a **transformed observation matrix** $Y = XV.$ The columns of this new matrix $Y$ are our new features.

Substituting $C = \dfrac{1}{n-1} X^T X$ into the expression $V^T\!CV$ and noting that $(XV)^T = V^T X^T{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{{{V}^{T}\,CV}_{⏟}}_{\text{diagonal}} & ={V}^{T}(\frac{1}{n-1}{X}^{T}X)V \\  & =\frac{1}{n-1}(XV)^{T}(XV) \\  & ={{\frac{1}{n-1}{Y}^{T}Y}_{⏟}}_{\text{covariance of [math]Y[/math]}}\end{aligned}
$$

The covariance matrix of $Y$ is diagonal, so the new features $y_1, y_2, \ldots, y_m$ are uncorrelated. The diagonal entries are the eigenvalues of $C,$ so $\text{Var}(y_i) = \lambda_i.$ By arranging the columns of $V$ in order of decreasing eigenvalue, the new features are also arranged in order of decreasing variance.

The columns of $V$ (the unit eigenvectors of $C$) are called the **principal components**. The $1$st *principal component* is the eigenvector corresponding to the largest eigenvalue, the $2$nd corresponds to the second-largest, and so on.

This procedure is the core of **Principal Component Analysis (PCA)**. To summarize:

*We define the change-of-variables $Y = XV,$ where the columns of $V$ are the **principal components** of the data, arranged in order of decreasing eigenvalue. This ensures that:*

- *The new features $y_1,y_2,\ldots,y_m$ are uncorrelated (diagonal covariance).*

- *The new features are arranged in order of decreasing variance ($\text{Var}(y_i) = \lambda_i$).*

Now let's understand what these vectors mean in terms of the original data." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186185305 :tutorial/content "The statistical interpretation of the principal components is as follows: 

- The $1$st principal component defines a direction along which the original data has the maximum variance.

- The $2$nd principal component is perpendicular to the $1$st component and defines a direction along which the remaining data has the maximum variance.

- The $3$rd principal component is perpendicular to both the $1$st and the $2$nd components and defines a direction along which the remaining data has the maximum variance.

$\vdots$ 

and so on.

To illustrate, let's consider the following scatter plot of a sample of two-dimensional (paired) observations.  

![](images/b9/b9db4d78847162a66cb3541387c9fed32ce7f717e069d9a6d6a7135bd87eda3f.png)

 

In our diagram, the direction along which the data varies the most corresponds (approximately) to the line shown below.

![](images/1c/1cab88d6f754736ec8a2f8c61861d9e5d24193b376dc6deed2591e44a75a8b72.png)

 

Therefore, the vectors corresponding to the first and second principal components of the data could be the unit vectors shown below. 

![](images/b4/b495503b421f2f1190595167bc031821d31b80b6bb95e0595bd8a7df41a60a1d.png)" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186185306 :tutorial/content "Suppose a physician measured two features, $x_1$ and $x_2,$ corresponding to height and weight for each athlete among a group who attended a particular competition. The collected data were stored in a standardized observation matrix, with each row containing both features for each athlete.

A scatter plot of the physician's results is shown below. 

![](images/df/df1dab6868232dd53da67b881c7de11cfd47cd84abe35ba94540e5ce038e9d1e.png)

 

Remember that the first and second principal components, denoted $\mathbf v_1$ and $\mathbf v_2,$ are the unit eigenvectors of the sample covariance matrix for the data set. The physician calculates that the first and second principal components of this data are approximately

The physician wants to combine the two features linearly into a single feature that preserves the maximum variance. What is the best candidate for the new feature?

The matrix of principal components, denoted $V,$ is given by

![](images/10/108e96292ad3af7d2d4a171925fd3554ed424e5f41b47eaeced4617affbdb695.svg)

Applying the change of variables $Y = XV,\,$ we can convert our observation matrix $X$ into a new matrix $Y$ of (linearly) transformed observations such that

- the covariance matrix of $Y$ is diagonal (meaning that the new features $y_1$ and $y_2$ are uncorrelated), and

- the features $y_1$ and $y_2$ are arranged in order of decreasing variance (meaning that most of the variance is concentrated in $y_1$).

Applying the change of variables to a single observation ![](images/17/170f8ecc20d8fab03e5a15749aefe7efa71b08671f99276a1261961040333185.svg) we have

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}{y}_{1} & {y}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]V \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & {x}_{2}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0.316 & -0.947 \\ 0.947 & 0.316\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0.316{x}_{1}+0.947{x}_{2} & -0.947{x}_{1}+0.316{x}_{2}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

As a result, $y_1 = 0.316 x_1 + 0.947 x_2$ will contain most of the variance of the data. Therefore, the best candidate for the new single feature is

$$

$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186184372 :activity/expected-seconds 480.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]} {:db/id 17592186198442 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-fd31a01e-94fe-56c0-b345-2a845f22f0d5"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id "question-fd31a01e-94fe-56c0-b345-2a845f22f0d5" :question/id #uuid "fd31a01e-94fe-56c0-b345-2a845f22f0d5" :question/math-academy-id "q-138131" :question/problem "The maximum  value of the quadratic form $Q(x)={x}_{1}^{2}+{x}_{2}^{2}+{x}_{3}^{2}-6{x}_{1}{x}_{2},$ when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to $4.$ Which of the following is a vector $x$ at which the maximum  is attained?" :question/worked-solution "Let $A$ be the matrix corresponding to our quadratic form. Recall that: 

- The maximum value of $Q(x),$ when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to the largest eigenvalue of $A:$

$$
max\{Q(x)\,|\,‖x‖=1\}={\lambda }_{\text{max}}
$$

 
The maximum is attained on the corresponding unit eigenvector ${u}_{\text{max}}.$

- The minimum value of $Q(x),$ when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to the smallest eigenvalue of $A:$

$$
min\{Q(x)\,|\,‖x‖=1\}={\lambda }_{\text{min}}
$$

 
The minimum is attained on the corresponding unit eigenvector ${u}_{\text{min}}.$

First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 & 0 \\ -3 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

Now, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{\text{min}}=4:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}A-4I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 & 0 \\ -3 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]-4[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-3 & -3 & 0 \\ -3 & -3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -3\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-4I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector $v=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$ 

Finally, dividing $v$ by its norm $‖v‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get 

$$
{u}_{\text{max}}=\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-fd3f9993-5662-5d10-ad04-17586e5bdd3b"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id Which of the following statements are true concerning the function $y=f(x)$ whose graph is shown above?

I. ${lim}_{x\to \,0}f(x)=3$

III. ${lim}_{x\to \,-2}f(x)={lim}_{x\to \,1}f(x)$" :question/worked-solution "Let's analyze each statement in turn.

- Statement I is false. As $x$ approaches $0,$ the function $f(x)$ approaches the value $y=2.$ Consequently, 

$$
{lim}_{x\to \,1}f(x)=2.
$$

- Statement II is true. As $x$ approaches $-1,$ the function $f(x)$ approaches the value $y=1.$ Consequently, 

$$
{lim}_{x\to \,-1}f(x)=1.
$$

- Statement III is false. As $x$ approaches $-2,$ the function $f(x)$ approaches the value $y=0,$ and consequently 

$$
{lim}_{x\to \,-2}f(x)=0.
$$

 
Similarly, as $x$ approaches $1,$ the function $f(x)$ approaches the value $y=1,$ and consequently,

$$
{lim}_{x\to \,1}f(x)=1.
$$

As a result,

$$
{lim}_{x\to \,-2}f(x)\ne {lim}_{x\to \,1}f(x).

:question/problem "![](images/67/6769c6590446a9599786758ba9cfaf17690f401d864b3ce5f2c3825d9ca432cd.png)

Which of the following statements are true concerning the function $y=f(x)$ whose graph is shown above?

I. ${lim}_{x\to \,-1}f(x)=1$

II. ${lim}_{x\to \,0}f(x)=0$

III. ${lim}_{x\to \,1}f(x)={lim}_{x\to \,2}f(x)$" :question/worked-solution "Let's analyze each statement in turn.

- Statement I is true. As $x$ approaches $-1,$ the function $f(x)$ approaches the value $y=1.$ Consequently, 

$$
{lim}_{x\to \,-1}f(x)=1.
$$

- Statement II is true. As $x$ approaches $0,$ the function $f(x)$ approaches the value $y=0.$ Consequently, 

$$
{lim}_{x\to \,0}f(x)=0.
$$

- Statement III is false. As $x$ approaches $1,$ the function $f(x)$ approaches the value $y=1,$ and consequently 

$$
{lim}_{x\to \,1}f(x)=1.
$$

 
Similarly, as $x$ approaches $2,$ the function $f(x)$ approaches the value $y=0,$ and consequently, 

$$
{lim}_{x\to \,2}f(x)=0.
$$

 As a result,

$$
{lim}_{x\to \,1}f(x)\ne {lim}_{x\to \,2}f(x).
$$

In conclusion, only statements I and II are true." :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-cf4a92b8-1b37-555c-b412-fdb7e36b861f"] :db/ensure Due to the symmetry of the student's $t$-distribution, we have that $P(|X|\ge x)=0.01$ is equivalent to

$$
2P(X\ge x)=0.01\,⟹\,P(X\ge x)=0.005.
$$

Now, since $X∼{T}_{25},$ we focus on the row of the table that corresponds to $k=25.$

| $k∖p$ | $0.100$ | $0.050$ | $0.025$ | $0.010$ | $0.005$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $24$ | $1.318$ | $1.711$ | $2.064$ | $2.492$ | $2.797$ |
| $25$ | $1.316$ | $1.708$ | $2.060$ | $2.485$ | $2.787$ |
| $26$ | $1.315$ | $1.706$ | $2.056$ | $2.479$ | $2.779$ |

From this row, we see that

$$
P(X\ge 2.787)=0.005.
$$

Therefore, our answer is $x=2.787.$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-8b63d849-ac8e-58fe-8d8d-780397c8a283"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} $$
\csch x = \dfrac{1}{\sinh x} = \dfrac {2}{e^{x} - e^{-x}}.

The definition of $\coth x$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{coth}⁡x & =\frac{1}{\operatorname{tanh}⁡x} \\  & =\frac{{e}^{x}+{e}^{-x}}{{e}^{x}-{e}^{-x}} \\  & =\frac{{e}^{2x}+1}{{e}^{2x}-1} \\  & =\frac{1+{e}^{-2x}}{1-{e}^{-2x}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the fourth definition, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{coth}⁡(-\operatorname{ln}⁡3) & =\frac{1+{e}^{-2(-\operatorname{ln}⁡3)}}{1-{e}^{-2(-\operatorname{ln}⁡3)}} \\  & =\frac{1+{e}^{2\operatorname{ln}⁡3}}{1-{e}^{2\operatorname{ln}⁡3}} \\  & =\frac{1+{e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡{3}^{2}}}{1-{e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡{3}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{1+{3}^{2}}{1-{3}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1+9}{1-9} \\  & =\frac{10}{(-8)} \\  & =-\frac{5}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "question-196ecf31-b7aa-5c38-b760-a54c4f34d305" :question/id #uuid "196ecf31-b7aa-5c38-b760-a54c4f34d305" :question/math-academy-id "q-96531" :question/problem "$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{csch}⁡(-2\operatorname{ln}⁡2) & =\frac{2}{{e}^{-2\operatorname{ln}⁡2}-{e}^{-(-2\operatorname{ln}⁡2)}} \\  & =\frac{2}{{e}^{-2\operatorname{ln}⁡2}-{e}^{2\operatorname{ln}⁡2}} \\  & =\frac{2}{{e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡{2}^{-2}}-{e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡{2}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{2}{{2}^{-2}-{2}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{2}{(\frac{1}{4}-4)} \\  & =\frac{2}{(-\frac{15}{4})} \\  & =-\frac{8}{15}.\end{aligned}

| $\,1.3\,$ | $\,0.9115\,$ | $\,0.9131\,$ | $\,0.9147\,$ | $\,0.9162\,$ | $\,0.9177\,$ |" :question/worked-solution "Recall that if ${X}_{1}$ and ${X}_{2}$ are independent random variables, where ${X}_{1}∼N({\mu }_{1},{\sigma }_{1}^{2})$ and ${X}_{2}∼N({\mu }_{2},{\sigma }_{2}^{2}),$ and $a$ and $b$ are constants, then 

$$
a{X}_{1}+b{X}_{2}∼N(a{\mu }_{1}+b{\mu }_{2},{a}^{2}{\sigma }_{1}^{2}+{b}^{2}{\sigma }_{2}^{2}).

Since ${X}_{1}$ and ${X}_{2}$ are independent, the distribution of $Y$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}Y=4{X}_{1}-2{X}_{2} & ∼N(4{\mu }_{1}-2{\mu }_{2},16{\sigma }_{1}^{2}+4{\sigma }_{2}^{2}) \\  & ∼N(20-16,48+16) \\  & ∼N(4,64).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $Y$ is normally distributed with mean $\mu =4$ and standard deviation $\sigma =\sqrt{64}=8.$ 

We want to find $P(Y<14).$ Thus, we convert $Y$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(Y<14) & =P(Z<\frac{14-4}{8}) \\  & =P(Z<1.25) \\  & =Φ(1.25)\end{aligned}
$$

Using the $z$-table, we see that

$$
Φ(1.25)≈0.8944.

$$

"question-9dd9198d-6665-5e5e-bf17-48bb8a7b15be" :question/id #uuid "9dd9198d-6665-5e5e-bf17-48bb8a7b15be" :question/math-academy-id "q-109748" :question/problem "The weights of some chocolate cookies are normally distributed with a mean of $10\,\text{g}$ and a variance of $1\,{\text{g}}^{2}.$ The weights of some oatcakes are normally distributed with a mean of $15\,\text{g}$ and a variance of $2\,{\text{g}}^{2}.$  If one chocolate cookie and one oatcake are randomly selected, what is the probability that $6$ times the weight of the cookie plus $4$ times the weight of oatcake is less than $120\,\text{g}$, but more than $100\,\text{g}?$ You may assume that the weights of the cookies and oatcakes are independent. 

*Hint: A table of values of $Φ(z)$ for different values of $z$ is given below, where $Φ(z)$ is the cumulative distribution function for the standard normal distribution. *

| $z$ | $\,0.00\,$ | $\,0.01\,$ | $\,0.02\,$ | $\,0.03\,$ | $\,0.04\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\,-2.5\,$ | $\,0.0062\,$ | $\,0.0060\,$ | $\,0.0059\,$ | $\,0.0057\,$ | $\,0.0055\,$ |
| $\,-2.4\,$ | $\,0.0082\,$ | $\,0.0080\,$ | $\,0.0078\,$ | $\,0.0075\,$ | $\,0.0073\,$ |
| $\,-2.3\,$ | $\,0.0107\,$ | $\,0.0104\,$ | $\,0.0102\,$ | $\,0.0099\,$ | $\,0.0096\,$ |" :question/worked-solution "Let $X$ denote the weight of a chocolate cookie, and let $Y$ denote the weight of an oatcake. We want to find 

$$
P(100<6X+4Y<120).
$$

Since $X$ and $Y$ are  independent random variables such that $X∼N(10,1)$ and $Y∼N(15,2),$ then 

$$
\begin{aligned}6X+4Y & ∼N(6\cdot 10+4\cdot 15,36\cdot 1+16\cdot 2) \\  & ∼N(120,68).\end{aligned}
$$

So, the variable $6X+4Y$ is normally distributed with mean $\mu =120$ and standard deviation $\sigma =\sqrt{68}.$

To find $P(100<6X+4Y<120),$ we convert $6X+4Y$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(100<6X+4Y<120) & =P(\frac{100-120}{\sqrt{68}}<Z<\frac{120-120}{\sqrt{68}}) \\  & ≈P(-2.43<Z<0) \\  & =P(Z<0)-P(Z\le -2.43) \\  & =P(Z\le 0)-P(Z\le -2.43) \\  & =Φ(0)-Φ(-2.43)\end{aligned}
$$

Using the $z$-table, we see that

$$
\begin{aligned}Φ(-2.43) & ≈0.0075,\end{aligned}
$$

and we know that

$$
\begin{aligned}Φ(0) & =0.5.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(100<6X+4Y<120) & ≈Φ(0)-Φ(-2.43) \\  & =0.5-0.0075 \\  & ≈0.4925.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-5f73640d-d4b8-5379-a9d2-f83257d2b179"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-5f73640d-d4b8-5379-a9d2-f83257d2b179" :answer-field/id #uuid "5f73640d-d4b8-5379-a9d2-f83257d2b179" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-3c7b928a-dbf0-5c53-8e9c-221cc73604b6" :answer-field/choices ["answer-953e7d4e-e884-5c5e-bebe-5d6c15fc8f60" "answer-1b7ed843-f01b-5ff0-9400-1f575ae46bc7" "answer-3c7b928a-dbf0-5c53-8e9c-221cc73604b6" "answer-c072162b-92cd-5039-9d7e-cf458cf7fc3b" "answer-a7650dd9-8eb4-5963-be58-a9d76c3de7ba"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-953e7d4e-e884-5c5e-bebe-5d6c15fc8f60" :answer/id #uuid "953e7d4e-e884-5c5e-bebe-5d6c15fc8f60" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "0.4639" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-1b7ed843-f01b-5ff0-9400-1f575ae46bc7" :answer/id #uuid "1b7ed843-f01b-5ff0-9400-1f575ae46bc7" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "0.4817" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-3c7b928a-dbf0-5c53-8e9c-221cc73604b6" :answer/id #uuid "3c7b928a-dbf0-5c53-8e9c-221cc73604b6" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "0.4925" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-c072162b-92cd-5039-9d7e-cf458cf7fc3b" :answer/id #uuid "c072162b-92cd-5039-9d7e-cf458cf7fc3b" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "0.5003" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-a7650dd9-8eb4-5963-be58-a9d76c3de7ba" :answer/id #uuid "a7650dd9-8eb4-5963-be58-a9d76c3de7ba" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "0.5153" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-666db65e-d2dd-5df6-aa61-3e935a25f26e" :question/id #uuid "666db65e-d2dd-5df6-aa61-3e935a25f26e" :question/math-academy-id "q-109755" :question/problem "A factory produces shovels, each consisting of a handle and a blade.
The length of a handle is normally distributed with a mean of $120$ centimeters and a variance of $0.14,$  while the length of a blade is normally distributed with a mean of $30$ centimeters and a variance of $0.02.$ If one shovel is randomly selected, what is the probability that its length is more than $150$ centimeters, but less than $150.5$ centimeters? You may assume that the lengths are independent.

*Hint: A table of values of $Φ(z)$ for different values of $z$ is given below, where $Φ(z)$ is the cumulative distribution function for the standard normal distribution. *

| $z$ | $\,0.05\,$ | $\,0.06\,$ | $\,0.07\,$ | $\,0.08\,$ | $\,0.09\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\,1.2\,$ | $\,0.8944\,$ | $\,0.8962\,$ | $\,0.8980\,$ | $\,0.8997\,$ | $\,0.9015\,$ |
| $\,1.3\,$ | $\,0.9115\,$ | $\,0.9131\,$ | $\,0.9147\,$ | $\,0.9162\,$ | $\,0.9177\,$ |
| $\,1.4\,$ | $\,0.9265\,$ | $\,0.9279\,$ | $\,0.9292\,$ | $\,0.9306\,$ | $\,0.9319\,$ |" :question/worked-solution "Let $X$ denote the length of a handle, and let $Y$ denote the length of a blade. We want to find 

$$
P(150<X+Y<150.5).
$$

Since $X$ and $Y$ are independent random variables such that $X∼N(120,0.14)$ and $Y∼N(30,0.02)$, then 

$$
\begin{aligned}X+Y & ∼N(120+30,0.14+0.02) \\  & ∼N(150,0.16).\end{aligned}
$$

So, the variable $X+Y$ is normally distributed with mean $\mu =150$ and standard deviation $\sigma =\sqrt{0.16}=0.4.$

In order to find $P(150<X+Y<150.5),$ we convert $X+Y$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(150<X+Y<150.5) & =P(\frac{150-150}{0.4}<Z<\frac{150.5-150}{0.4}) \\  & ≈P(0<Z<1.25) \\  & =P(Z\le 1.25)-P(Z\le 0) \\  & =Φ(1.25)-Φ(0)\end{aligned}
$$

Using the $z$-table, we see that

$$
\begin{aligned}Φ(1.25) & ≈0.8944,\end{aligned}
$$

and we know that

$$
\begin{aligned}Φ(0) & =0.5.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(150<X+Y<150.5) & ≈Φ(1.25)-Φ(0) \\  & ≈0.8944-0.5 \\  & ≈0.3944.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we conclude that the probability that the length of a randomly selected shovel is more than $150$ centimeters, but less than $150.5$ centimeters is $0.3944.$" :question/difficulty The number of prey {{field-3}} and the number of predators {{field-4}}." :question/worked-solution "The Lotka-Volterra predator-prey model is given by

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}=ax-bxy \\ {y}^{′}=-cy+dxy\end{aligned}
$$

where $a,b,c,d$ are positive real constants. Here, $x=x(t)$ represents the prey and $y=y(t)$ represents the predators.

With that in mind, let's examine the statements:

- The trajectory $\text{circles around}$ $\text{the nonzero equilibrium}.$

- From $A$ to $B,$ the number of prey $\text{decreases}$ and the number of predators $\text{increases}.$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186370186 :question/problem "$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}=-2x+3xy \\ {y}^{′}=7y-5xy\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the Lotka-Volterra model above, where $x=x(t)$ represents the predators and $y=y(t)$ represents the prey. Find the nonzero equilibrium of the model.

$(${{field-1}}
$,$
{{field-2}}$)$" :question/worked-solution "The equilibrium (fixed) points of a system ${x}^{′}(t)=f(x,y)$ are the points for which $f(x,y)=0.$ So, we get the following system of linear equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}-2x+3xy=0 \\ 7y-5xy=0\end{aligned}
$$

Solving the first equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}-2x+3xy & =0 \\ x(-2+3y) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, $x=0$ or $y=\frac{2}{3}.$ We consider both cases separately.

- If $x=0,$ substituting it into the second equation, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}7y-5(0)y=0\,⇒\,y=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, one equilibrium is $(0,0).$

- If $y=\frac{2}{3},$ substituting it into the second equation, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}7y-5xy & =0 \\ y(7-5x) & =0 \\ \frac{2}{3}(7-5x) & =0 \\ 7-5x & =0 \\ x & =\frac{7}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, another equilibrium is $(\frac{7}{5},\frac{2}{3}).$

Therefore, the nonzero equilibrium of the model is
$(\frac{7}{5},\frac{2}{3}).$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186166924 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-9ec6a2eb-63e4-55a4-849b-ba0f89289e7d"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id "question-9ec6a2eb-63e4-55a4-849b-ba0f89289e7d" :question/id #uuid "9ec6a2eb-63e4-55a4-849b-ba0f89289e7d" :question/math-academy-id "q-335018" :question/problem "$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}=-0.5x+0.5xy \\ {y}^{′}=y-5xy\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the Lotka-Volterra model above, where $x=x(t)$ represents the predators and $y=y(t)$ represents the prey. Select the correct options in the reasoning below.

$\,$ Evaluating the Jacobian of the system at the equilibrium ${x}^{∗}=[0.2,\,1]^{T},$ we get

<tbody><tr>
<td align="center" height="30px" rowspan="2">$J({x}^{∗})=\,\,$</td>
<td align="center" height="40px" width="5px"></td>
<td align="center" width="40px">{{field-1}}</td>
<td align="center" width="40px">{{field-2}}</td>
<td align="center" width="5px"></td>

</tr>
</tbody></table>

$\,$ The eigenvalues of the Jacobian matrix are 
{{field-5}}.

$\,$ Therefore, the equilibrium at ${x}^{∗}$ is
{{field-6}}{{field-7}}." :question/worked-solution "Let's denote ${f}_{1}(x,y)=-0.5x+0.5xy$ and ${f}_{2}(x,y)=y-5xy.$

Now, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(-0.5x+0.5xy)=-0.5+0.5y,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(-0.5x+0.5xy)=0.5x \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(y-5xy)=-5y,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(y-5xy)=1-5x\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the Jacobian matrix is

$$
J=[\begin{aligned}-0.5+0.5y & 0.5x \\ -5y & 1-5x\end{aligned}].
$$

Next, we evaluate the Jacobian at the equilibrium ${x}^{∗}=[\begin{aligned}0.2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$ to get

$$
J({x}^{∗})=[\begin{aligned}-0.5+0.5(1) & 0.5(0.2) \\ -5(1) & 1-5(0.2)\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 & 0.1 \\ -5 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

To find the eigenvalues of the Jacobian matrix, we write down the characteristic equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}-\lambda  & 0.1 \\ -5 & -\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (-\lambda )(-\lambda )-(-5)\cdot 0.1 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}+0.5 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Solving the equation, we get the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1,2}=\pm 0.5\sqrt{2}\,\text{i}.$ Since the eigenvalues are purely imaginary, our equilibrium is $\text{a stable}$ $\text{center}.$

**Note:**
For the Lotka-Volterra model (as in this problem), it is safe to classify the nonzero equilibrium as a center when the linearization has purely imaginary eigenvalues. 

**Watch out!** 
In contrast, for a general nonlinear system, the Jacobian test alone is inconclusive (additional analysis is required to determine whether the equilibrium is a true center or a spiral sink/source)." $a = b^x$ is equivalent to $\log_{b}{a} = x$

If we compare $2^4 = 16$ with $a = b^x,$ we get $a = 16,$ $b = 2,$ and $x = 4.$

$a = b^x$ is equivalent to $\log_{b}{a} = x$

If we compare $7^0 = 1$ with $a = b^x,$ we get $a = 1, b = 7,$ and $x=0.$

Therefore, the equation $7^0 = 1$ is equivalent to $\log_{7}{1}= 0.$

In general, $\log_n(1) = 0$ for any $n>0, n\neq 1.$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186064187 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-bb68a7c2-cb48-5196-952e-fea6e54d1914" "question-277ed942-8515-5af5-8070-395ac017b6ed"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186064062 :question/worked-solution "The logarithm of $a$ with base $b$ is defined as follows:

:answer.type/math :answer/value "{log}_{2}⁡(\frac{1}{2})≈1.414" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186065354 :tutorial/content "A **logarithm** (or log) is an operation that's the *inverse* of exponentiation. 

For example, we know that ${\color{blue}{2}}^{\color{red}{3}} = 8.$ But we can also write this using a logarithm as

$$
\log_{\color{blue}{2}}(8) = {\color{red}{3}}.
$$

In words, we would say "log of $8$ with base ${\color{blue}{2}}$ equals ${\color{red}{3}}$". The **base** of the logarithm is always the base of the exponential expression.

Since exponents and logarithms are opposite operations, an exponential equation can always be expressed in logarithmic form, and vice versa.

In general, the logarithm of $a$ with positive base $b \neq 1$ is defined as follows:

$a = {\color{blue}b}^{\color{red}x}$ is equivalent to $\log_{\color{blue}b}{a} = {\color{red}x}.$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186065351 :tutorial/content "What logarithmic equation is equivalent to the equation $\sqrt{4} = 2 ?$

Notice that the given equation can be written using exponents as

$$
4^{1/2} = 2.
$$

The logarithm of $a$ with base $b$ is defined as follows:

$a = b^x$ is equivalent to $\log_{b}{a} = x$

If we compare $4^{1/2} = 2$ with $a = b^x,$ we get $a = 2, b = 4,$ and $x=\dfrac{1}{2}.$

Therefore, the equation $\sqrt{4} = 2$ is equivalent to $\log_{4}{2}= \dfrac{1}{2}.$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186064463 :activity/expected-seconds 420.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]} {:db/id 17592186133885 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-9d632f6e-3556-5d97-834c-4e1de9c56681"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id "question-9d632f6e-3556-5d97-834c-4e1de9c56681" :question/id #uuid "9d632f6e-3556-5d97-834c-4e1de9c56681" :question/math-academy-id "q-109858" :question/problem "Which of the following subspaces must be orthogonal to $\text{Col}({A}^{T}+{B}^{T})$ for all compatible matrices $A$ and $B?$

I. $\text{Null}(A+B)$

II. $\text{Col}(A+B)$

III. $\text{Null}({A}^{T}+{B}^{T})$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that $\text{Col}({A}^{T}+{B}^{T})$ is the row space of $({A}^{T}+{B}^{T})^{T}=A+B.$ This consists of all linear combinations of the rows of $A+B.$

If a vector is orthogonal to every linear combination of the rows of $A+B,$ it must be orthogonal to each row of $A+B.$
But notice that when pre-multiplying a vector by $A+B,$ we actually multiply each row of $A+B$ by that vector.
So, $\text{Col}({A}^{T}+{B}^{T})$ must be orthogonal to the null space of $A+B,$ which is $\text{Null}(A+B).$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only."

:question/worked-solution "Substituting $3$ for $x$ in the polynomial and evaluating, we get the following result:

$$
\eqalign{
		2(3)^3+8(3)^2-2(3)-8 &= \
		2(27)+8(9)-6-8 &= \
		54+72-14 &= \
		112
	}
$$

The polynomial does *not* equal $0$ when $3$ is substituted for $x.$

Therefore, $3$ is *not* a root." :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186068750 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-6dc4cf16-d154-5217-ba51-01445eca1e9d"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186068583 :question/problem "Find $p$ if $3$ is a root of $x^3-3x+p.$" :question/worked-solution "Since $x=3$ is a root, we have $f(3)=0.$ Therefore, we can evaluate the polynomial at $x=3,$ set it equal to $0,$ and solve the equation for the parameter $p\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}(3)^{3}-3(3)+p & =0 \\ 27-9+p & =0 \\ p & =-18\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "question-01d0ba8c-f3fb-52e6-bc68-8e1659694309" :question/id #uuid "01d0ba8c-f3fb-52e6-bc68-8e1659694309" :question/math-academy-id "q-114096" :question/problem "Which of the following is **NOT** a root of the polynomial ${x}^{3}-{x}^{2}-21x+45?$

II. $x=4$

III. $x=5$" :question/worked-solution "- Substituting $3$ for $x$ in the polynomial and evaluating, we get the following result:

$$
\begin{aligned}{3}^{3}-{3}^{2}-21(3)+45 & = \\ 27-9-63+45 & = \\ 0\end{aligned}
$$

The polynomial is $0$ when $3$ is substituted for $x.$ Therefore, $3$ is a root.

- Substituting $4$ for $x$ in the polynomial and evaluating, we get the following result:

$$
\begin{aligned}{4}^{3}-{4}^{2}-21(4)+45 & = \\ 64-16-84+45 & = \\ 9\end{aligned}
$$

The polynomial does *not* equal $0$ when $4$ is substituted for $x.$ Therefore, $4$ is *not*  a root.

- Substituting $5$ for $x$ in the polynomial and evaluating, we get the following result:

$$
\begin{aligned}{5}^{3}-{5}^{2}-21(5)+45 & = \\ 125-25-105+45 & = \\ 40\end{aligned}
$$

The polynomial does *not* equal $0$ when $5$ is substituted for $x.$ Therefore, $5$ is *not*  a root.

Therefore, the values that are *not* roots are $x=4$ and $x=5,$ so the correct answer is "II and III only"." :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-973ef37b-f85d-515c-b5ff-cf8e3417a87e"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-973ef37b-f85d-515c-b5ff-cf8e3417a87e" :answer-field/id #uuid "973ef37b-f85d-515c-b5ff-cf8e3417a87e" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-e3d73040-b6a3-590a-8f1a-f21f92d2e834" :answer-field/choices ["answer-26aca2b6-27fd-5137-9f5a-b761d0340f16" "answer-bfaf3574-1d71-5d97-bc40-fa0a286b8c0d" "answer-e3d73040-b6a3-590a-8f1a-f21f92d2e834" "answer-fed866e1-3125-5187-99bc-41e67b687920" "answer-c90944c5-320d-596d-8f3d-d4daa4e170c5"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-26aca2b6-27fd-5137-9f5a-b761d0340f16" :answer/id #uuid "26aca2b6-27fd-5137-9f5a-b761d0340f16" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "I and III only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-bfaf3574-1d71-5d97-bc40-fa0a286b8c0d" :answer/id #uuid "bfaf3574-1d71-5d97-bc40-fa0a286b8c0d" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "I only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-e3d73040-b6a3-590a-8f1a-f21f92d2e834" :answer/id #uuid "e3d73040-b6a3-590a-8f1a-f21f92d2e834" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "II and III only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-fed866e1-3125-5187-99bc-41e67b687920" :answer/id #uuid "fed866e1-3125-5187-99bc-41e67b687920" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "II only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-c90944c5-320d-596d-8f3d-d4daa4e170c5" :answer/id #uuid "c90944c5-320d-596d-8f3d-d4daa4e170c5" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "III only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186069316 :question/problem "Which of the following is **NOT** a root of the polynomial ${x}^{4}-13{x}^{2}+36?$

III. $x=-4$" :question/worked-solution "- Substituting $4$ for $x$ in the polynomial and evaluating, we get the following result:

$$
\begin{aligned}{4}^{4}-13(4)^{2}+36 & = \\ 256-13(16)+36 & = \\ 256-208+36 & = \\ 84\end{aligned}

The polynomial does *not* equal $0$ when $4$ is substituted for $x.$ Therefore, $4$ is *not*  a root.

- Substituting $2$ for $x$ in the polynomial and evaluating, we get the following result:

$$
\begin{aligned}{2}^{4}-13(2)^{2}+36 & = \\ 16-13(4)+36 & = \\ 16-52+36 & = \\ 0\end{aligned}
$$

The polynomial is $0$ when $2$ is substituted for $x.$ Therefore, $2$ is a root.

- Substituting $-4$ for $x$ in the polynomial and evaluating, we get the following result:

$$
\begin{aligned}(-4)^{4}-13(-4)^{2}+36 & = \\ 256-13(16)+36 & = \\ 256-208+36 & = \\ 84\end{aligned}
$$

The polynomial does *not* equal $0$ when $-4$ is substituted for $x.$ Therefore, $-4$ is *not*  a root.

Therefore, the values that are *not* roots are $x=4$ and $x=-4,$ so the correct answer is "I and III only"." :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186067066 :answer-field/correct 17592186067070 :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id 17592186069305 :question/problem "Find $a$ if $-2$ is a root of ${x}^{4}+a{x}^{3}-11{x}^{2}+60x+100.$" :question/worked-solution "Since  $x=-2$ is a root, we have $f(-2)=0.$ Therefore, we can evaluate the polynomial at $x=-2,$ set it equal to $0,$ and solve the equation for the parameter $a:$

For example, consider the polynomial $x^2-9.$ This polynomial has two roots, $x=3$ and $x=-3,$ because the polynomial evaluates to $0$ when either of these values is substituted for $x\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}x=3\,⇒\,{x}^{2}-9 & = \\ (3)^{2}-9 & = \\ 9-9 & = \\ 0 & \,✓ \\ x=-3\,⇒\,{x}^{2}-9 & = \\ (-3)^{2}-9 & = \\ 9-9 & = \\ 0 & \,✓\end{aligned}
$$

On the other hand, a number like $x=1$ is *not* a root of the polynomial because the polynomial does not evaluate to $0$ when this value is substituted for $x\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}x=1\,⇒\,{x}^{2}-9 & = \\ (1)^{2}-9 & = \\ 1-9 & = \\ -8 & \,\times \end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186069969 :tutorial/content "A **parametric polynomial** is a polynomial in which one of the coefficients is itself represented as another variable.

For example, the polynomial below is a parametric polynomial:

$$
f(x)=2x^2 -px
$$

Here, $p$ is a **parameter**,  which means that it corresponds to a certain constant value. Unlike the variable $x,$ the parameter is treated exactly like any other coefficient. It's only special in that we don't know its numerical value.

If we're given the root of a polynomial, we can find the numerical value of a parameter. Let's say, for instance, that a root of the above polynomial is $x=1.$ This means that the polynomial is zero for that value:

$$
f(1)=0
$$

Therefore, we can evaluate the polynomial at $x=1,$ set it equal to $0,$ and solve the equation for the parameter $p\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(1) & =0 \\ 2(1)^{2}-p(1) & =0 \\ 2-p & =0 \\ p & =2\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186068994 :activity/expected-seconds 480.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]} [:db/retract 17592186164942 :answer-field/choices 17592186164944] [:db/retract 17592186164942 :answer-field/choices 17592186164945] [:db/retract 17592186164942 :answer-field/choices 17592186164946] [:db/retract 17592186164942 :answer-field/choices 17592186164947] [:db/retract 17592186164942 :answer-field/choices 17592186164943] {:db/id 17592186167287 :question/problem "$$
f(x)∼\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)
$$

Let $F(x)=-5x$ for $x\in [0,\pi ).$ The Fourier cosine series of the **even** $2\pi $-periodic extension $f(x)$ of $F(x)$ is shown above. Find the expression for ${a}_{n}.$

$\,{a}_{n}=$ {{field-1}}
for $n\ge 1$" :question/worked-solution "For our Fourier cosine series, the coefficients are given by

$$
{a}_{n}=\frac{2}{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{\pi }f(x)\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)\,\text{d}x.
$$

In our case, $f(x)=-5x$ for $x\in (0,\pi ).$ So, substituting into the formula, we get

$$
{a}_{n}=-\frac{10}{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{\pi }x\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)\,\text{d}x.
$$

We use the integration by parts: 

$$
\begin{aligned}u=x\, & ⇒\,{u}^{′}=1 \\ {v}^{′}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)\, & ⇒\,v=\frac{1}{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & =-\frac{10}{\pi }(uv\,{|}_{0}^{\pi }-{\int }_{0}^{\pi }v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x) \\  & =-\frac{10}{\pi }(\frac{1}{n}[x\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)]_{0}^{\pi }-\frac{1}{n}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)\,\text{d}x) \\  & =-\frac{10}{n\pi }((\pi \cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡(n\pi )-0\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡(0))+\frac{1}{n}[\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)]_{0}^{\pi }) \\  & =-\frac{10}{n\pi }(0+\frac{1}{n}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi )-\operatorname{cos}⁡(0))) \\  & =\frac{10(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi ))}{{n}^{2}\pi }.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since $\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi )=(-1)^{n},$ we have

$$
{a}_{n}=\frac{10(1-(-1)^{n})}{\pi {n}^{2}}.
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186164942 :answer-field/correct "answer-6d8b9a94-844b-5230-8dbb-b4c344711de3" :answer-field/choices standardized observation matrix $X$ are the unit eigenvectors of the covariance matrix $C.$ If 

$$
\lambda_1 \gt \lambda_2 \gt \cdots\gt \lambda_n
$$

are the eigenvalues of $C$ written in descending order, then: 

- the $1$st principal component is the unit eigenvector $\mathbf u_1$ corresponding to the $1$st eigenvalue $\lambda_1,$

- the $2$nd principal component is the unit eigenvector $\mathbf u_2$ corresponding to the $2$nd eigenvalue $\lambda_2,$

- $\cdots$

and so on.

For example, suppose that the covariance matrix $C$ of some particular observations is 

![](images/e4/e40cd1a0df89ba171b921ab971e8eee25e284265df13b7e031ea32fc28d2c27b.svg)

It's easy to show that the eigenvalues of the covariance matrix $C,$ in descending order, are 

$$
\lambda_1=10, \qquad
\lambda_2=8.
$$

To find the first principal component of the data, we need the unit eigenvector corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda_1=10.$ 

Applying our usual algorithm for finding eigenvectors, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}C-10I & =[\begin{aligned}9 & 1 \\ 1 & 9\end{aligned}]-10[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Now, seeking a non-zero solution of $(C-10I)\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}$ gives the eigenvector 

![](images/c7/c7050bbb395b939b1b0559b3e7515c4be4f572aed61090f1a4489e126763240f.svg) 

Finally, dividing $\mathbf{v}_1$ by its norm $\| \mathbf{v}_1 \| = \sqrt{2},$ we get 

![](images/7b/7b0a41deb385aa2471cae701c9f87938085256879a8d834535f8ec0e3f431f27.svg) 

Therefore, the $1$st principal component of the data is ![](images/94/9490f2e5105592fa3976ae506cbdf64d70c3372d1cc9295eaa6c6580a4ac75aa.svg)

**Note:** The opposite vector ![](images/e2/e2b366cfb8cb5b708eb5ba443dfc61c05b498d4eb737b375c8ebc86b96e8eea6.svg) also works in the example above." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186192865 :activity/expected-seconds 420.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]} {:db/id 17592186124463 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-cc4d5cf2-890e-5aaa-adb5-f60e0888df55"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id "question-cc4d5cf2-890e-5aaa-adb5-f60e0888df55" :question/id #uuid "cc4d5cf2-890e-5aaa-adb5-f60e0888df55" :question/math-academy-id "q-71405" :question/problem "For the function $f(x,y,z)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(yz)$, find a vector that's perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(1,\frac{\pi }{2},0).$" :question/worked-solution "A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(1,\frac{\pi }{2},0)$ can be found by computing

So, we first find the gradient and evaluate it at $(x,y,z)=(1,\frac{\pi }{2},0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(yz))\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(yz))\,j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(yz))\,k \\  & =-y\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy)\text{ }i+(-x\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy)+z\operatorname{cos}⁡(yz))\text{ }j+y\operatorname{cos}⁡(yz)\text{ }k \\ ∇f(1,\frac{\pi }{2},0) & =-\frac{\pi }{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(1\cdot \frac{\pi }{2})\,i+(-(1)\operatorname{sin}⁡(1\cdot \frac{\pi }{2})+0\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}\cdot 0))\,j+\frac{\pi }{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}\cdot 0)\,k \\  & =-\frac{\pi }{2}\,i-j+\frac{\pi }{2}\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $-\frac{\pi }{2}\,i-j+\frac{\pi }{2}\,k$ is perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(1,\frac{\pi }{2},0).$" :question/difficulty For the given problem, we have

$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186054620 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-683bbf9d-fe44-596b-9cba-6b07323bd6d5" "question-40969b77-0e08-50d1-86b5-46f58976876a" "question-bbd97f04-776a-53ed-8d9f-1d2d316080bc"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186054531 :question/problem "Evaluate $\left( \dfrac{1}{2} + \sqrt{-9} \right) + (3 - \sqrt{-16}).$" :question/worked-solution "First, we simplify the two complex numbers:

$$
\begin{aligned}(\frac{1}{2}+\sqrt{-9})+(3-\sqrt{-16}) & =(\frac{1}{2}+3\,\text{i})+(3-4\,\text{i})\end{aligned}
$$

{{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "We have the piecewise function

$$
p(x)=\{\begin{aligned}k+10, & \,x\le 3, \\ 8x-\frac{2}{3}{x}^{3}, & \,x>3.\end{aligned}

At $x=3,$ the left-sided limit is

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {3}^{-}}p(x) & =p(3) \\  & =k+10,\end{aligned}
$$

 

and the right-sided limit is

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {3}^{+}}p(x) & ={lim}_{x\to {3}^{+}}(8x-\frac{2}{3}{x}^{3}) \\  & =8(3)-\frac{2}{3}(3)^{3} \\  & =24-18 \\  & =6.\end{aligned}
$$

In order for $p(x)$ to be continuous at $x=3,$ we require that

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {3}^{-}}p(x) & ={lim}_{x\to {3}^{+}}p(x) \\ k+10 & =6 \\ k & =-4.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $p(x)$ is continuous at $x=3$ when $k=-4.$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-43939460-e1b0-596e-a7b7-ed6180d6c370"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-43939460-e1b0-596e-a7b7-ed6180d6c370" :answer-field/id #uuid "43939460-e1b0-596e-a7b7-ed6180d6c370" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-6c3822e0-7f7b-5338-85bf-9c5070788c44" :answer-field/choices ["answer-6c3822e0-7f7b-5338-85bf-9c5070788c44"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-6c3822e0-7f7b-5338-85bf-9c5070788c44" :answer/id #uuid "6c3822e0-7f7b-5338-85bf-9c5070788c44" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-4" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186059675 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-83dc5138-e470-5b8f-b97c-b3006ebeb428"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id "question-83dc5138-e470-5b8f-b97c-b3006ebeb428" :question/id #uuid "83dc5138-e470-5b8f-b97c-b3006ebeb428" :question/math-academy-id "q-166071" :question/problem "$\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}x}\,=${{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "We know that

{{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "We differentiate using the product rule. Recall that $f(x)=\frac{1}{2}{e}^{x}$ and $h(x)=-4\operatorname{sin}⁡x.$ Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{e}^{x})=\frac{1}{2}{e}^{x} \\ \frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(-4\operatorname{sin}⁡x)=-4\operatorname{cos}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the product rule gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =f\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}x}+h\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{e}^{x}\cdot (-4\operatorname{cos}⁡x)+(-4\operatorname{sin}⁡x)\cdot \frac{1}{2}{e}^{x} \\  & =-2{e}^{x}(\operatorname{cos}⁡x+\operatorname{sin}⁡x).\end{aligned}
$$

To find the slope of the tangent line, we now substitute $x=\pi $ into the formula and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}|}_{x=\pi } & =-2{e}^{\pi }(\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi +\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi ) \\  & =-2{e}^{\pi }(-1+0) \\  & =2{e}^{\pi }.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of the tangent line is $2{e}^{\pi }.$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-f49d4659-1c96-5a65-a285-84ed00e2cd31"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-f49d4659-1c96-5a65-a285-84ed00e2cd31" :answer-field/id #uuid "f49d4659-1c96-5a65-a285-84ed00e2cd31" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-e2f634bf-1fab-5c5c-9faf-cca696e95edd" :answer-field/choices ["answer-e2f634bf-1fab-5c5c-9faf-cca696e95edd"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-e2f634bf-1fab-5c5c-9faf-cca696e95edd" :answer/id #uuid "e2f634bf-1fab-5c5c-9faf-cca696e95edd" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "2e^{\pi}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186092240 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-745a29fd-db69-5896-9d5f-b9b3dcaa95b6"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id "question-745a29fd-db69-5896-9d5f-b9b3dcaa95b6" :question/id #uuid "745a29fd-db69-5896-9d5f-b9b3dcaa95b6" :question/math-academy-id "q-166074" :question/problem "The equation of the normal to the curve $y=f(x)\cdot h(x)$ at the point where $x=\pi $ is$\,y=$

We apply the quotient rule, as follows:

$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-bb0216fd-fe08-5818-afd9-7fc21cfab6bb"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-bb0216fd-fe08-5818-afd9-7fc21cfab6bb" :answer-field/id #uuid "bb0216fd-fe08-5818-afd9-7fc21cfab6bb" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-c73650fb-8ca5-5747-bbe3-f451e92a6a69" :answer-field/choices ["answer-c73650fb-8ca5-5747-bbe3-f451e92a6a69"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-c73650fb-8ca5-5747-bbe3-f451e92a6a69" :answer/id #uuid "c73650fb-8ca5-5747-bbe3-f451e92a6a69" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-2e^{-4\sin x}\cos x" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186064273 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-d78b3b66-caba-5b75-9179-7631fdc0e796"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id "question-d78b3b66-caba-5b75-9179-7631fdc0e796" :question/id #uuid "d78b3b66-caba-5b75-9179-7631fdc0e796" :question/math-academy-id "q-166077" :question/problem "![](images/5d/5d2bfbefca5ce0a0b04accad183d0f43537d600c72000058b59f692398259a80.png)

$+\,C,\,$ where $C$ is an arbitrary constant." :question/worked-solution "Recall that

$$
det({A}^{-1})=\frac{1}{det(A)}=-\frac{1}{10}.

$$

$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-c336fca6-9149-5cbc-a19d-a2bfb6cf6d63"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id $$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}-2{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+12x & =22 \\ {y}^{2}-2{x}^{2}+12x & =22 \\ {y}^{2}-2[{x}^{2}-6x] & =22 \\ {y}^{2}-2[(x-3)^{2}-9] & =22 \\ {y}^{2}-2(x-3)^{2}+18 & =22 \\ {y}^{2}-2(x-3)^{2} & =4 \\ \frac{{y}^{2}}{4}-\frac{(x-3)^{2}}{2} & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem "Calculate $\displaystyle \int x^2 \,\textrm d x.$" :question/worked-solution "We apply the power rule with $n=2$, and we get

$$
\int x^2 \,\textrm d x = \dfrac{x^{2+1}}{2+1} + C = \dfrac{x^3}{3}+C.
$$

Let's check by differentiating:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}+C) & = \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{{x}^{3}}{3})+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(C) & = \\ \frac{1}{3}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{3})+0 & = \\ \frac{1}{3}\cdot 3{x}^{2} & = \\ {x}^{2}\,✓\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186064168 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-34621fcb-1a0d-5d3e-9880-09e09830a08f" "question-37cc1eff-0240-5120-ba5e-14ada8bc6fca"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186064039 :question/problem "Find the antiderivative of  $\sqrt x.$" :question/worked-solution "We start by writing the square root as a rational power, $\sqrt x= x^{1/2}.$ So, we can apply the power rule with $n=\dfrac{1}{2}$ and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \sqrt{x}\,\text{d}x & =\int {x}^{1/2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{x}^{1/2+1}}{(\frac{1}{2}+1)}+C \\  & =\frac{{x}^{3/2}}{(\frac{3}{2})}+C \\  & =\frac{2{x}^{3/2}}{3}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Again, let's check by differentiating:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{2{x}^{3/2}}{3}+C) & = \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{2{x}^{3/2}}{3})+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(C) & = \\ \frac{2}{3}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{3/2})+0 & = \\ \frac{2}{3}\cdot \frac{3}{2}{x}^{3/2-1} & = \\ {x}^{1/2}\,✓\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186064169 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-3ce88619-593c-543d-be7b-78867655bb11" "question-28f4ccc6-88e6-5461-934d-fc36db9c8ad4"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186064040 :question/problem "Given that $f(x) = \dfrac 1 {x^3}$ and that $F'(x) = f(x)$, calculate $F(x).$" :question/worked-solution "Remember that integration is the opposite of differentiation. So, if $F'(x) = f(x),$ then integrating both sides of this equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{F}^{′}(x) & =f(x) \\ \int {F}^{′}(x)\,\text{d}x & =\int f(x)\,\text{d}x \\ F(x) & =\int f(x)\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $\dfrac 1 {x^3}= x^{-3}.$ So, we can use the power rule with $n=-3$ and get

$$
\begin{aligned}F(x) & =\int f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{1}{{x}^{3}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int {x}^{-3}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{x}^{-3+1}}{-3+1}+C \\  & =-\frac{{x}^{-2}}{2}+C \\  & =-\frac{1}{2{x}^{2}}+C.\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "question-7c1117fb-96ed-5032-8c50-48772b44cf5c" :question/id #uuid "7c1117fb-96ed-5032-8c50-48772b44cf5c" :question/math-academy-id "q-113668" :question/problem "Calculate $F(x)$ given that $f(x)={x}^{13}$ and ${F}^{′}(x)=f(x).$" :question/worked-solution "Remember that integration is the opposite of differentiation. So, if ${F}^{′}(x)=f(x),$ then integrating both sides of this equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{F}^{′}(x) & =f(x) \\ \int {F}^{′}(x)\,\text{d}x & =\int f(x)\,\text{d}x \\ F(x) & =\int f(x)\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

We apply the power rule with $n=13$, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}F(x) & =\int f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int {x}^{13}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{x}^{13+1}}{13+1}+C \\  & =\frac{{x}^{14}}{14}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Let's check by differentiating:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{{x}^{14}}{14}+C) & = \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{{x}^{14}}{14})+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(C) & = \\ \frac{1}{14}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{14})+0 & = \\ \frac{1}{14}\cdot 14\,{x}^{13} & = \\ {x}^{13}\,✓\end{aligned}
