:question.difficulty/hard} :question/problem "The minimum value of $Q(x)=4{x}_{1}^{2}-36{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+9{x}_{2}^{2},$ when $4{x}_{1}^{2}+9{x}_{2}^{2}=36,$ is $-72.$ Which of the following is a vector $x$ at which the minimum is attained?" :question/worked-solution "First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}4 & -18 \\ -18 & 9\end{bmatrix}
$$

Notice that we can write the constraint equation as follows:

$$
\frac{{x}_{1}^{2}}{{3}^{2}}+\frac{{x}_{2}^{2}}{{2}^{2}}=1
$$

This is an ellipse with semiaxes $a=3$ (along the ${x}_{1}$-axis) and $b=2$ (along the ${x}_{2}$-axis). If we introduce new variables

$\,$ ${y}_{1}=\frac{{x}_{1}}{3}\,$ and $\,{y}_{2}=\frac{{x}_{2}}{2},$

the equation of the ellipse will transform into ${y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}=1$ or $‖y‖=1.$

So, introducing a change-of-coordinate matrix 

$$
P=\begin{bmatrix}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix},
$$

 

we obtain that $x=Py.$ Substituting this into the expression of the quadratic form, we get

$$
Q(x)={x}^{T}\,Ax=(Py)^{T}A\,(Py)={y}^{T}\,({P}^{T}AP)y={Q}^{′}(y).
$$

As a result, since ${P}^{T}=P,$ the matrix of our quadratic form in new coordinates is 

$$
\begin{aligned}B & ={P}^{T}\,AP \\  & =PAP \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}4 & -18 \\ -18 & 9\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}12 & -54 \\ -36 & 18\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}36 & -108 \\ -108 & 36\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we minimize ${Q}^{′}(y)$ when $‖y‖=1,$ as usual.

Since we are told that the minimum value of the quadratic form is $-72,$ we have

$$
min\{{Q}^{′}(y)\,|\,‖y‖=1\}={\lambda }_{min}=-72.
$$

Next, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{\text{min}}=-72:$

$$
\begin{aligned}B-(-72)I & =\begin{bmatrix}36 & -108 \\ -108 & 36\end{bmatrix}+72\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}108 & -108 \\ -108 & 108\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(B-(-72)I)x=0$ gives the  eigenvector $v=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.$ Dividing $v$ by its norm $‖v‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get 

$$
{u}_{\text{min}}=\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

 

Finally, we map this vector back to the initial coordinate  system using the change-of-coordinates matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{\text{min}} & =P{u}_{\text{min}} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix}\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186389643 :question/id #uuid "546ae5ae-d06c-5386-b960-6a8c9d016f97" :question/math-academy-id "q-170514" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "e97a677c-7cd3-5ab4-a853-3e58af95ef68" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\begin{bmatrix}5 \\ 4\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186389645} {:answer/id #uuid "d626e8f2-6f92-5b4c-b77d-4433976b4f8c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 4\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186389646} {:answer/id #uuid "388c0d7a-2358-5cd2-b7be-8784a5eb4f83" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 4\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186389647} {:answer/id #uuid "5bee8a5d-5168-5c30-886c-aa5b72b8ba65" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\begin{bmatrix}5 \\ 6\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186389648} {:answer/id #uuid "34eaf1be-fb4e-53d6-9abd-f05704e7c071" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186389649}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186389648} :answer-field/id #uuid "807b9eea-f22c-56a9-981a-517ef2430f4c" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186389644}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/problem "The minimum value of $Q(x)=8{x}_{1}^{2}-30{x}_{1}{x}_{2}-50{x}_{2}^{2},$ when $4{x}_{1}^{2}+25{x}_{2}^{2}=100,$ is $-250.$ Which of the following is a vector $x$ at which the minimum is attained?" :question/worked-solution "First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$

$$
\frac{{x}_{1}^{2}}{{5}^{2}}+\frac{{x}_{2}^{2}}{{2}^{2}}=1
$$

$\,$ ${y}_{1}=\frac{{x}_{1}}{5}\,$ and $\,{y}_{2}=\frac{{x}_{2}}{2},$

the equation of the ellipse will transform into ${y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}=1$ or $‖y‖=1.$

So, introducing a change-of-coordinate matrix 

$$
P=\begin{bmatrix}5 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix},
$$

 

we obtain that $x=Py.$ Substituting this into the expression of the quadratic form, we get

$$
Q(x)={x}^{T}\,Ax=(Py)^{T}A\,(Py)={y}^{T}\,({P}^{T}AP)y={Q}^{′}(y).
$$

As a result, since ${P}^{T}=P,$ the matrix of our quadratic form in new coordinates is 

$$
\begin{aligned}B & ={P}^{T}\,AP \\  & =PAP \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}5 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}8 & -15 \\ -15 & -50\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}5 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}40 & -75 \\ -30 & -100\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}5 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}200 & -150 \\ -150 & -200\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}B-(-250I) & =\begin{bmatrix}200 & -150 \\ -150 & -200\end{bmatrix}+250\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}450 & -150 \\ -150 & 50\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}

$$
{u}_{\text{min}}=\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}.

$$

at which the maximum is attained?" :question/worked-solution "First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 8 \\ 8 & 4\end{bmatrix}
$$

Notice that we can write the constraint equation as follows:

$$
\frac{{x}_{1}^{2}}{{2}^{2}}+\frac{{x}_{2}^{2}}{{1}^{2}}=1
$$

This is an ellipse with semiaxes $a=2$ (along the ${x}_{1}$-axis) and $b=1$ (along the ${x}_{2}$-axis). If we introduce new variables

$\,$ ${y}_{1}=\frac{{x}_{1}}{2}\,$ and $\,{y}_{2}={x}_{2},$

the equation of the ellipse will transform into ${y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}=1$ or $‖y‖=1.$

So, introducing a change-of-coordinate matrix 

$$
P=\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix},
$$

 

we obtain that $x=Py.$ Substituting this into the expression of the quadratic form, we get

$$
Q(x)={x}^{T}\,Ax=(Py)^{T}A\,(Py)={y}^{T}\,({P}^{T}AP)y={Q}^{′}(y).
$$

 

As a result, since ${P}^{T}=P,$ the matrix of our quadratic form in new coordinates is 

$$
\begin{aligned}B & ={P}^{T}\,AP \\  & =PAP \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 8 \\ 8 & 4\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 16 \\ 8 & 4\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}4 & 16 \\ 16 & 4\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we maximize ${Q}^{′}(y)$ when $‖y‖=1,$ as usual.

Since we are told that the maximum value of the quadratic form is $20,$ we have

$$
max\{{Q}^{′}(y)\,|\,‖y‖=1\}={\lambda }_{max}=20.
$$

Next, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{\text{max}}=20:$

$$
\begin{aligned}B-20I & =\begin{bmatrix}4 & 16 \\ 16 & 4\end{bmatrix}-20\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-16 & 16 \\ 16 & -16\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(B-20I)y=0$ gives the eigenvector $v=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.$ Dividing $v$ by its norm $‖v‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get  

$$
{u}_{\text{max}}=\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

 

Finally, we map this vector back to the initial coordinate  system using the change-of-coordinates matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{\text{max}} & =P{u}_{\text{max}} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186410197 :question/id #uuid "dea55e7b-1cc0-500b-8640-ae39dddce75c" :question/math-academy-id "q-170560" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "27fa6c83-fea5-559c-b3af-e6a7e1618346" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{5}\begin{bmatrix}8 \\ 9\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186410169} {:answer/id #uuid "3bb153c6-9455-5e09-b9d4-e4c936682c6a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}-3 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186410172} {:answer/id #uuid "566bcdea-96b1-557a-bdcd-81a53378a8b5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\begin{bmatrix}4 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186410173} {:answer/id #uuid "a93b100e-c392-5adc-a3ed-bee963bcaac6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186410185} {:answer/id #uuid "b119d151-632a-5e08-8a6e-94f8c7ba763c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186410186}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186410169} :answer-field/id #uuid "b5b0d1a4-b3d8-5bd2-80e4-83dea5aa94c3" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186410194}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/problem "The maximum value of $Q(x)=4{x}_{1}^{2}+4{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+{x}_{2}^{2},$ when $9{x}_{1}^{2}+4{x}_{2}^{2}=36,$ is $25.$ Which of the following is a vector $x$ at which the maximum is attained?" :question/worked-solution "First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}4 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{bmatrix}
$$

$$
\frac{{x}_{1}^{2}}{{2}^{2}}+\frac{{x}_{2}^{2}}{{3}^{2}}=1
$$

This is an ellipse with semiaxes $a=2$ (along the ${x}_{1}$-axis) and $b=3$ (along the ${x}_{2}$-axis). If we introduce new variables

$\,$ ${y}_{1}=\frac{{x}_{1}}{2}\,$ and $\,{y}_{2}=\frac{{x}_{2}}{3},$

the equation of the ellipse will transform into ${y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}=1$ or $‖y‖=1.$

So, introducing a change-of-coordinate matrix 

$$
P=\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{bmatrix},
$$

 

we obtain that $x=Py.$ Substituting this into the expression of the quadratic form, we get

$$
Q(x)={x}^{T}\,Ax=(Py)^{T}A\,(Py)={y}^{T}\,({P}^{T}AP)y={Q}^{′}(y).
$$

As a result, since ${P}^{T}=P,$ the matrix of our quadratic form in new coordinates is 

$$
\begin{aligned}B & ={P}^{T}\,AP \\  & =PAP \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}4 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}8 & 4 \\ 6 & 3\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}16 & 12 \\ 12 & 9\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we maximize ${Q}^{′}(y)$ when $‖y‖=1,$ as usual.

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}B-25I & =\begin{bmatrix}16 & 12 \\ 12 & 9\end{bmatrix}-25\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-9 & 12 \\ 12 & -16\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

$$"} {:db/id 17592186492837 :question/id #uuid "1e463920-832a-54ce-b343-95505e40d97a" :question/math-academy-id "q-170527"} {:db/id 17592186050205} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid 17592186199393 :step/content {:db/id 17592186199515 :tutorial/content "If $A$ is the matrix corresponding to the quadratic form $Q(\mathbf{x}),$ then:  

- The maximum value of $Q(\mathbf{x}),$ when $\| \mathbf{x} \|=1,$ is equal to the largest eigenvalue $\lambda_{\textrm{max}}$ of $A,$ and the maximum is attained on the corresponding unit eigenvector $\mathbf{u}_{\textrm{max}}.$

- The minimum value of $Q(\mathbf{x}),$ when $\| \mathbf{x} \|=1,$ is equal to the smallest eigenvalue $\lambda_{\textrm{min}}$ of $A,$ and the minimum is attained on the corresponding unit eigenvector $\mathbf{u}_{\textrm{min}}.$

We'll prove this result at the end of the lesson.

Suppose we're given that the maximum value of the quadratic form 

$$
Q(\mathbf{x})=x_1^2-10\: \! x_1x_2+x_2^2
$$

 

when $\| \mathbf{x} \| = 1$ is $6.$ Let's use this to find a unit vector $\mathbf{u}_{\textrm{max}}$ where this maximum value is attained. 

So first, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

![](images/a6/a6165f41eb43e8f6e8fd4399f1c428f73481de9d4b5ec41293f3ec0e4f062fc6.svg)

Next, we find the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue $\lambda_{\textrm{max}}=6{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}A-6I & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & -5 \\ -5 & 1\end{bmatrix}-6\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-5 & -5 \\ -5 & -5\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-6I)\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}$ gives the eigenvector ![](images/30/30699c4f0abcb099a6f7a76cbd76674757c3f7de313e034d0870d1fce27fdd8c.svg) 

Finally, dividing $\mathbf{v}$ by its norm $\| \mathbf{v} \| = \sqrt{2},$ we get 

![](images/ef/ef14ea5facf5010b99721cf915f44162dfa52e089508fb78c2d02d9aad66f1a4.svg)  

Let's check that this is indeed the vector we were looking for: 

$$
\begin{aligned}Q({u}_{\text{max}}) & ={(\frac{-1}{\sqrt{2}})}^{2}-10(\frac{-1}{\sqrt{2}})(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}})+{(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}})}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}+\frac{10}{2}+\frac{1}{2} \\  & =6\,✓\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "c50ae6a7-1f29-5274-bd82-d2d8acfef6b7" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7954 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "08dd4ae6-a6ab-54da-a4ca-840835781b76" :step/math-academy-id {:db/id 17592186199516 :tutorial/content "Suppose we're given that the maximum value of the quadratic form 

$$
Q(\mathbf{x})=x_1^2-2x_1x_2+x_2^2,
$$

 over the ellipse $4x_1^2+x_2^2=4$ equals $5.$ How can we find a vector $\mathbf{x}$ at which this maximum is attained?

We can find this vector by applying a suitable change of variable. This change of variable should transform our problem into one where we need to maximize a related quadratic form $Q'$ on the unit circle. Let's see how this is done.

First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

![](images/7b/7b1fd813963e16887c57d6c10be1bfe288e3209fd3a02ca6e6236b7261feb7b1.svg)

Notice that we can write the constraint equation as follows:

$$
{x_1^2}+ \dfrac{x_2^2}{2^2}=1
$$

which  represents an ellipse with semiaxes $a=1$ (along the $x_1$-axis) and $b=2$ (along the $x_2$-axis). 

If we introduce new variables

$$
y_1={x_1}, \qquad y_2 = \dfrac{x_2}{2},
$$

the equation of the ellipse will transform into $y_1^2+y_2^2 = 1,$ or $\|\mathbf{y}\|=1.$

So, introducing a change-of-coordinate matrix 

![](images/80/80f8e821a60b63dde0f314460adfd31faca5d82315243fb2a3ebdec75bc61538.svg) 

we obtain that $\mathbf{x} = P \mathbf{y}.$ Substituting this into the expression of the quadratic form, we get

$$
Q(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{x}^T \! A \mathbf{x} = (P\mathbf{y})^T A \, (P\mathbf{y}) = \mathbf{y}^T \! (P^TAP) \mathbf{y}=Q'(\mathbf{y}).
$$

As a result, since $P^T=P,$ the matrix of our quadratic form in the new coordinates is 

$$
\begin{aligned}B & ={P}^{T}\,AP \\  & =PAP \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 \\ -1 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 \\ -2 & 2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 \\ -2 & 4\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, the goal is to maximize $Q'(\mathbf{y})$ when $\| \mathbf{y} \|=1,$ which we do using our usual methods.  

Since we are told that the maximum value of the quadratic form is $5,$ we have

$$
\max \{ Q'(\mathbf{y}) \: | \: \| \mathbf{y} \|=1 \} = \lambda_{\max} = 5.
$$

Next, we find the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue $\lambda_{\textrm{max}}=5{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}B-5I & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 \\ -2 & 4\end{bmatrix}-5\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-4 & -2 \\ -2 & -1\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(B-5I)\mathbf{y}=\mathbf{0}$ gives the eigenvector ![](images/4b/4b51afece6e21c2fe073a5346557f42f9f03ae3400407d18ed6af3af8f32e310.svg) Dividing $\mathbf{v}$ by its norm $\| \mathbf{v} \| = \sqrt{5},$ we get 

![](images/ce/ce571338fc1d83f0b0892a356bca56073c096a1f5191a21a4baef56b6d5a399f.svg) 

Finally, we map this vector back to the initial coordinate  system using the change-of-coordinates matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{\text{max}} & =P{u}_{\text{max}} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix}\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 4\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "e750f422-509a-598a-858a-c11360c80eea" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7955 :tutorial/title "Constrained Optimization of Quadratic Forms Over Ellipses"} :step/id #uuid "f3b4db0d-8fec-573f-8597-7e9b0d0a4474" :step/math-academy-id 45758 :step/next {:db/id 17592186199395}} {:db/id 17592186199404 :step/content {:db/id 17592186199547 :tutorial/content "To complete the picture, let's prove the main theorem of this lesson:

*The maximum value of a quadratic form $Q(\mathbf{x})=\mathbf{x}^T A \mathbf{x},$ when $\| \mathbf{x} \|=1,$ is equal to the largest eigenvalue of $A{:}$* 

$$
\max \{ Q(\mathbf{x}) \: | \:  \| \mathbf{x} \| = 1 \} = \lambda_{\textrm{max}}
$$

*The maximum is attained on the corresponding unit eigenvector $\mathbf{u}_{\textrm{max}}.$*

**Note:** We'll show only the first part (about the maximum value) since a similar argument can be used to prove the second part (about the minimum value).

Let $A$ be a real $n \times n$ symmetric matrix corresponding to a quadratic form $Q(\mathbf x)\mathbin.$ As a result, there must be an *orthonormal* matrix $P$ such that 

- $D=P^{-1}AP=P^TAP,$ where $D$ is a diagonal matrix.

- The diagonal entries of $D$ are the eigenvalues of $A$. Without loss of generality, we can assume that the eigenvalues are $\lambda_1 \geq \lambda_2 \geq \ldots \geq \lambda_n,$ where $\lambda_{\textrm{max}} = \lambda_1.$

- The columns $\mathbf{u}_1,\mathbf{u}_2, \ldots, \mathbf{u}_n$ of $P$ form an orthonormal set of unit eigenvectors of $A.$ So, $\mathbf{u}_{\textrm{max}} = \mathbf{u}_1.$

Take $\mathbf x=P\mathbf y.$ Since, $P$ is orthonormal, we have

$$
\|\mathbf x\| = \|P \mathbf y \| = \|\mathbf y\|
$$

and

$$
Q(\mathbf x) = \mathbf x^T\!A\mathbf x = (P\mathbf y)^T\!A(P\mathbf y) = \mathbf{y}^T (P^T\!AP) \mathbf{y} = \mathbf{y}^T D \mathbf{y}
$$

for all $\mathbf{y} \in \mathbb{R}^n.$

Therefore, we can conclude the following:

- $\|\mathbf x\| =1 \Longleftrightarrow \|\mathbf y\| =1$ for all $\mathbf y$ such that $\mathbf x=P\mathbf y$

- Restricted to the unit sphere of $\Bbb R^n,$ the images of the quadratic forms $Q(\mathbf x)$  and $Q'(\mathbf y)= \mathbf y^T D\mathbf y$ coincide: 

$$
\{\mathbf x^TA\mathbf x: \: \: \|\mathbf x\|=1\}= \{\mathbf y^TD\mathbf y: \: \: \|\mathbf y\|=1\}  \subset \mathbb R
$$

Now, for any unit vector $\mathbf{y} \in \mathbb{R}^n,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(x) & ={Q}^{′}(y) \\  & ={\lambda }_{1}{y}_{1}^{2}+{\lambda }_{2}{y}_{2}^{2}+⋯+{\lambda }_{n}{y}_{n}^{2} \\  & \le {\lambda }_{\text{max}}\,{y}_{1}^{2}+{\lambda }_{\text{max}}\,{y}_{2}^{2}+⋯+{\lambda }_{\text{max}}\,{y}_{n}^{2} \\  & ={\lambda }_{\text{max}}({y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}+⋯+{y}_{n}^{2}) \\  & ={\lambda }_{\text{max}}\,‖y{‖}^{2} \\  & ={\lambda }_{\text{max}}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have that  that 

$$
M = \max \{ Q(\mathbf{x}) \: | \:  \| \mathbf{x} \| = 1 \} = \max \{ Q'(\mathbf{y}) \: | \:  \| \mathbf{y} \| = 1 \} \le \lambda_{\textrm{max}}.
$$

 

On the other hand, if we take ![](images/53/53a051ea36059c9222e717c65adc6531bc313c9807d44a39b262433acfdcbc5c.svg) then $Q(P\mathbf{e}_1) = Q'(\mathbf{e}_1) = \lambda_{\textrm{max}}.$ So, we conclude that $M = \lambda_{\textrm{max}}.$

Finally, since $\mathbf{u}_1 = P\mathbf{e}_1$ we have that 
$Q(\mathbf u_1) =  \mathbf e_1^T D \mathbf e_1 = \lambda_{\textrm{max}}.$ 
Therefore, the maximum value is attained at $\mathbf u_{\textrm{max}}.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "364005f5-f0fc-5d17-9d6b-288d52abe715" :tutorial/math-academy-id 8176 :tutorial/title "Proof of the Main Theorem"} :step/id #uuid "3a8e9986-4b85-5793-91b8-d47f73b67205" :step/math-academy-id 54038}] :activity/title "Constrained Optimization of Quadratic Forms: Determining Where Extrema are Attained" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186198510} {:db/id 17592186199393 :step/content {:db/id 17592186199515 :tutorial/content "If $A$ is the matrix corresponding to the quadratic form $Q(\mathbf{x}),$ then:  

- The maximum value of $Q(\mathbf{x}),$ when $\| \mathbf{x} \|=1,$ is equal to the largest eigenvalue $\lambda_{\textrm{max}}$ of $A,$ and the maximum is attained on the corresponding unit eigenvector $\mathbf{u}_{\textrm{max}}.$

- The minimum value of $Q(\mathbf{x}),$ when $\| \mathbf{x} \|=1,$ is equal to the smallest eigenvalue $\lambda_{\textrm{min}}$ of $A,$ and the minimum is attained on the corresponding unit eigenvector $\mathbf{u}_{\textrm{min}}.$

We'll prove this result at the end of the lesson.

Suppose we're given that the maximum value of the quadratic form 

$$
Q(\mathbf{x})=x_1^2-10\: \! x_1x_2+x_2^2
$$

$$
Q(\mathbf{x})=x_1^2-2x_1x_2+x_2^2,
$$

 over the ellipse $4x_1^2+x_2^2=4$ equals $5.$ How can we find a vector $\mathbf{x}$ at which this maximum is attained?

We can find this vector by applying a suitable change of variable. This change of variable should transform our problem into one where we need to maximize a related quadratic form $Q'$ on the unit circle. Let's see how this is done.

First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

![](images/7b/7b1fd813963e16887c57d6c10be1bfe288e3209fd3a02ca6e6236b7261feb7b1.svg)

Notice that we can write the constraint equation as follows:

$$
{x_1^2}+ \dfrac{x_2^2}{2^2}=1
$$

which  represents an ellipse with semiaxes $a=1$ (along the $x_1$-axis) and $b=2$ (along the $x_2$-axis). 

If we introduce new variables

$$
y_1={x_1}, \qquad y_2 = \dfrac{x_2}{2},
$$

the equation of the ellipse will transform into $y_1^2+y_2^2 = 1,$ or $\|\mathbf{y}\|=1.$

So, introducing a change-of-coordinate matrix 

![](images/80/80f8e821a60b63dde0f314460adfd31faca5d82315243fb2a3ebdec75bc61538.svg) 

we obtain that $\mathbf{x} = P \mathbf{y}.$ Substituting this into the expression of the quadratic form, we get

$$
Q(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{x}^T \! A \mathbf{x} = (P\mathbf{y})^T A \, (P\mathbf{y}) = \mathbf{y}^T \! (P^TAP) \mathbf{y}=Q'(\mathbf{y}).
$$

As a result, since $P^T=P,$ the matrix of our quadratic form in the new coordinates is 

$$
\begin{aligned}B & ={P}^{T}\,AP \\  & =PAP \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 \\ -1 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 \\ -2 & 2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 \\ -2 & 4\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, the goal is to maximize $Q'(\mathbf{y})$ when $\| \mathbf{y} \|=1,$ which we do using our usual methods.  

Since we are told that the maximum value of the quadratic form is $5,$ we have

$$
\max \{ Q'(\mathbf{y}) \: | \: \| \mathbf{y} \|=1 \} = \lambda_{\max} = 5.
$$

Next, we find the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue $\lambda_{\textrm{max}}=5{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}B-5I & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 \\ -2 & 4\end{bmatrix}-5\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-4 & -2 \\ -2 & -1\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(B-5I)\mathbf{y}=\mathbf{0}$ gives the eigenvector ![](images/4b/4b51afece6e21c2fe073a5346557f42f9f03ae3400407d18ed6af3af8f32e310.svg) Dividing $\mathbf{v}$ by its norm $\| \mathbf{v} \| = \sqrt{5},$ we get 

![](images/ce/ce571338fc1d83f0b0892a356bca56073c096a1f5191a21a4baef56b6d5a399f.svg) 

Finally, we map this vector back to the initial coordinate  system using the change-of-coordinates matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{\text{max}} & =P{u}_{\text{max}} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix}\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 4\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "e750f422-509a-598a-858a-c11360c80eea" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7955 :tutorial/title "Constrained Optimization of Quadratic Forms Over Ellipses"} :step/id #uuid "f3b4db0d-8fec-573f-8597-7e9b0d0a4474" :step/math-academy-id 45758 :step/next {:db/id 17592186199395}} {:db/id 17592186199515 :tutorial/content "If $A$ is the matrix corresponding to the quadratic form $Q(\mathbf{x}),$ then:  

- The maximum value of $Q(\mathbf{x}),$ when $\| \mathbf{x} \|=1,$ is equal to the largest eigenvalue $\lambda_{\textrm{max}}$ of $A,$ and the maximum is attained on the corresponding unit eigenvector $\mathbf{u}_{\textrm{max}}.$

- The minimum value of $Q(\mathbf{x}),$ when $\| \mathbf{x} \|=1,$ is equal to the smallest eigenvalue $\lambda_{\textrm{min}}$ of $A,$ and the minimum is attained on the corresponding unit eigenvector $\mathbf{u}_{\textrm{min}}.$

*The maximum value of a quadratic form $Q(\mathbf{x})=\mathbf{x}^T A \mathbf{x},$ when $\| \mathbf{x} \|=1,$ is equal to the largest eigenvalue of $A{:}$* 

$$
\max \{ Q(\mathbf{x}) \: | \:  \| \mathbf{x} \| = 1 \} = \lambda_{\textrm{max}}
$$

*The maximum is attained on the corresponding unit eigenvector $\mathbf{u}_{\textrm{max}}.$*

**Note:** We'll show only the first part (about the maximum value) since a similar argument can be used to prove the second part (about the minimum value).

Let $A$ be a real $n \times n$ symmetric matrix corresponding to a quadratic form $Q(\mathbf x)\mathbin.$ As a result, there must be an *orthonormal* matrix $P$ such that 

- $D=P^{-1}AP=P^TAP,$ where $D$ is a diagonal matrix.

- The diagonal entries of $D$ are the eigenvalues of $A$. Without loss of generality, we can assume that the eigenvalues are $\lambda_1 \geq \lambda_2 \geq \ldots \geq \lambda_n,$ where $\lambda_{\textrm{max}} = \lambda_1.$

- The columns $\mathbf{u}_1,\mathbf{u}_2, \ldots, \mathbf{u}_n$ of $P$ form an orthonormal set of unit eigenvectors of $A.$ So, $\mathbf{u}_{\textrm{max}} = \mathbf{u}_1.$

Take $\mathbf x=P\mathbf y.$ Since, $P$ is orthonormal, we have

$$
\|\mathbf x\| = \|P \mathbf y \| = \|\mathbf y\|
$$

and

$$
Q(\mathbf x) = \mathbf x^T\!A\mathbf x = (P\mathbf y)^T\!A(P\mathbf y) = \mathbf{y}^T (P^T\!AP) \mathbf{y} = \mathbf{y}^T D \mathbf{y}
$$

for all $\mathbf{y} \in \mathbb{R}^n.$

Therefore, we can conclude the following:

- $\|\mathbf x\| =1 \Longleftrightarrow \|\mathbf y\| =1$ for all $\mathbf y$ such that $\mathbf x=P\mathbf y$

- Restricted to the unit sphere of $\Bbb R^n,$ the images of the quadratic forms $Q(\mathbf x)$  and $Q'(\mathbf y)= \mathbf y^T D\mathbf y$ coincide: 

$$
\{\mathbf x^TA\mathbf x: \: \: \|\mathbf x\|=1\}= \{\mathbf y^TD\mathbf y: \: \: \|\mathbf y\|=1\}  \subset \mathbb R
$$

Now, for any unit vector $\mathbf{y} \in \mathbb{R}^n,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(x) & ={Q}^{′}(y) \\  & ={\lambda }_{1}{y}_{1}^{2}+{\lambda }_{2}{y}_{2}^{2}+⋯+{\lambda }_{n}{y}_{n}^{2} \\  & \le {\lambda }_{\text{max}}\,{y}_{1}^{2}+{\lambda }_{\text{max}}\,{y}_{2}^{2}+⋯+{\lambda }_{\text{max}}\,{y}_{n}^{2} \\  & ={\lambda }_{\text{max}}({y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}+⋯+{y}_{n}^{2}) \\  & ={\lambda }_{\text{max}}\,‖y{‖}^{2} \\  & ={\lambda }_{\text{max}}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have that  that 

$$
M = \max \{ Q(\mathbf{x}) \: | \:  \| \mathbf{x} \| = 1 \} = \max \{ Q'(\mathbf{y}) \: | \:  \| \mathbf{y} \| = 1 \} \le \lambda_{\textrm{max}}.
$$

 

On the other hand, if we take ![](images/53/53a051ea36059c9222e717c65adc6531bc313c9807d44a39b262433acfdcbc5c.svg) then $Q(P\mathbf{e}_1) = Q'(\mathbf{e}_1) = \lambda_{\textrm{max}}.$ So, we conclude that $M = \lambda_{\textrm{max}}.$

Finally, since $\mathbf{u}_1 = P\mathbf{e}_1$ we have that 
$Q(\mathbf u_1) =  \mathbf e_1^T D \mathbf e_1 = \lambda_{\textrm{max}}.$ 
Therefore, the maximum value is attained at $\mathbf u_{\textrm{max}}.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "364005f5-f0fc-5d17-9d6b-288d52abe715" :tutorial/math-academy-id 8176 :tutorial/title "Proof of the Main Theorem"} :step/id #uuid "3a8e9986-4b85-5793-91b8-d47f73b67205" :step/math-academy-id 54038} {:db/id 17592186199516 :tutorial/content "Suppose we're given that the maximum value of the quadratic form

quadratic form $Q(x)=7{x}_{1}^{2}+8{x}_{2}^{2}+5{x}_{3}^{2}-4{x}_{2}{x}_{3},$ when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to $4.$ Which of the following is a vector $x$ at which the minimum is attained?" :question/worked-solution "Let $A$ be the matrix corresponding to our quadratic form. Recall that: 

- The maximum value of $Q(x),$ when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to the largest eigenvalue of $A:$

$$
max{Q(x)\,|\,‖x‖=1}={\lambda }_{\text{max}}
$$

 
The maximum is attained on the corresponding unit eigenvector ${u}_{\text{max}}.$

- The minimum value of $Q(x),$ when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to the smallest eigenvalue of $A:$

$$
min{Q(x)\,|\,‖x‖=1}={\lambda }_{\text{min}}
$$

 
The minimum is attained on the corresponding unit eigenvector ${u}_{\text{min}}.$

First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}7 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 8 & -2 \\ 0 & -2 & 5\end{bmatrix}
$$

Now, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{\text{min}}=4:$

$$
\begin{aligned}A-4I & =\begin{bmatrix}7 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 8 & -2 \\ 0 & -2 & 5\end{bmatrix}-4\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}3 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & -2 \\ 0 & -2 & 1\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-4I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector $v=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}.$ 

Finally, dividing $v$ by its norm $‖v‖=\sqrt{5},$ we get 

$$
{u}_{\text{min}}=\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "0d7e6a3a-4e90-51f7-9e6d-1f36e15dea08" :step/next {:db/id 17592186410203}} {:db/id 17592186410200 :step/content {:db/id 17592186410197 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "27fa6c83-fea5-559c-b3af-e6a7e1618346" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{5}\begin{bmatrix}8 \\ 9\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186410169} {:answer/id #uuid "3bb153c6-9455-5e09-b9d4-e4c936682c6a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}-3 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186410172} {:answer/id #uuid "566bcdea-96b1-557a-bdcd-81a53378a8b5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\begin{bmatrix}4 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186410173} {:answer/id #uuid "a93b100e-c392-5adc-a3ed-bee963bcaac6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186410185} {:answer/id #uuid "b119d151-632a-5e08-8a6e-94f8c7ba763c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186410186}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186410169} :answer-field/id #uuid "b5b0d1a4-b3d8-5bd2-80e4-83dea5aa94c3" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186410194}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "dea55e7b-1cc0-500b-8640-ae39dddce75c" :question/math-academy-id "q-170560" :question/problem "The maximum value of $Q(x)=4{x}_{1}^{2}+4{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+{x}_{2}^{2},$ when $9{x}_{1}^{2}+4{x}_{2}^{2}=36,$ is $25.$ Which of the following is a vector $x$ at which the maximum is attained?" :question/worked-solution "First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}4 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{bmatrix}
$$

Notice that we can write the constraint equation as follows:

$$
\frac{{x}_{1}^{2}}{{2}^{2}}+\frac{{x}_{2}^{2}}{{3}^{2}}=1
$$

This is an ellipse with semiaxes $a=2$ (along the ${x}_{1}$-axis) and $b=3$ (along the ${x}_{2}$-axis). If we introduce new variables

$\,$ ${y}_{1}=\frac{{x}_{1}}{2}\,$ and $\,{y}_{2}=\frac{{x}_{2}}{3},$

the equation of the ellipse will transform into ${y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}=1$ or $‖y‖=1.$

So, introducing a change-of-coordinate matrix 

$$
P=\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{bmatrix},
$$

 

we obtain that $x=Py.$ Substituting this into the expression of the quadratic form, we get

$$
Q(x)={x}^{T}\,Ax=(Py)^{T}A\,(Py)={y}^{T}\,({P}^{T}AP)y={Q}^{′}(y).
$$

As a result, since ${P}^{T}=P,$ the matrix of our quadratic form in new coordinates is 

$$
\begin{aligned}B & ={P}^{T}\,AP \\  & =PAP \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}4 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}8 & 4 \\ 6 & 3\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}16 & 12 \\ 12 & 9\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we maximize ${Q}^{′}(y)$ when $‖y‖=1,$ as usual.

Since we are told that the maximum value of the quadratic form is $25,$ we have

$$
max\{{Q}^{′}(y)\,|\,‖y‖=1\}={\lambda }_{max}=25.
$$

Next, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{\text{max}}=25:$

$$
\begin{aligned}B-25I & =\begin{bmatrix}16 & 12 \\ 12 & 9\end{bmatrix}-25\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-9 & 12 \\ 12 & -16\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(B-25I)y=0$ gives the eigenvector $v=\begin{bmatrix}4 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}.$ Dividing $v$ by its norm $‖v‖=5,$ we get 

$$
{u}_{\text{max}}=\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{5}\begin{bmatrix}4 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}.
$$

 

Finally, we map this vector back to the initial coordinate  system using the change-of-coordinates matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{\text{max}} & =P{u}_{\text{max}} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{bmatrix}\cdot \frac{1}{5}\begin{bmatrix}4 \\ 3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{5}\begin{bmatrix}8 \\ 9\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "3781c4aa-7e7b-5b51-9af4-d354711b0091"} {:db/id 17592186410201 :step/content {:db/id 17592186410195 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1579c753-1597-556d-8bd8-51a8deed3084" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\begin{bmatrix}-3 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186410166} {:answer/id #uuid "1c96736a-b709-578c-8d05-cc73305aecdc" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186410168} {:answer/id #uuid "31146e93-a5b1-5fe1-90a1-7f9c284f1056" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186410171} {:answer/id #uuid "5dd5c912-e67d-530f-a2c1-baaeaac814c2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186410177} {:answer/id #uuid "a21806c6-2164-532f-ac84-142d42881117" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186410184}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186410168} :answer-field/id #uuid "5dc24884-5d5e-5b11-b5e7-3763c0022ada" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186410191}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "3f433543-b9f1-5f20-b0ed-749a73af3fa7" :question/math-academy-id "q-170506" :question/problem "The maximum value of $Q(x)={x}_{1}^{2}+16{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+4{x}_{2}^{2},$ when ${x}_{1}^{2}+4{x}_{2}^{2}=4,$ is $20.$ Which of the following is a vector $x$ at which the maximum is attained?" :question/worked-solution "First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}4 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{bmatrix}
$$

Notice that we can write the constraint equation as follows:

$$
\frac{{x}_{1}^{2}}{{2}^{2}}+\frac{{x}_{2}^{2}}{{3}^{2}}=1
$$

This is an ellipse with semiaxes $a=2$ (along the ${x}_{1}$-axis) and $b=3$ (along the ${x}_{2}$-axis). If we introduce new variables

$\,$ ${y}_{1}=\frac{{x}_{1}}{2}\,$ and $\,{y}_{2}=\frac{{x}_{2}}{3},$

the equation of the ellipse will transform into ${y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}=1$ or $‖y‖=1.$

So, introducing a change-of-coordinate matrix 

$$
P=\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{bmatrix},
$$

 

we obtain that $x=Py.$ Substituting this into the expression of the quadratic form, we get

$$
Q(x)={x}^{T}\,Ax=(Py)^{T}A\,(Py)={y}^{T}\,({P}^{T}AP)y={Q}^{′}(y).
$$

As a result, since ${P}^{T}=P,$ the matrix of our quadratic form in new coordinates is 

$$
\begin{aligned}B & ={P}^{T}\,AP \\  & =PAP \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}4 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}8 & 4 \\ 6 & 3\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}16 & 12 \\ 12 & 9\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we maximize ${Q}^{′}(y)$ when $‖y‖=1,$ as usual.

Since we are told that the maximum value of the quadratic form is $25,$ we have

$$
max\{{Q}^{′}(y)\,|\,‖y‖=1\}={\lambda }_{max}=25.
$$

Next, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{\text{max}}=25:$

$$
\begin{aligned}B-25I & =\begin{bmatrix}16 & 12 \\ 12 & 9\end{bmatrix}-25\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-9 & 12 \\ 12 & -16\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(B-25I)y=0$ gives the eigenvector $v=\begin{bmatrix}4 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}.$ Dividing $v$ by its norm $‖v‖=5,$ we get 

$$
{u}_{\text{max}}=\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{5}\begin{bmatrix}4 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}.
$$

 

Finally, we map this vector back to the initial coordinate  system using the change-of-coordinates matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{\text{max}} & =P{u}_{\text{max}} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{bmatrix}\cdot \frac{1}{5}\begin{bmatrix}4 \\ 3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{5}\begin{bmatrix}8 \\ 9\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "3781c4aa-7e7b-5b51-9af4-d354711b0091"} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "27fa6c83-fea5-559c-b3af-e6a7e1618346" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value ${x}_{1}^{2}+9{x}_{2}^{2}=9.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}1 & -9 \\ -9 & 81\end{bmatrix}
$$

Notice that we can write the constraint equation as follows:

$$
\frac{{x}_{1}^{2}}{{3}^{2}}+\frac{{x}_{2}^{2}}{{1}^{2}}=1
$$

This is an ellipse with semiaxes $a=3$ (along the ${x}_{1}$-axis) and $b=1$ (along the ${x}_{2}$-axis). If we introduce new variables

$\,$ ${y}_{1}=\frac{{x}_{1}}{3}\,$ and $\,{y}_{2}={x}_{2},$ 

the equation of the ellipse will transform into ${y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}=1$ or $‖y‖=1.$

So, introducing a change-of-coordinates matrix 

$$
P=\begin{bmatrix}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix},
$$

 

we obtain that $x=Py.$ Substituting this into the expression of the quadratic form, we get

$$
Q(x)={x}^{T}\,Ax=(Py)^{T}A\,(Py)={y}^{T}\,({P}^{T}AP)y={Q}^{′}(y).
$$

 

As a result, since ${P}^{T}=P,$ the matrix of our quadratic form in new coordinates is 

$$
\begin{aligned}B & ={P}^{T}\,AP \\  & =PAP \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 & -9 \\ -9 & 81\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}3 & -27 \\ -9 & 81\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}9 & -27 \\ -27 & 81\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we maximize ${Q}^{′}(y)$ when $‖y‖=1,$ as usual. Calculating the eigenvalues $B,$ we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}|B-\lambda I| & =0 \\ \begin{vmatrix}9-\lambda  & -27 \\ -27 & 81-\lambda \end{vmatrix} & =0 \\ (9-\lambda )(81-\lambda )-729 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-90\lambda  & =0 \\ \lambda (\lambda -90) & =0 \\ \lambda  & =0,\,90\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
max\{{Q}^{′}(y)\,|\,‖y‖=1\}={\lambda }_{\text{max}}=90.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "14546d02-e8ca-5bbd-82f2-37c20dd8c152" :step/next {:db/id 17592186414675}} {:db/id 17592186414675 :step/content {:db/id 17592186410197 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "27fa6c83-fea5-559c-b3af-e6a7e1618346" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{5}\begin{bmatrix}8 \\ 9\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186410169} {:answer/id #uuid "3bb153c6-9455-5e09-b9d4-e4c936682c6a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}-3 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186410172} {:answer/id #uuid "566bcdea-96b1-557a-bdcd-81a53378a8b5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\begin{bmatrix}4 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186410173} {:answer/id #uuid "a93b100e-c392-5adc-a3ed-bee963bcaac6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186410185} {:answer/id #uuid "b119d151-632a-5e08-8a6e-94f8c7ba763c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186410186}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186410169} :answer-field/id #uuid "b5b0d1a4-b3d8-5bd2-80e4-83dea5aa94c3" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186410194}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "dea55e7b-1cc0-500b-8640-ae39dddce75c" :question/math-academy-id "q-170560" :question/problem "The maximum value of $Q(x)=4{x}_{1}^{2}+4{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+{x}_{2}^{2},$ when $9{x}_{1}^{2}+4{x}_{2}^{2}=36,$ is $25.$ Which of the following is a vector $x$ at which the maximum is attained?" :question/worked-solution "First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}4 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{bmatrix}
$$

Notice that we can write the constraint equation as follows:

$$
\frac{{x}_{1}^{2}}{{2}^{2}}+\frac{{x}_{2}^{2}}{{3}^{2}}=1
$$

This is an ellipse with semiaxes $a=2$ (along the ${x}_{1}$-axis) and $b=3$ (along the ${x}_{2}$-axis). If we introduce new variables

$\,$ ${y}_{1}=\frac{{x}_{1}}{2}\,$ and $\,{y}_{2}=\frac{{x}_{2}}{3},$

the equation of the ellipse will transform into ${y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}=1$ or $‖y‖=1.$

So, introducing a change-of-coordinate matrix 

$$
P=\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{bmatrix},
$$

 

we obtain that $x=Py.$ Substituting this into the expression of the quadratic form, we get

$$
Q(x)={x}^{T}\,Ax=(Py)^{T}A\,(Py)={y}^{T}\,({P}^{T}AP)y={Q}^{′}(y).
$$

As a result, since ${P}^{T}=P,$ the matrix of our quadratic form in new coordinates is 

$$
\begin{aligned}B & ={P}^{T}\,AP \\  & =PAP \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}4 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}8 & 4 \\ 6 & 3\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}16 & 12 \\ 12 & 9\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we maximize ${Q}^{′}(y)$ when $‖y‖=1,$ as usual.

Since we are told that the maximum value of the quadratic form is $25,$ we have

$$
max\{{Q}^{′}(y)\,|\,‖y‖=1\}={\lambda }_{max}=25.
$$

Next, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{\text{max}}=25:$

$$
\begin{aligned}B-25I & =\begin{bmatrix}16 & 12 \\ 12 & 9\end{bmatrix}-25\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-9 & 12 \\ 12 & -16\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(B-25I)y=0$ gives the eigenvector $v=\begin{bmatrix}4 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}.$ Dividing $v$ by its norm $‖v‖=5,$ we get 

$$
{u}_{\text{max}}=\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{5}\begin{bmatrix}4 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}.
$$

 

Finally, we map this vector back to the initial coordinate  system using the change-of-coordinates matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{\text{max}} & =P{u}_{\text{max}} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{bmatrix}\cdot \frac{1}{5}\begin{bmatrix}4 \\ 3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{5}\begin{bmatrix}8 \\ 9\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}

"First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}4 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{bmatrix}
$$

Notice that we can write the constraint equation as follows:

$$
\frac{{x}_{1}^{2}}{{2}^{2}}+\frac{{x}_{2}^{2}}{{3}^{2}}=1
$$

This is an ellipse with semiaxes $a=2$ (along the ${x}_{1}$-axis) and $b=3$ (along the ${x}_{2}$-axis). If we introduce new variables

$\,$ ${y}_{1}=\frac{{x}_{1}}{2}\,$ and $\,{y}_{2}=\frac{{x}_{2}}{3},$

the equation of the ellipse will transform into ${y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}=1$ or $‖y‖=1.$

So, introducing a change-of-coordinate matrix 

$$
P=\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{bmatrix},
$$

 

we obtain that $x=Py.$ Substituting this into the expression of the quadratic form, we get

$$
Q(x)={x}^{T}\,Ax=(Py)^{T}A\,(Py)={y}^{T}\,({P}^{T}AP)y={Q}^{′}(y).
$$

As a result, since ${P}^{T}=P,$ the matrix of our quadratic form in new coordinates is 

$$
\begin{aligned}B & ={P}^{T}\,AP \\  & =PAP \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}4 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}8 & 4 \\ 6 & 3\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}16 & 12 \\ 12 & 9\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we maximize ${Q}^{′}(y)$ when $‖y‖=1,$ as usual.

Since we are told that the maximum value of the quadratic form is $25,$ we have

$$
max\{{Q}^{′}(y)\,|\,‖y‖=1\}={\lambda }_{max}=25.
$$

Next, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{\text{max}}=25:$

$$
\begin{aligned}B-25I & =\begin{bmatrix}16 & 12 \\ 12 & 9\end{bmatrix}-25\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-9 & 12 \\ 12 & -16\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(B-25I)y=0$ gives the eigenvector $v=\begin{bmatrix}4 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}.$ Dividing $v$ by its norm $‖v‖=5,$ we get 

$$
{u}_{\text{max}}=\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{5}\begin{bmatrix}4 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}.
$$

 

Finally, we map this vector back to the initial coordinate  system using the change-of-coordinates matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{\text{max}} & =P{u}_{\text{max}} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{bmatrix}\cdot \frac{1}{5}\begin{bmatrix}4 \\ 3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{5}\begin{bmatrix}8 \\ 9\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "310e7c10-e8a2-5719-93d8-e4b398b84456"} {:db/id 17592186414676 :step/content {:db/id 17592186389629 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "33fcc9d7-da26-566b-892f-8ca0dccbf100" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186389631} {:answer/id #uuid "a86affbe-00af-5daa-9d5d-d6b4c732cb8c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186389632} {:answer/id #uuid "da2b263a-4cb7-517f-88b9-8ca97ec6707e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186389633} {:answer/id #uuid "b5f8b750-04ea-55ad-b825-30a6ece0925e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186389634} {:answer/id #uuid "0ceac102-859c-568b-8eb7-f0592356b505" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186389635}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186389631} :answer-field/id #uuid "205f15e5-0108-5b4a-888b-1b37b338482c" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186389630}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "8daa1f82-58aa-5738-bbe7-9b509869abcc" :question/math-academy-id "q-170411" :question/problem "The minimum value of the quadratic form $Q(x)={x}_{1}^{2}+{x}_{2}^{2}+{x}_{3}^{2}+4{x}_{1}{x}_{2},$ when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to $-1.$ Which of the following is a vector $x$ at which the minimum is attained?" :question/worked-solution "Let $A$ be the matrix corresponding to our quadratic form. $$

$$

Now, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{\text{max}}=4:$

$$
\begin{aligned}A-4I & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 3 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 3 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}-4\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-3 & 0 & 3 \\ 0 & -3 & 0 \\ 3 & 0 & -3\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}

$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}-3 & 8 \\ 8 & 12\end{bmatrix}
$$

Notice that we can write the constraint equation as follows:

$$
\frac{{x}_{1}^{2}}{{2}^{2}}+\frac{{x}_{2}^{2}}{{1}^{2}}=1
$$

This is an ellipse with semiaxes $a=2$ (along the ${x}_{1}$-axis) and $b=1$ (along the ${x}_{2}$-axis). If we introduce new variables

$\,$ ${y}_{1}=\frac{{x}_{1}}{2}\,$ and $\,{y}_{2}={x}_{2},$ 

the equation of the ellipse will transform into ${y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}=1$ or $‖y‖=1.$

So, introducing a change-of-coordinates matrix 

$$
P=\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix},
$$

 

we obtain that $x=Py.$ Substituting this into the expression of the quadratic form, we get

$$
Q(x)={x}^{T}\,Ax=(Py)^{T}A\,(Py)={y}^{T}\,({P}^{T}AP)y={Q}^{′}(y).
$$

 

As a result, since ${P}^{T}=P,$ the matrix of our quadratic form in new coordinates is 

$$
\begin{aligned}B & ={P}^{T}\,AP \\  & =PAP \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}-3 & 8 \\ 8 & 12\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-6 & 16 \\ 8 & 12\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-12 & 16 \\ 16 & 12\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}|B-\lambda I| & =0 \\ \begin{vmatrix}-12-\lambda  & 16 \\ 16 & 12-\lambda \end{vmatrix} & =0 \\ (-12-\lambda )(12-\lambda )-256 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-400 & =0 \\ (\lambda -20)(\lambda +20) & =0 \\ \lambda  & =20,\,-20\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$

$$"} :step/id #uuid "0b1d2308-18cf-5d1f-9792-a558d12df58b"} {:db/id 17592186422487 :step/content {:db/id 17592186198560 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "5991713d-c756-5033-8e5a-4d4d4ed69367" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186410175} {:answer/id #uuid "5dd4da5f-a084-569f-9c7d-65ba6f2fa2d4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186410176} {:answer/id #uuid "7a09264a-e062-5b32-b960-ce1fdd0596f3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186410180} {:answer/id #uuid "a18e2980-f7b3-5399-bdf5-0e6bab2f2d73" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186410183} {:answer/id #uuid "f781d714-082f-5b5c-9033-4f6f86bf4d82" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186410188}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186410176} :answer-field/id #uuid "9a69a67c-d671-56dc-a201-31f05adf2afb" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186410193}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "13f589cb-239b-530f-99ce-e58d907d8d98" :question/math-academy-id "q-136828" :question/problem "The minimum value of the quadratic form $Q(x)=-{x}_{1}^{2}-{x}_{2}^{2}+2{x}_{3}^{2}+2{x}_{1}{x}_{2},$ when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to $-2.$ Which of the following is a vector $x$ at which the minimum is attained?" :question/worked-solution "Let $A$ be the matrix corresponding to our quadratic form. $$
A=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 8 \\ 8 & 4\end{bmatrix}
$$

Notice that we can write the constraint equation as follows:

$$
\frac{{x}_{1}^{2}}{{2}^{2}}+\frac{{x}_{2}^{2}}{{1}^{2}}=1
$$

This is an ellipse with semiaxes $a=2$ (along the ${x}_{1}$-axis) and $b=1$ (along the ${x}_{2}$-axis). If we introduce new variables

$\,$ ${y}_{1}=\frac{{x}_{1}}{2}\,$ and $\,{y}_{2}={x}_{2},$

the equation of the ellipse will transform into ${y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}=1$ or $‖y‖=1.$

So, introducing a change-of-coordinate matrix 

$$
P=\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix},
$$

 

we obtain that $x=Py.$ Substituting this into the expression of the quadratic form, we get

$$
Q(x)={x}^{T}\,Ax=(Py)^{T}A\,(Py)={y}^{T}\,({P}^{T}AP)y={Q}^{′}(y).
$$

 

As a result, since ${P}^{T}=P,$ the matrix of our quadratic form in new coordinates is 

$$
\begin{aligned}B & ={P}^{T}\,AP \\  & =PAP \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 8 \\ 8 & 4\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 16 \\ 8 & 4\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}4 & 16 \\ 16 & 4\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we maximize ${Q}^{′}(y)$ when $‖y‖=1,$ as usual.

Since we are told that the maximum value of the quadratic form is $20,$ we have

$$
max\{{Q}^{′}(y)\,|\,‖y‖=1\}={\lambda }_{max}=20.
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}B-20I & =\begin{bmatrix}4 & 16 \\ 16 & 4\end{bmatrix}-20\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-16 & 16 \\ 16 & -16\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

$$
{u}_{\text{max}}=\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

$$

$$"} :step/id #uuid "5f8ca3b8-f2b1-5dda-8678-447d69f170dd" :step/next {:db/id 17592186442119}} {:db/id 17592186442118 :step/content {:db/id 17592186442114 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "2daa7e54-1e63-51fd-a83f-c84ab1ec9d14" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 3 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186442108} {:answer/id #uuid "44864e9b-3b6d-5ead-83f1-bf2b06aa99bb" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186442109} {:answer/id #uuid "47e556d0-ace5-5cd4-bce8-0b8edffbc42a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186442110} {:answer/id #uuid "b628a5cd-923e-5683-b6ff-5e0fdf447fc2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186442111} {:answer/id #uuid "f5d0fa24-c8cf-52e6-90a5-639dbcfbac97" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186442112}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186442108} :answer-field/id #uuid "9a8a33df-b62e-5f61-90ea-9cf4c2ac4093" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186442113}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "95026062-b044-5134-829b-f9813c55ce41" :question/math-academy-id "q-170503" :question/problem "The minimum value of the quadratic form $Q(x)={x}_{1}^{2}-9{x}_{2}^{2}-{x}_{3}^{2}-6{x}_{2}{x}_{3},$ when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to $-10.$ Which of the following is a vector $x$ at which the minimum is attained?" :question/worked-solution "Let $A$ be the matrix corresponding to our quadratic form. $$
A=\begin{bmatrix}4 & -18 \\ -18 & 9\end{bmatrix}
$$

Notice that we can write the constraint equation as follows:

$$
\frac{{x}_{1}^{2}}{{3}^{2}}+\frac{{x}_{2}^{2}}{{2}^{2}}=1
$$

This is an ellipse with semiaxes $a=3$ (along the ${x}_{1}$-axis) and $b=2$ (along the ${x}_{2}$-axis). If we introduce new variables

$\,$ ${y}_{1}=\frac{{x}_{1}}{3}\,$ and $\,{y}_{2}=\frac{{x}_{2}}{2},$

the equation of the ellipse will transform into ${y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}=1$ or $‖y‖=1.$

So, introducing a change-of-coordinate matrix 

$$
P=\begin{bmatrix}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix},
$$

 

we obtain that $x=Py.$ Substituting this into the expression of the quadratic form, we get

$$
Q(x)={x}^{T}\,Ax=(Py)^{T}A\,(Py)={y}^{T}\,({P}^{T}AP)y={Q}^{′}(y).
$$

As a result, since ${P}^{T}=P,$ the matrix of our quadratic form in new coordinates is 

$$
\begin{aligned}B & ={P}^{T}\,AP \\  & =PAP \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}4 & -18 \\ -18 & 9\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}12 & -54 \\ -36 & 18\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}36 & -108 \\ -108 & 36\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we minimize ${Q}^{′}(y)$ when $‖y‖=1,$ as usual.

Since we are told that the minimum value of the quadratic form is $-72,$ we have

$$
min\{{Q}^{′}(y)\,|\,‖y‖=1\}={\lambda }_{min}=-72.
$$

Next, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{\text{min}}=-72:$

$$
\begin{aligned}B-(-72)I & =\begin{bmatrix}36 & -108 \\ -108 & 36\end{bmatrix}+72\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}108 & -108 \\ -108 & 108\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

$$
{u}_{\text{min}}=\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

 

Finally, we map this vector back to the initial coordinate  system using the change-of-coordinates matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{\text{min}} & =P{u}_{\text{min}} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix}\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "e31c99b8-71b1-5ecf-a2b4-f70c0a3c9f33"}] :activity/title "Constrained Optimization of Quadratic Forms: Determining Where Extrema are Attained" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045464 :db/ident :activity.type/review} :db/id 17592186442107} {:db/id 17592186442115 :step/content {:db/id 17592186388524 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "659e6953-7cee-5b96-970f-fa397b86ee27" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186388526} {:answer/id #uuid "326d7edd-18b0-5a3b-b08d-0b77a365bbd8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186388527} {:answer/id #uuid "b7f8657c-b325-5796-aed4-2807063c509c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186388528} {:answer/id #uuid "aeba8346-f317-5cca-9056-2ca0f6aec458" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186388529} {:answer/id #uuid "76dc6aea-81a8-5e26-8056-6496647263c1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186388530}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186388530} :answer-field/id #uuid "43aa64d2-1826-583b-afa1-0a5a086f07b0" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186388525}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "aacc9ef4-d33c-5e64-bc37-708eaf7597fc" :question/math-academy-id "q-138090" :question/problem "The minimum value of the quadratic form $Q(x)=3{x}_{1}^{2}+{x}_{2}^{2}+3{x}_{3}^{2}-2{x}_{1}{x}_{3},$ when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to $1.$ Which of the following is a vector $x$ at which the minimum is attained?" :question/worked-solution "Let $A$ be the matrix corresponding to our quadratic form. $\,$ ${y}_{1}=\frac{{x}_{1}}{2}\,$ and $\,{y}_{2}={x}_{2},$

the equation of the ellipse will transform into ${y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}=1$ or $‖y‖=1.$

So, introducing a change-of-coordinate matrix 

$$
P=\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix},
$$

 

we obtain that $x=Py.$ Substituting this into the expression of the quadratic form, we get

$$
Q(x)={x}^{T}\,Ax=(Py)^{T}A\,(Py)={y}^{T}\,({P}^{T}AP)y={Q}^{′}(y).
$$

 

As a result, since ${P}^{T}=P,$ the matrix of our quadratic form in new coordinates is 

$$
\begin{aligned}B & ={P}^{T}\,AP \\  & =PAP \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 8 \\ 8 & 4\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 16 \\ 8 & 4\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}4 & 16 \\ 16 & 4\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we maximize ${Q}^{′}(y)$ when $‖y‖=1,$ as usual.

Since we are told that the maximum value of the quadratic form is $20,$ we have

$$
max\{{Q}^{′}(y)\,|\,‖y‖=1\}={\lambda }_{max}=20.
$$

Next, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{\text{max}}=20:$

$$
\begin{aligned}B-20I & =\begin{bmatrix}4 & 16 \\ 16 & 4\end{bmatrix}-20\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-16 & 16 \\ 16 & -16\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(B-20I)y=0$ gives the eigenvector $v=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.$ Dividing $v$ by its norm $‖v‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get  

$$
{u}_{\text{max}}=\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

 

Finally, we map this vector back to the initial coordinate  system using the change-of-coordinates matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{\text{max}} & =P{u}_{\text{max}} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "5f8ca3b8-f2b1-5dda-8678-447d69f170dd" :step/next {:db/id 17592186442119}} {:db/id 17592186442119 :step/content {:db/id 17592186378969 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "fea291ee-6497-5ad3-94fc-370909961651" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186378971} {:answer/id #uuid "d36d82c5-f411-510f-b777-9fca82b43277" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186378972} {:answer/id #uuid "34611fcc-fc75-5837-8815-4b563c9bc527" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186378973} {:answer/id #uuid "a08c13c3-88ad-550d-9cc8-cabd76a06564" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{5}\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186378974} {:answer/id #uuid "a6d304bd-fbab-5bd6-8c82-afcb34c6646e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186378975}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186378971} :answer-field/id #uuid "59fbad7d-97f9-581f-9baa-b0e8b8e58fe8" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186378970}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "6d3c8fe2-1d6d-57e9-bf5c-5e70cb30abf3" :question/math-academy-id "q-170561" :question/problem "The minimum value of $Q(x)=4{x}_{1}^{2}-36{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+9{x}_{2}^{2},$ when $4{x}_{1}^{2}+9{x}_{2}^{2}=36,$ is $-72.$ Which of the following is a vector $x$ at which the minimum is attained?" :question/worked-solution "First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$

$$

First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$

Finally, dividing $v$ by its norm $‖v‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get 

$$
{u}_{\text{max}}=\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "203e3740-ec3e-5f05-bb23-784b804df740" :step/next {:db/id 17592186502182}} {:db/id 17592186502174 :step/content {:db/id 17592186284645 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "58e43fd8-bedb-54d5-9723-4873762018ec" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "20" :db/id 17592186282444} {:answer/id #uuid "6080b967-b1e5-508e-9eb9-b06f08ffc56b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "21" :db/id 17592186282507} {:answer/id #uuid "b44dda1b-d74d-5302-ac25-2322f81791f4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "18" :db/id 17592186283250} {:answer/id #uuid "f9c243a3-3d78-5363-a946-67271923a982" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "9" :db/id 17592186283874} {:answer/id #uuid "fdac630b-fc7e-5910-8320-fe5c826d997e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "17" :db/id 17592186283913}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186282444} :answer-field/id #uuid "b28de760-832c-5bd3-997a-40bc410c2fcb" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186284244}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "315ff370-acb2-54c0-a94c-7932c53e50d7" :question/math-academy-id "q-170525" :question/problem "Find the maximum value of $Q(x)=-3{x}_{1}^{2}+16{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+12{x}_{2}^{2}$ given that ${x}_{1}^{2}+4{x}_{2}^{2}=4.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

![](images/c0/c0ed78e2e640611d70263e17a76eb4a13e9e2816efba02494b53e540d38065d6.png)" :question/worked-solution "As $x$ approaches $0,$ the value of $f(x)$ approaches $1.$ Consequently,

Remember, it does not matter that the actual value of $f(0)$ is $2.$ All that matters is that as $x$ approaches $0,$ the function $f(x)$ *looks like* it is getting closer and closer to $1$."} {:db/id 17592186069093 :question/id #uuid "4b624718-54bc-577c-bda1-017c8cf28e46" :question/math-academy-id "q-16261"} {:db/id 17592186069094 :question/id #uuid "9fa81edb-a127-519d-b9d1-759d92ae8eee" :question/math-academy-id "q-16266"} {:db/id 17592186068795 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186068534 :question/id #uuid "ab95d805-958c-5de3-99bd-41368cc57080" :question/math-academy-id "e-3"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "851c841f-6e27-5f81-8a0d-0f2439ae3e61" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186069274 :question/id #uuid "bbc80124-17c2-585a-8280-2acdc4c9d707" :question/math-academy-id "q-34840"} {:db/id 17592186069276 :question/id #uuid "7a5fdf11-243e-52ee-a4a4-937c2603f07f" :question/math-academy-id "q-34932"} {:db/id 17592186233090 :question/id #uuid "7dee115c-2d20-5ec2-8285-ad5a690a282f" :question/math-academy-id "q-106090"}] :knowledge-point/title "Identifying True Statements About Limits"} {:db/id 17592186068534 :question/id #uuid "ab95d805-958c-5de3-99bd-41368cc57080" :question/math-academy-id "e-3" :knowledge-point/_canonical-example [{:db/id 17592186068795 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "851c841f-6e27-5f81-8a0d-0f2439ae3e61" :knowledge-point/title "Identifying True Statements About Limits"}] :question/problem "Which of the following statements are true concerning the function $y=f(x)$ whose graph is shown below? 

I. $\lim_\limits{x\rightarrow \,0}f(x)=0$

II. $\lim_\limits{x\rightarrow \,3}f(x)=0$

III. $\lim_\limits{x\rightarrow \,-1}f(x)=\lim_\limits{x\rightarrow \,1}f(x)$

![](images/68/68241f3cd913cd91d10765499dc4ce4398fb3e8a81ec4bcfb65b47c0d77731d6.png)" :question/worked-solution "Let's analyze each statement in turn.

- Statement I is false. As $x$ approaches $0,$ the function $f(x)$ approaches the value $y=-1.$ Consequently, 

$$
\lim_\limits{x\rightarrow \,0}f(x)=-1.
$$

- Statement II is true. As $x$ approaches $3,$ the function $f(x)$ approaches the value $y=0.$ Consequently,

$$
\lim_\limits{x\rightarrow \,3}f(x)=0.
$$

- Statement III is false. As $x$ approaches $-1$ the function $f(x)$ approaches the value $y=2,$ and consequently

$$
\lim_\limits{x\rightarrow \,-1}f(x)=2.
$$

Similiarly, as $x$ approaches $1,$ the function $f(x)$ approaches the value $y=-2,$ and consequently

$$
\lim_\limits{x\rightarrow \,1}f(x)=-2.
$$

As a result,

$$
\lim_\limits{x\rightarrow \,-1}f(x)\ne\lim_\limits{x\rightarrow \,1}f(x).
$$

In conclusion, only statement II is true."} {:db/id 17592186069274 :question/id #uuid "bbc80124-17c2-585a-8280-2acdc4c9d707" :question/math-academy-id "q-34840"} {:db/id 17592186069276 :question/id #uuid "7a5fdf11-243e-52ee-a4a4-937c2603f07f" :question/math-academy-id "q-34932"} {:db/id 17592186233090 :question/id #uuid "7dee115c-2d20-5ec2-8285-ad5a690a282f" :question/math-academy-id "q-106090"} {:db/id 17592186050259} {:db/id 17592186050454} {:activity/expected-seconds 420.0 :activity/first-step {:db/id 17592186069709} :activity/id #uuid "c2e3d487-c981-55e6-ba25-8949d030cfa3" :activity/scope {:db/id 17592186050274 :topic/id #uuid "3bdc5470-2e0b-5f3c-9875-854353ddeb19" :topic/math-academy-id 461} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186069709 :step/content {:db/id 17592186069928 :tutorial/content "The **limit** of a function is the value that the function approaches. For example, the function $y=f(x)$ shown below is not defined at $x=2,$ as represented by the open circle there $-$ but when we *approach* $x=2$, we see that $f(x)$ *approaches* the value $y=1.$

![](images/f7/f7081d649c6cdfa0a19a0fb2de93b97ee700ad922f34530c7f3e5c2a3228c9fb.png)

As $x$ approaches $2$, the value of $f(x)$ approaches $1.$ In other words, the limit of $f(x),$ as $x$ approaches $2,$ is $1$. We can express this mathematically as 

$$
\lim_\limits{x\rightarrow 2}f(x)=1 \, .
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "e52528a2-ed6a-5d07-89d4-1a74d70eb6b9" :tutorial/math-academy-id 138 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "309b25fa-6c05-5421-8f80-e956e2975682" :step/math-academy-id 256 :step/next {:db/id 17592186069713}} {:db/id 17592186069713 :step/content {:db/id 17592186068791 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186068428 :question/id #uuid "282add39-5184-589e-bb7b-b87a59cd41e6" :question/math-academy-id "e-1"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "607443d5-b1dd-56b1-919b-fcc652ac3bc9" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048652} {:db/id 17592186049534}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186069091} {:db/id 17592186069092} {:db/id 17592186510368} {:db/id 17592186510431} {:db/id 17592186510453} {:db/id 17592186510473}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding a Limit When the Function Value is Not Defined"} :step/id #uuid "01fbff48-2ebc-5e33-a1b9-e271896f5340" :step/math-academy-id 257 :step/next {:db/id 17592186069717}} {:db/id 17592186069714 :step/content {:db/id 17592186068792 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186068533 :question/id #uuid "fb401fbe-a718-5ea7-b598-139ef837b047" :question/math-academy-id "e-2"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "e5fe1482-00d6-5738-b56a-8c082912d8d7" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186069093} {:db/id 17592186069094}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding a Limit When the Limit is Not Equal to the Function Value"} :step/id #uuid "9144fd7b-81d4-5cb5-8051-0619e464002c" :step/math-academy-id 260 :step/next {:db/id 17592186069718}} {:db/id 17592186069717 :step/content {:db/id 17592186069924 :tutorial/content "The limit of a function at some point has **nothing to do** with the value of the function at that point.

For example, the following functions $g(x)$ and $h(x)$ have *different values* at $x=2,$ but they have the *same limit* at $x=2.$

![](images/6a/6a73b74072a8a990c91a38553d519f4913370d34ef0251b7e45cc664da40517d.png)

![](images/06/06e150aacae774b4fe883a2750ef13cebbddf2ea871e5a682f2587c47a54615a.png)

The actual values of $g(2)$ and $h(2)$ are irrelevant for determining the limit at $x=2$. All that matters is what values the functions *look like* they are approaching as $x$ approaches $2$. 

Near $x=2,$ both $g(x)$ and $h(x)$ appear to be approaching $y=1$. Therefore,

$$
\lim_\limits{x\rightarrow 2}g(x)=1
$$

and

$$
\lim_\limits{x\rightarrow 2}h(x)=1 \, .
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "ea300af0-adfe-5df2-8b4d-ae23430245a7" :tutorial/math-academy-id 1333 :tutorial/title "Limit Has Nothing to Do With the Function Value"} :step/id #uuid "d21275b2-0542-5145-8c14-535a8c0db329" :step/math-academy-id 2621 :step/next {:db/id 17592186069714}} {:db/id 17592186069718 :step/content {:db/id 17592186068795 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186068534 :question/id #uuid "ab95d805-958c-5de3-99bd-41368cc57080" :question/math-academy-id "e-3"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "851c841f-6e27-5f81-8a0d-0f2439ae3e61" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186069274} {:db/id 17592186069276} {:db/id 17592186233090}] :knowledge-point/title "Identifying True Statements About Limits"} :step/id #uuid "0447b7b5-01f2-52cd-851f-84ee0d719836" :step/math-academy-id 263}] :activity/title "The Finite Limit of a Function" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186068988} {:db/id 17592186069709 :step/content {:db/id 17592186069928 :tutorial/content "The **limit** of a function is the value that the function approaches. For example, the function $y=f(x)$ shown below is not defined at $x=2,$ as represented by the open circle there $-$ but when we *approach* $x=2$, we see that $f(x)$ *approaches* the value $y=1.$

![](images/f7/f7081d649c6cdfa0a19a0fb2de93b97ee700ad922f34530c7f3e5c2a3228c9fb.png)

As $x$ approaches $2$, the value of $f(x)$ approaches $1.$ In other words, the limit of $f(x),$ as $x$ approaches $2,$ is $1$. We can express this mathematically as 

$$
\lim_\limits{x\rightarrow 2}f(x)=1 \, .
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "e52528a2-ed6a-5d07-89d4-1a74d70eb6b9" :tutorial/math-academy-id 138 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} {:db/id 17592186069713 :step/content {:db/id 17592186068791 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186068428 :question/id #uuid "282add39-5184-589e-bb7b-b87a59cd41e6" :question/math-academy-id "e-1"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "607443d5-b1dd-56b1-919b-fcc652ac3bc9" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048652} {:db/id 17592186049534}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186069091} {:db/id 17592186069092} {:db/id 17592186510368} {:db/id 17592186510431} {:db/id 17592186510453} {:db/id 17592186510473}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding a Limit When the Function Value is Not Defined"} :step/id #uuid "01fbff48-2ebc-5e33-a1b9-e271896f5340" :step/math-academy-id 257 :step/next {:db/id 17592186069717}} {:db/id 17592186069717 :step/content {:db/id 17592186069924 :tutorial/content "The limit of a function at some point has **nothing to do** with the value of the function at that point.

For example, the following functions $g(x)$ and $h(x)$ have *different values* at $x=2,$ but they have the *same limit* at $x=2.$

![](images/6a/6a73b74072a8a990c91a38553d519f4913370d34ef0251b7e45cc664da40517d.png)

![](images/06/06e150aacae774b4fe883a2750ef13cebbddf2ea871e5a682f2587c47a54615a.png)

The actual values of $g(2)$ and $h(2)$ are irrelevant for determining the limit at $x=2$. All that matters is what values the functions *look like* they are approaching as $x$ approaches $2$. 

Near $x=2,$ both $g(x)$ and $h(x)$ appear to be approaching $y=1$. Therefore,

$$
\lim_\limits{x\rightarrow 2}g(x)=1
$$

and

$$
\lim_\limits{x\rightarrow 2}h(x)=1 \, .
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "ea300af0-adfe-5df2-8b4d-ae23430245a7" :tutorial/math-academy-id 1333 :tutorial/title "Limit Has Nothing to Do With the Function Value"} :step/id #uuid "d21275b2-0542-5145-8c14-535a8c0db329" :step/math-academy-id 2621 :step/next {:db/id 17592186069714}} {:db/id 17592186069714 :step/content {:db/id 17592186068792 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186068533 :question/id #uuid "fb401fbe-a718-5ea7-b598-139ef837b047" :question/math-academy-id "e-2"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "e5fe1482-00d6-5738-b56a-8c082912d8d7" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186069093} {:db/id 17592186069094}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding a Limit When the Limit is Not Equal to the Function Value"} :step/id #uuid "9144fd7b-81d4-5cb5-8051-0619e464002c" :step/math-academy-id 260 :step/next {:db/id 17592186069718}} {:db/id 17592186069718 :step/content {:db/id 17592186068795 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186068534 :question/id #uuid "ab95d805-958c-5de3-99bd-41368cc57080" :question/math-academy-id "e-3"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "851c841f-6e27-5f81-8a0d-0f2439ae3e61" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186069274} {:db/id 17592186069276} {:db/id 17592186233090}] :knowledge-point/title "Identifying True Statements About Limits"} :step/id #uuid "0447b7b5-01f2-52cd-851f-84ee0d719836" :step/math-academy-id 263} {:db/id 17592186069924 :tutorial/content "The limit of a function at some point has **nothing to do** with the value of the function at that point.

:tutorial/content "An important family of distributions in probability and statistics is the **student's $t$-distribution** (or $t$-**distribution**). The diagram below shows the probability density functions for some members of this family.

![](images/08/08b2d66fda68155c6440568508dde075812a7fe0e7a855e1efe175df52830719.png)

Each family member has an associated positive integer parameter $k,$ known as the **degrees of freedom**. 

The probability density function of a student's $t$-distribution is symmetric and bell-shaped, similar to the standard normal distribution. However, $t$-distribution curves have fatter "tails." A consequence is that extreme events (i.e., events far from the mean) are more likely with a $t$-distribution than a standard normal distribution.

To see how the student's $t$-distribution comes about, consider a large random sample of size $n$

$$
X_1, \: X_2, \: \ldots, \: X_{n}
$$

 

drawn from a population with mean $\mu$ and variance $\sigma^2.$ According to the central limit theorem, 

$$
\dfrac{\overline{X}-\mu}{\sigma/\sqrt{n}} \approx N(0,1),
$$

where $\overline{X}$ is the sample mean. 

In reality, it's unlikely that the population variance $\sigma^2$ is known, in which case it must be estimated. 

Recall that an unbiased estimator for $\sigma^2,$ known as the sample variance, is given by

$$
S^2 = \dfrac{1}{n-1} \sum_{i=1}^n \left( X_i - \overline{X} \right)^2.
$$

If we estimate $\sigma^2$ using $S^2,$ then it can be shown that

$$
\dfrac{\overline{X}-\mu}{S/\sqrt{n}} \approx T_{n-1}
$$

where $T_{n-1}$ is a $t$-distributed random variable with $n-1$ degrees of freedom. 

The $t$-distribution is widely used in statistical estimation problems. We'll learn more about the practical applications of this important distribution in future lessons." :tutorial/id #uuid "86069b59-4cfe-5965-9f08-bd7cbfca0b5f" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6250 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "9e43698a-bcd5-5e90-92a2-a01cfff08635" :step/math-academy-id 37900 :step/next {:db/id 17592186163059}} {:db/id 17592186163059 :step/content {:db/id 17592186163323 :tutorial/content "When working with $t$-distributed random variables, we often want to find a value that gives rise to a specific probability. 

For example, let $X\sim T_{21}$ be a $t$-distributed random variable with $21$ degrees of freedom. Suppose we want to find the value of $x$ such that 

$$
P(X\geq x) = 0.01.
$$

In other words, we wish to find the $x$-value corresponding to the shaded area shown below.

![](images/3c/3c3ef041152494232ecb60408580965018132a024c406dcde0506ff519d7ed73.png)

To compute these probabilities, we use a **percentage points table**. A typical percentage points table for the student's $t$-distribution is shown below.

| $k \setminus p$ | $0.100$ | $0.050$ | $0.025$ | $0.010$ | $0.005$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\cdots$ | $\cdots$ | $\cdots$ | $\cdots$ | $\cdots$ | $\cdots$ |
| $20$ | $1.325$ | $1.725$ | $2.086$ | $2.528$ | $2.845$ |
| $21$ | $1.323$ | $1.721$ | $2.080$ | $2.518$ | $2.831$ |
| $22$ | $1.321$ | $1.717$ | $2.074$ | $2.508$ | $2.819$ |
| $\cdots$ | $\cdots$ | $\cdots$ | $\cdots$ | $\cdots$ | $\cdots$ |

The rows correspond to different degrees of freedom $k.$ Each cell in the table gives a value $x$ such that 

$$
P(X\geq x) = p
$$

for a particular value of $p.$

Since $X \sim T_{21},$ we focus on the table row corresponding to $k=21.$

| $k \setminus p$ | $0.100$ | $0.050$ | $0.025$ | $\bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}0.010}$ | $0.005$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $20$ | $1.325$ | $1.725$ | $2.086$ | $2.528$ | $2.845$ |
| $21$ | $1.323$ | $1.721$ | $2.080$ | $\bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{red}2.518}$ | $2.831$ |
| $22$ | $1.321$ | $1.717$ | $2.074$ | $2.508$ | $2.819$ |

From this row, we see that

$$
P(X \geq {\color{red}2.518}) = {\color{blue}0.01}.
$$

Therefore, $x = 2.518,$ shown below.
