:question/worked-solution "First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}xy & ={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-7 \\ 0 & ={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-xy-7\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y)={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-xy-7$, our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=0.$  

A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(2,-1)$ can be found by computing $∇f(2,-1).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(2,-1):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-xy-7)\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-xy-7)\,j \\  & =(2x-y)\,i+(2y-x)\,j \\ ∇f(2,-1) & =(2(2)-(-1))\,i+(2(-1)-2)\,j \\  & =5\,i-4\,j \\  & =⟨5,-4⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $∇f(2,-1)=⟨5,-4⟩$ is a normal vector to the curve at $(2,-1).$

Finally, the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to $v=⟨{v}_{x},{v}_{y}⟩$ and passes through the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0})$ can be written as:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-{x}_{0}}{{v}_{x}} & =\frac{y-{y}_{0}}{{v}_{y}} \\ \frac{x-2}{5} & =\frac{y-(-1)}{-4} \\ -4(x-2) & =5(y+1) \\ -4x-5y+8-5 & =0 \\ -4x-5y+3 & =0 \\ 4x+5y-3 & =0\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186265960 :question/id #uuid "c80428ab-daca-506e-aca7-d4e40b0d604c" :question/math-academy-id "q-130718" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186124462 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "3b2f7fab-cebe-519a-83e3-a0831cac289d" :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Equation of the Normal Line to a Plane Curve Using the Gradient"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "076ccae2-d102-5ad8-b1c2-ac28978e3e97" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "x-3y=0" :db/id 17592186263068} {:answer/id #uuid "1b3882de-2108-52bf-b5e1-4c3304b9a5c3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "x-y-2=0" :db/id 17592186263257} {:answer/id #uuid "a00ce4f7-3888-5dba-a972-b715615f1421" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "x+y-4=0" :db/id 17592186264362} {:answer/id #uuid "cf2a0770-0459-500c-aa32-352ae1667e03" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "x+3y-6=0" :db/id 17592186264813} {:answer/id #uuid "d493ac59-d9ae-5896-bd9e-006d111d56b9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "2x+y-7=0" :db/id 17592186264850}] :answer-field/correct {:answer/id #uuid "a00ce4f7-3888-5dba-a972-b715615f1421" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "x+y-4=0" :db/id 17592186264362} :answer-field/id #uuid "cb7e101e-fe81-5db4-a578-c892744685d7" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186265605}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "Consider the plane curve ${x}^{2}-3{y}^{2}=6.$  Find the equation of the normal line to the curve at the point $(3,1).$" :question/worked-solution "If we set $f(x,y)={x}^{2}-3{y}^{2},$ our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=6.$  

A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(3,1)$ can be found by computing $∇f(3,1).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(3,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}-3{y}^{2})\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}-3{y}^{2})\,j \\  & =2x\,i-6y\,j \\ ∇f(3,1) & =2(3)\,i-6(1)\,j \\  & =6\,i-6\,j \\  & =⟨6,-6⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $∇f(3,1)=⟨6,-6⟩$ is a normal vector to the curve at $(3,1).$

Finally, the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to $v=⟨{v}_{x},{v}_{y}⟩$ and passes through the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0})$ can be written as:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-{x}_{0}}{{v}_{x}} & =\frac{y-{y}_{0}}{{v}_{y}} \\ \frac{x-3}{6} & =\frac{y-1}{(-6)} \\ -6(x-3) & =6(y-1) \\ -(x-3) & =y-1 \\ -x+3 & =y-1 \\ x+y-4 & =0\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186265961 :question/id #uuid "d42d4bf9-4eef-57b6-b4ed-d5448bfe2b61" :question/math-academy-id "q-130723" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0029eb5c-a868-5b35-b213-3fa6e3a04a1d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2x-y-5=0" :db/id 17592186263005} {:answer/id #uuid "2d9853cb-1b4d-5d99-b740-f207d47a13c3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x-3y-5=0" :db/id 17592186263384} {:answer/id #uuid "62cb3b0d-c5e0-5140-9b14-0b73eecbc9ac" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x+y-1=0" :db/id 17592186263854} {:answer/id #uuid "70e32100-046e-5e0e-b9f2-eac7fe211b6f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x-2y-4=0" :db/id 17592186263976} {:answer/id #uuid "b5d5900d-9aee-5b56-aa97-4e95d9c8f10a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x+2y=0" :db/id 17592186264575}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186263005} :answer-field/id #uuid "263638a6-9832-58e0-a5f7-da0d13d29e2d" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186265316}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "Consider the plane curve $4xy+2{x}^{2}=x+2y.$  Find the equation of the normal line to the curve at the point $(2,-1).$" :question/worked-solution "First, we bring all variables to one side: 

$$
\begin{aligned}4xy+2{x}^{2} & =x+2y \\ 4xy+2{x}^{2}-x-2y & =0\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y)=4xy+2{x}^{2}-x-2y$, our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=0.$   

A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(2,-1)$ can be found by computing $∇f(2,-1).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(2,-1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(4xy+2{x}^{2}-x-2y)\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(4xy+2{x}^{2}-x-2y)\,j \\  & =(4y+4x-1)\,i+(4x-2)\,j \\ ∇f(2,-1) & =(4(-1)+4(2)-1)\,i+(4(2)-2)\,j \\  & =3\,i+6\,j \\  & =⟨3,6⟩\end{aligned}
$$

 Hence, $∇f(2,-1)=⟨3,6⟩$ is a normal vector to the curve at $(2,-1).$

$$
\begin{aligned}2y-x & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{x}{2y}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{x}{2y})-2y+x & =0\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{x}{2y})-2y+x,$ our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=0.$  

A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(2,1)$ can be found by computing $∇f(2,1).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(2,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{x}{2y})-2y+x)i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{x}{2y})-2y+x)j \\  & =(\frac{2y}{x}\cdot \frac{1}{2y}+1)i+(\frac{2y}{x}\cdot (-\frac{x}{2{y}^{2}})-2)j \\  & =(\frac{1}{x}+1)i+(-\frac{1}{y}-2)j \\ ∇f(2,1) & =(\frac{1}{2}+1)i+(-\frac{1}{1}-2)j \\  & =\frac{3}{2}\,i-3\,j \\  & =⟨\frac{3}{2},-3⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $∇f(3,1)=⟨\frac{3}{2},-3⟩$ is a normal vector to the curve at $(2,1).$

Finally, the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to $v=⟨{v}_{x},{v}_{y}⟩$ and passes through the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0})$ can be written as:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-{x}_{0}}{{v}_{x}} & =\frac{y-{y}_{0}}{{v}_{y}} \\ \frac{x-2}{(\frac{3}{2})} & =\frac{y-1}{(-3)} \\ -3(x-2) & =\frac{3}{2}(y-1) \\ -6(x-2) & =3(y-1) \\ -2(x-2) & =y-1 \\ -2x+4 & =y-1 \\ 2x+y-5 & =0\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186423051 :question/id #uuid "6f16c0b1-b80b-5067-adaf-a65b04fb7bb4" :question/math-academy-id "q-130721" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "364ddf2b-cdd1-5e21-88c2-478a7d637e32" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2x+3y-4=0" :db/id 17592186423045} {:answer/id #uuid "415a3975-289f-5c0a-aa48-bc85b813f82a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2x-y-4=0" :db/id 17592186423046} {:answer/id #uuid "6321cb0e-8e68-5a7b-9a36-ac871cc17b89" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x+2y-2=0" :db/id 17592186423047} {:answer/id #uuid "82ce7cc2-be21-5dc4-9b04-e941ddd03d24" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x-3y-2=0" :db/id 17592186423048} {:answer/id #uuid "ba63a292-9d83-540d-ac68-00ce4812ebb4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x+3y-2=0" :db/id 17592186423049}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186423048} :answer-field/id #uuid "02401848-522e-501b-82ff-6e5cb3f48ab9" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186423050}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "Consider the plane curve ${e}^{{x}^{2}y}={y}^{2}-{x}^{3}+9.$  Find the equation of the normal line to the curve at the point $(2,0).$" :question/worked-solution "First, we bring all variables to one side:

$f(x,y,z)={x}^{2}y+{y}^{2}z+{z}^{2}x.$ Then, our surface can be viewed as the level surface $f(x,y,z)=5.$ 

A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point $(1,-1,2)$ can be found by computing $∇f(1,-1,2).$

$$

Finally, the vector equation of the line that is parallel to $∇f(1,-1,2)$ and passes through the point $(1,-1,2)$ can be written as

$$

$$

surface $x={y}^{2}-{z}^{2}$ at the point $(3,2,1).$" :question/worked-solution "First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & ={y}^{2}-{z}^{2} \\ {y}^{2}-{z}^{2}-x & =0\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y,z)={y}^{2}-{z}^{2}-x$, our surface can be viewed as the level surface $f(x,y,z)=0.$ 

A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point $(3,2,1)$ can be found by computing $∇f(3,2,1).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(3,2,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({y}^{2}-{z}^{2}-x)i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({y}^{2}-{z}^{2}-x)j+\frac{∂}{∂z}({y}^{2}-{z}^{2}-x)k \\  & =-i+2y\,j-2z\,k \\ ∇f(3,2,1) & =-i+2(2)\,j-2(1)\,k \\  & =-i+4\,j-2\,k \\  & =⟨-1,4,-2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to $v=⟨{v}_{x},{v}_{y},{v}_{z}⟩$ and passes through the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ can be written as:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-{x}_{0}}{{v}_{x}}=\frac{y-{y}_{0}}{{v}_{y}}=\frac{z-{z}_{0}}{{v}_{z}} \\ \frac{x-3}{(-1)}=\frac{y-2}{4}=\frac{z-1}{(-2)} \\ \frac{x-3}{1}=\frac{y-2}{-4}=\frac{z-1}{2} \\ x-3=\frac{2-y}{4}=\frac{z-1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186338940 :question/id #uuid "5b6f2dff-79f7-5470-a733-d919ff7c2a24" :question/math-academy-id "q-71411"} {:db/id 17592186373006 :question/id #uuid "a1e0fe3a-1bd3-5ee4-ab1a-74e46b29c2c8" :question/math-academy-id "q-36351" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "9dd151b9-79f9-5a66-8557-365b16a9535a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{x-1}{2}=\frac{y+1}{2}=-z" :db/id 17592186373008} {:answer/id #uuid "e407b4cd-b0e3-5ef2-a3e1-1c2c4a208e39" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x-1=\frac{y}{2}=-z" :db/id 17592186373009} {:answer/id #uuid "2042c239-c608-579c-a356-780f349dc015" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{x-1}{2}=y+1=-z" :db/id 17592186373010} {:answer/id #uuid "e11362e5-c68a-5d93-8627-d0fe7c1b9816" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x-1=\frac{y+1}{2}=z" :db/id 17592186373011} {:answer/id #uuid "dad753bd-efc6-5cc5-bf02-04d7fe01e2cb" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{x+1}{2}=\frac{y-1}{2}=z" :db/id 17592186373012}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186373010} :answer-field/id #uuid "f074ec94-f4ab-59e4-98e4-6833b7d43d47" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186373007}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/problem "Find the equation of the normal line to the surface $z=\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x+y)$ at the point $(1,-1,0).$" :question/worked-solution "First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}z & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x+y) \\ 0 & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x+y)-z\end{aligned}
$$

 

So, if we set $f(x,y,z)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x+y)-z$, then our surface can be viewed as the level surface $f(x,y,z)=0.$ 

A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point $(1,-1,0)$ can be found by computing $∇f(1,-1,0).$

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(1,-1,0):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x+y)-z)i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x+y)-z)j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x+y)-z)k \\  & =\frac{2}{2x+y}\text{ }i+\frac{1}{2x+y}\text{ }j-1\text{ }k \\ ∇f(1,-1,0) & =\frac{2}{2(1)+(-1)}\text{ }i+\frac{1}{2(1)+(-1)}\text{ }j-k \\  & =2\text{ }i+\,j-k \\  & =⟨2,\,1,\,-1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, by using the symmetric form of the equation of the line that is parallel to the vector $v=⟨{v}_{x},{v}_{y},{v}_{z}⟩$ and passes through the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$,  we get: 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-{x}_{0}}{{v}_{x}}=\frac{y-{y}_{0}}{{v}_{y}}=\frac{z-{z}_{0}}{{v}_{z}} \\ \frac{x-1}{2}=\frac{y-(-1)}{1}=\frac{z-0}{-1} \\ \frac{x-1}{2}=y+1=-z\end{aligned}

:question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "Find a vector equation of the normal line to the surface $\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y+z)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)-xyz$ at the point $(1,0,1).$" :question/worked-solution "First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y+z) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)-xyz \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y+z)+xyz & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y,z)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y+z)+xyz$, our surface can be viewed as the level surface $f(x,y,z)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(2).$ 

A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point $(1,0,1)$ can be found by computing $∇f(1,0,1).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(1,0,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y+z)+xyz)i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y+z)+xyz)j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y+z)+xyz)k \\  & =(\frac{1}{x+y+z}+yz)\text{ }i+(\frac{1}{x+y+z}+xz)\text{ }j+(\frac{1}{x+y+z}+xy)\text{ }k \\ ∇f(1,0,1) & =(\frac{1}{1+0+1}+(0)(1))\,i+(\frac{1}{1+0+1}+(1)(1))\text{ }j+(\frac{1}{1+0+1}+(1)(0))\,k \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\,i+\frac{3}{2}\,j+\frac{1}{2}\,k \\  & =⟨\frac{1}{2},\frac{3}{2},\frac{1}{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the vector equation of the line that is parallel to $∇f(1,0,1)$ and passes through the point $(1,0,1)$ can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =⟨1,0,1⟩+t\,∇f(1,0,1)=⟨1,0,1⟩+t\,⟨\frac{1}{2},\frac{3}{2},\frac{1}{2}⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

where $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).$"} {:db/id 17592186510365 :question/id #uuid "056dc885-9ad1-5245-b1aa-85becac66885" :question/math-academy-id "q-131125"} {:db/id 17592186510409 :question/id #uuid partial derivatives $f_x,$ $f_y$ exist and are continuous in a neighborhood of a point $P(x_0,y_0)$ in the domain of the function, and if $\nabla \! f(x_0,y_0) \neq \mathbf 0,$ then we have the following result:

*$\nabla \! f(x_0,y_0)$ is a normal vector to the level curve $C$ that passes through the point $P.$ *

This property is one of the most important facts in multivariable calculus since it gives a fundamental  link between
calculus and geometry!

Let's illustrate this property with a concrete example. Consider the paraboloid $z = f (x, y)=  x^2 + y^2$ and the level curve $\color{red}C$ of $f(x,y)$ corresponding to the point $P(1,-1).$  It is easy to see that  $\color{red}C$ is a circle of radius $\sqrt{2}$ with equation $x^2+y^2 = 2.$ 

![](images/f2/f2461dbfcde2403e6ed7de9d6288d33a4deb52319d35b7036628c3fa8b3789dc.png)

In this particular instance, the property says that

*$\nabla \! f(1,-1)$ is a normal vector to the level curve $\color{red}C$ that passes through the point $P(1,-1).$ *

![](images/48/481b68af522b9144e232d9c775f734cd998b31a21571cbfd983c23d0f68c3688.png)

Looking at the situation in the $xy$-plane, we see the following:

![](images/ce/ceb353d5164d6aa089a37e77c9469d747ef4430e363e42f9d35ee6d769d9a4e4.png)

Let's verify that $\nabla f(1,-1)$ is a normal line to the level curve $C$ at the point $P(1,-1).$

- First, computing the gradient, we find that $\nabla f = \langle 2x, 2y \rangle.$ Therefore, 

$$
\nabla f(1,-1) = \langle 2, -2 \rangle.
$$

To illustrate, let's consider the function  

$$
w = f (x, y, z)= \dfrac 1 2\left(x^2 + y^2 + z^2-1\right).
$$

 

The level surface corresponding to $w=0$ is the sphere $\mathcal S$ with equation $x^2 + y^2 +z^2 =1.$ 

The point $P(0,0,1)$ lies on $\mathcal S.$ Computing $\nabla f(0,0,1),$ we get

$$
\eqalign{
\nabla f(x,y,z) &= \langle f_x, \: f_y, \:f_z\rangle \[5pt]
&= \dfrac12\langle2x, \: 2y, \: 2z\rangle\[5pt]
&= \langle x, \: y, \: z\rangle\[10pt]

\nabla f(0,0,1) &= \langle 0,\: 0,\: 1 \rangle.
}

17592186125735 :tutorial/content "Given a function $z=f(x,y)$, if both partial derivatives $f_x,$ $f_y$ exist and are continuous in a neighborhood of a point $P(x_0,y_0)$ in the domain of the function, and if $\nabla \! f(x_0,y_0) \neq \mathbf 0,$ then we have the following result:

*$\nabla \! f(x_0,y_0)$ is a normal vector to the level curve $C$ that passes through the point $P.$ *

This property is one of the most important facts in multivariable calculus since it gives a fundamental  link between
calculus and geometry!

Let's illustrate this property with a concrete example. Consider the paraboloid $z = f (x, y)=  x^2 + y^2$ and the level curve $\color{red}C$ of $f(x,y)$ corresponding to the point $P(1,-1).$  It is easy to see that  $\color{red}C$ is a circle of radius $\sqrt{2}$ with equation $x^2+y^2 = 2.$ 

![](images/f2/f2461dbfcde2403e6ed7de9d6288d33a4deb52319d35b7036628c3fa8b3789dc.png)

In this particular instance, the property says that

*$\nabla \! f(1,-1)$ is a normal vector to the level curve $\color{red}C$ that passes through the point $P(1,-1).$ *

![](images/48/481b68af522b9144e232d9c775f734cd998b31a21571cbfd983c23d0f68c3688.png)

Looking at the situation in the $xy$-plane, we see the following:

![](images/ce/ceb353d5164d6aa089a37e77c9469d747ef4430e363e42f9d35ee6d769d9a4e4.png)

Let's verify that $\nabla f(1,-1)$ is a normal line to the level curve $C$ at the point $P(1,-1).$

- First, computing the gradient, we find that $\nabla f = \langle 2x, 2y \rangle.$ Therefore, 

$$
\nabla f(1,-1) = \langle 2, -2 \rangle.
$$

- Then, using elementary calculus, we can show that the equation of the tangent to $C$ at $P$ is $y=x-2.$ Since this line has slope $m=1,$ it follows that the vector $\langle 1,1 \rangle$  is parallel to the level curve.

- Finally, taking the dot product between the gradient and the tangent vector, we obtain

$$
\nabla f(1,-1)\cdot  \langle 1,1 \rangle = \langle 2, -2\rangle \cdot \langle 1,1 \rangle = 0.
$$

This means that $\nabla f(1,-1)$ is *perpendicular* to the tangent line to $C$ at $(1,-1).$" :tutorial/id #uuid "68a96106-e224-5989-af04-8d464b6e58d5" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2499 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "35b375f8-a01b-56db-97b7-ac88f2a7883a" :step/math-academy-id 11200 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125306}} {:db/id 17592186125735 :tutorial/content "Given a function $z=f(x,y)$, if both partial derivatives $f_x,$ $f_y$ exist and are continuous in a neighborhood of a point $P(x_0,y_0)$ in the domain of the function, and if $\nabla \! f(x_0,y_0) \neq \mathbf 0,$ then we have the following result:

that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(-2,-3,1).$" :question/worked-solution "A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(-2,-3,1)$ can be found by computing 
$∇f(-2,-3,1).$ 

So, we first find the gradient and evaluate it at $(x,y,z)=(-2,-3,1):$

$$

Therefore, $3\,i-2\,j$ is perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(1,-1,-1).$"} :step/id #uuid "1470ea07-3b96-5965-8beb-c2e0041edd4a"} {:db/id 17592186423053 :step/content {:db/id 17592186373139 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "fd12d1d6-f236-57c3-bd6d-b0a476bef5f3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x-1=y+1=\frac{z-1}{-1}" :db/id 17592186373141} {:answer/id #uuid "e0818182-cafe-552e-a4a0-98b0c1314881" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x+1=y+1=\frac{z+1}{-1}" :db/id 17592186373142} {:answer/id #uuid "df5c957f-327c-59b5-a275-854f61c6c1b1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x+1=y-1=z-1" :db/id 17592186373143} {:answer/id #uuid "4643467a-d570-58d2-ac66-45f1f209b1ac" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x+1=y+1=z-1" :db/id 17592186373144} {:answer/id #uuid "c777726a-c485-5a89-bead-338bff4761cc" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x+1=y+1=\frac{z-1}{-1}" :db/id 17592186373145}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186373145} :answer-field/id #uuid "31f112b8-6ada-53ff-b6b3-be00d57b76b2" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186373140}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "d41ffa1d-b743-559f-b433-9851a75bb790" :question/math-academy-id "q-71408" :question/problem "Find the equation of the normal line to the surface ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}=3$ at the point $(-1,-1,1).$" :question/worked-solution "If we set $f(x,y,z)={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}$, our surface can be viewed as the level surface $f(x,y,z)=3.$ 

A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point $(-1,-1,1)$ can be found by computing $∇f(-1,-1,1).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(-1,-1,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2})i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2})j+\frac{∂}{∂z}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2})k \\  & =2x\text{ }i+2y\text{ }j+2z\text{ }k \\ ∇f(-1,-1,1) & =2(-1)\text{ }i+2(-1)\text{ }j+2(1)\text{ }k \\  & =-2\,i-2\,j+2\,k \\  & =⟨-2,-2,2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to $v=⟨{v}_{x},{v}_{y},{v}_{z}⟩$ and passes through the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ can be written as:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-{x}_{0}}{{v}_{x}}=\frac{y-{y}_{0}}{{v}_{y}}=\frac{z-{z}_{0}}{{v}_{z}} \\ \frac{x-(-1)}{-2}=\frac{y-(-1)}{-2}=\frac{z-1}{2} \\ \frac{x+1}{-2}=\frac{y+1}{-2}=\frac{z-1}{2} \\ \frac{x+1}{1}=\frac{y+1}{1}=\frac{z-1}{-1} \\ x+1=y+1=\frac{z-1}{-1}\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "20ee70ca-88be-504d-b7aa-237d8d22e58a" :step/next {:db/id 17592186423054}} {:db/id 17592186423054 :step/content {:db/id 17592186423051 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "364ddf2b-cdd1-5e21-88c2-478a7d637e32" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2x+3y-4=0" :db/id 17592186423045} {:answer/id #uuid "415a3975-289f-5c0a-aa48-bc85b813f82a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2x-y-4=0" :db/id 17592186423046} {:answer/id #uuid "6321cb0e-8e68-5a7b-9a36-ac871cc17b89" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x+2y-2=0" :db/id 17592186423047} {:answer/id #uuid "82ce7cc2-be21-5dc4-9b04-e941ddd03d24" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x-3y-2=0" :db/id 17592186423048} {:answer/id #uuid "ba63a292-9d83-540d-ac68-00ce4812ebb4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x+3y-2=0" :db/id 17592186423049}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186423048} :answer-field/id #uuid "02401848-522e-501b-82ff-6e5cb3f48ab9" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186423050}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "6f16c0b1-b80b-5067-adaf-a65b04fb7bb4" :question/math-academy-id "q-130721" :question/problem "Consider the plane curve ${e}^{{x}^{2}y}={y}^{2}-{x}^{3}+9.$  Find the equation of the normal line to the curve at the point $(2,0).$" :question/worked-solution "First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{{x}^{2}y} & ={y}^{2}-{x}^{3}+9 \\ {e}^{{x}^{2}y}-{y}^{2}+{x}^{3} & =9\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y)={e}^{{x}^{2}y}-{y}^{2}+{x}^{3}$, our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=9.$  

A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(2,0)$ can be found by computing $∇f(2,0).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(2,0):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({e}^{{x}^{2}y}-{y}^{2}+{x}^{3})i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({e}^{{x}^{2}y}-{y}^{2}+{x}^{3})j \\  & =(2xy{e}^{{x}^{2}y}+3{x}^{2})i+({x}^{2}{e}^{{x}^{2}y}-2y)j \\ ∇f(2,0) & =(2(2)(0){e}^{({2}^{2})(0)}+3({2}^{2}))i+(({2}^{2}){e}^{({2}^{2})(0)}-2(0))j \\  & =12\,i+4\,j \\  & =⟨12,4⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $∇f(2,0)=⟨12,4⟩$ is a normal vector to the curve at $(2,0).$

Finally, the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to $v=⟨{v}_{x},{v}_{y}⟩$ and passes through the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0})$ can be written as:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-{x}_{0}}{{v}_{x}} & =\frac{y-{y}_{0}}{{v}_{y}} \\ \frac{x-2}{12} & =\frac{y-0}{4} \\ 4(x-2) & =12y \\ x-2 & =3y \\ x-3y-2 & =0\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "68e1c4ea-40a6-5a21-ae75-071da89109f6" :step/next {:db/id 17592186423052}} {:db/id 17592186423055 :step/content {:db/id 17592186373006 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "9dd151b9-79f9-5a66-8557-365b16a9535a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{x-1}{2}=\frac{y+1}{2}=-z" :db/id 17592186373008} {:answer/id #uuid "e407b4cd-b0e3-5ef2-a3e1-1c2c4a208e39" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x-1=\frac{y}{2}=-z" :db/id 17592186373009} {:answer/id #uuid "2042c239-c608-579c-a356-780f349dc015" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{x-1}{2}=y+1=-z" :db/id 17592186373010} {:answer/id #uuid "e11362e5-c68a-5d93-8627-d0fe7c1b9816" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x-1=\frac{y+1}{2}=z" :db/id 17592186373011} {:answer/id #uuid "dad753bd-efc6-5cc5-bf02-04d7fe01e2cb" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{x+1}{2}=\frac{y-1}{2}=z" :db/id 17592186373012}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186373010} :answer-field/id #uuid "f074ec94-f4ab-59e4-98e4-6833b7d43d47" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186373007}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "a1e0fe3a-1bd3-5ee4-ab1a-74e46b29c2c8" :question/math-academy-id "q-36351" :question/problem "Find the equation of the normal line to the surface $z=\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x+y)$ at the point $(1,-1,0).$" :question/worked-solution "First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}z & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x+y) \\ 0 & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x+y)-z\end{aligned}
$$

 

So, if we set $f(x,y,z)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x+y)-z$, then our surface can be viewed as the level surface $f(x,y,z)=0.$ 

A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point $(1,-1,0)$ can be found by computing $∇f(1,-1,0).$

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(1,-1,0):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x+y)-z)i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x+y)-z)j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x+y)-z)k \\  & =\frac{2}{2x+y}\text{ }i+\frac{1}{2x+y}\text{ }j-1\text{ }k \\ ∇f(1,-1,0) & =\frac{2}{2(1)+(-1)}\text{ }i+\frac{1}{2(1)+(-1)}\text{ }j-k \\  & =2\text{ }i+\,j-k \\  & =⟨2,\,1,\,-1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, by using the symmetric form of the equation of the line that is parallel to the vector $v=⟨{v}_{x},{v}_{y},{v}_{z}⟩$ and passes through the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$,  we get: 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-{x}_{0}}{{v}_{x}}=\frac{y-{y}_{0}}{{v}_{y}}=\frac{z-{z}_{0}}{{v}_{z}} \\ \frac{x-1}{2}=\frac{y-(-1)}{1}=\frac{z-0}{-1} \\ \frac{x-1}{2}=y+1=-z\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "6fe264a7-c045-5612-8184-b7672b802421" :step/next {:db/id 17592186423056}} {:db/id 17592186423056 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125189 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "a68112ca-e7ee-5f12-8c6b-6f964b2fce64" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-3\,i+4j+2\,k" :db/id 17592186398915} {:answer/id #uuid "5739b0cd-fba7-5818-952f-616d15f8cd4f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\,i-4j+3\,k" :db/id 17592186398916} {:answer/id #uuid "fc61dd7b-3fa9-5347-ad13-eae563990528" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2\,i-j+3\,k" :db/id 17592186398917} {:answer/id #uuid "9e270cd2-2ed5-5ff9-a8d2-046b4683fe91" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "12\,i+4j+3\,k" :db/id 17592186398918} {:answer/id #uuid "12f59294-d897-5332-9fd4-6a0a58840be5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3\,i-2j+6\,k" :db/id 17592186398919}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186398916} :answer-field/id #uuid "027e0dd0-8fb0-53bb-95b9-27c1e0e20a6a" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186398914}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "15fe86f3-62bf-5e0d-8567-00ad11df9f8d" :question/math-academy-id "q-65167" :question/problem "For the function $f(x,y,z)=x{y}^{2}-2yz+z$, find a vector that's perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(1,-1,1).$" :question/worked-solution "A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(1,-1,1)$ can be found by computing

$$
\begin{aligned}z & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x+y) \\ 0 & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x+y)-z\end{aligned}
$$

point $(2,-1).$" :question/worked-solution "First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}xy & ={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-7 \\ 0 & ={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-xy-7\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y)={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-xy-7$, our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=0.$  

A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(2,-1)$ can be found by computing $∇f(2,-1).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(2,-1):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-xy-7)\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-xy-7)\,j \\  & =(2x-y)\,i+(2y-x)\,j \\ ∇f(2,-1) & =(2(2)-(-1))\,i+(2(-1)-2)\,j \\  & =5\,i-4\,j \\  & =⟨5,-4⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $∇f(2,-1)=⟨5,-4⟩$ is a normal vector to the curve at $(2,-1).$

Finally, the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to $v=⟨{v}_{x},{v}_{y}⟩$ and passes through the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0})$ can be written as:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-{x}_{0}}{{v}_{x}} & =\frac{y-{y}_{0}}{{v}_{y}} \\ \frac{x-2}{5} & =\frac{y-(-1)}{-4} \\ -4(x-2) & =5(y+1) \\ -4x-5y+8-5 & =0 \\ -4x-5y+3 & =0 \\ 4x+5y-3 & =0\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "053dd984-66f7-5e60-a777-6ca3631e9fa4" :step/next {:db/id 17592186497423}} {:db/id 17592186497423 :step/content {:db/id 17592186398954 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "4643060a-8d1d-5789-a362-102d70382db9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2\,i+2\,j+2\,k" :db/id 17592186398956} {:answer/id #uuid "8070bb66-d16c-505c-85ee-2a417bc81d72" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2\,i+2\,j+k" :db/id 17592186398957} {:answer/id #uuid "0bdcaf70-4358-5973-a594-026557c83288" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2\,i+j+2\,k" :db/id 17592186398958} {:answer/id #uuid "61e68fe8-0332-53d0-b214-d38a39b52899" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "i+2\,j+2\,k" :db/id 17592186398959} {:answer/id #uuid "b9c9c882-083f-5978-8947-be71bba2f10e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2\,i+j+k" :db/id 17592186398960}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186398956} :answer-field/id #uuid "91095769-6695-5735-bdf7-d8d4bfdca38b" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186398955}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "58a67c4a-aa8b-5b64-8268-56928e2716de" :question/math-academy-id "q-71399" :question/problem "For the function $f(x,y,z)={e}^{x+y+z}+x+y+z$, find a vector that's perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(0,0,0).$" :question/worked-solution "A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(0,0,0)$ can be found by computing

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y+z) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)-xyz \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y+z)+xyz & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y,z)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y+z)+xyz$, our surface can be viewed as the level surface $f(x,y,z)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(2).$ 

A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point $(1,0,1)$ can be found by computing $∇f(1,0,1).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(1,0,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y+z)+xyz)i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y+z)+xyz)j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y+z)+xyz)k \\  & =(\frac{1}{x+y+z}+yz)\text{ }i+(\frac{1}{x+y+z}+xz)\text{ }j+(\frac{1}{x+y+z}+xy)\text{ }k \\ ∇f(1,0,1) & =(\frac{1}{1+0+1}+(0)(1))\,i+(\frac{1}{1+0+1}+(1)(1))\text{ }j+(\frac{1}{1+0+1}+(1)(0))\,k \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\,i+\frac{3}{2}\,j+\frac{1}{2}\,k \\  & =⟨\frac{1}{2},\frac{3}{2},\frac{1}{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the vector equation of the line that is parallel to $∇f(1,0,1)$ and passes through the point $(1,0,1)$ can be written as

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}xy & ={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-7 \\ 0 & ={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-xy-7\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y)={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-xy-7$, our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=0.$  

A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(2,-1)$ can be found by computing $∇f(2,-1).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(2,-1):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-xy-7)\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-xy-7)\,j \\  & =(2x-y)\,i+(2y-x)\,j \\ ∇f(2,-1) & =(2(2)-(-1))\,i+(2(-1)-2)\,j \\  & =5\,i-4\,j \\  & =⟨5,-4⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $∇f(2,-1)=⟨5,-4⟩$ is a normal vector to the curve at $(2,-1).$

Finally, the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to $v=⟨{v}_{x},{v}_{y}⟩$ and passes through the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0})$ can be written as:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-{x}_{0}}{{v}_{x}} & =\frac{y-{y}_{0}}{{v}_{y}} \\ \frac{x-2}{5} & =\frac{y-(-1)}{-4} \\ -4(x-2) & =5(y+1) \\ -4x-5y+8-5 & =0 \\ -4x-5y+3 & =0 \\ 4x+5y-3 & =0\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "053dd984-66f7-5e60-a777-6ca3631e9fa4" :step/next {:db/id 17592186497423}} {:db/id 17592186497423 :step/content {:db/id 17592186398954 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "4643060a-8d1d-5789-a362-102d70382db9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2\,i+2\,j+2\,k" :db/id 17592186398956} {:answer/id #uuid "8070bb66-d16c-505c-85ee-2a417bc81d72" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2\,i+2\,j+k" :db/id 17592186398957} {:answer/id #uuid "0bdcaf70-4358-5973-a594-026557c83288" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2\,i+j+2\,k" :db/id 17592186398958} {:answer/id #uuid "61e68fe8-0332-53d0-b214-d38a39b52899" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "i+2\,j+2\,k" :db/id 17592186398959} {:answer/id #uuid "b9c9c882-083f-5978-8947-be71bba2f10e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2\,i+j+k" :db/id 17592186398960}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186398956} :answer-field/id #uuid "91095769-6695-5735-bdf7-d8d4bfdca38b" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186398955}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "58a67c4a-aa8b-5b64-8268-56928e2716de" :question/math-academy-id "q-71399" :question/problem "For the function $f(x,y,z)={e}^{x+y+z}+x+y+z$, find a vector that's perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(0,0,0).$" :question/worked-solution "A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(0,0,0)$ can be found by computing

:question/worked-solution "First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y+z) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)-xyz \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y+z)+xyz & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y,z)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y+z)+xyz$, our surface can be viewed as the level surface $f(x,y,z)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(2).$ 

A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point $(1,0,1)$ can be found by computing $∇f(1,0,1).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(1,0,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y+z)+xyz)i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y+z)+xyz)j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y+z)+xyz)k \\  & =(\frac{1}{x+y+z}+yz)\text{ }i+(\frac{1}{x+y+z}+xz)\text{ }j+(\frac{1}{x+y+z}+xy)\text{ }k \\ ∇f(1,0,1) & =(\frac{1}{1+0+1}+(0)(1))\,i+(\frac{1}{1+0+1}+(1)(1))\text{ }j+(\frac{1}{1+0+1}+(1)(0))\,k \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\,i+\frac{3}{2}\,j+\frac{1}{2}\,k \\  & =⟨\frac{1}{2},\frac{3}{2},\frac{1}{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the vector equation of the line that is parallel to $∇f(1,0,1)$ and passes through the point $(1,0,1)$ can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =⟨1,0,1⟩+t\,∇f(1,0,1)=⟨1,0,1⟩+t\,⟨\frac{1}{2},\frac{3}{2},\frac{1}{2}⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

where $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).$"} :step/id #uuid "bf1f0a54-a2e4-5d5b-9366-b7874e2b2325" :step/next {:db/id 17592186497425}} {:db/id 17592186497425 :step/content {:db/id 17592186265960 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "076ccae2-d102-5ad8-b1c2-ac28978e3e97" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x-3y=0" :db/id 17592186263068} {:answer/id #uuid "1b3882de-2108-52bf-b5e1-4c3304b9a5c3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x-y-2=0" :db/id 17592186263257} {:answer/id #uuid "a00ce4f7-3888-5dba-a972-b715615f1421" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x+y-4=0" :db/id 17592186264362} {:answer/id #uuid "cf2a0770-0459-500c-aa32-352ae1667e03" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x+3y-6=0" :db/id 17592186264813} {:answer/id #uuid "d493ac59-d9ae-5896-bd9e-006d111d56b9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2x+y-7=0" :db/id 17592186264850}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186264362} :answer-field/id #uuid "cb7e101e-fe81-5db4-a578-c892744685d7" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186265605}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "c80428ab-daca-506e-aca7-d4e40b0d604c" :question/math-academy-id "q-130718" :question/problem "Consider the plane curve ${x}^{2}-3{y}^{2}=6.$  Find the equation of the normal line to the curve at the point $(3,1).$" :question/worked-solution "If we set $f(x,y)={x}^{2}-3{y}^{2},$ our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=6.$

$$
\begin{aligned}
(\frac{1}{2} + \sqrt{-9}) + (3 - \sqrt{-16}) &= (\frac{1}{2} + 3\textrm{i}) + (3 - 4\textrm{i})
\end{aligned}
$$

To add these two complex numbers, we just add the real parts and add the imaginary parts separately:

$$
\begin{aligned}
(\frac{1}{2} + 3\textrm{i}) + (3 - 4\textrm{i}) &= (\frac{1}{2} + 3) + (3 + (-4))\textrm{i} \\
&= (\frac{1}{2} + 3) + (3 - 4)\textrm{i} \\
&= \frac{7}{2} - 1\textrm{i} \\
&= \frac{7}{2} - \textrm{i}
\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186054994 :question/id #uuid "f6f39940-95a6-5ce3-a464-3e2e2d5607a1" :question/math-academy-id "q-126"} {:db/id 17592186055440 :question/id #uuid "807d76c0-edcd-5c5c-80a8-2ab4e68dedd2" :question/math-academy-id "q-617"} {:db/id 17592186332981 :question/id #uuid "73b4f61a-d5e0-5e61-ba69-b272e9ac2be5" :question/math-academy-id "q-641"} {:db/id 17592186054621 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186054532 :question/id #uuid "90553ebc-846c-5cac-8402-8370e5619e3e" :question/math-academy-id "e-4039"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "182eba72-4c11-5e90-8533-77cf3cd86f4c" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186055453 :question/id #uuid "71ef0350-927f-5ce0-b4d0-f74d53fe8c9b" :question/math-academy-id "q-66349"} {:db/id 17592186055454 :question/id #uuid "364e62b3-17d8-5120-8d1a-de45f9f1ea81" :question/math-academy-id "q-66351"}] :knowledge-point/title "Adding Purely Imaginary Numbers"} {:db/id 17592186054532 :question/id #uuid "90553ebc-846c-5cac-8402-8370e5619e3e" :question/math-academy-id "e-4039" :knowledge-point/_canonical-example [{:db/id 17592186054621 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "182eba72-4c11-5e90-8533-77cf3cd86f4c" :knowledge-point/title "Adding Purely Imaginary Numbers"}] :question/problem "Find the value of $5\,\textrm{i} - 8\,\textrm{i}$." :question/worked-solution "To subtract two complex numbers, we just subtract the real parts and subtract the imaginary parts separately.

For example,

$$
\begin{aligned}
(3 + 5\textrm{i}) + (2 - 3\textrm{i}) &= (3 + 5\textrm{i}) + (2 - 3\textrm{i}) \\
&= (3 + 2) + (5 + (-3))\textrm{i} \\
&= (3 + 2) + (5 - 3)\textrm{i} \\
&= 5 + 2\textrm{i}
\end{aligned}
$$

In general, we write

$$
(a + b\textrm{i}) + (c + d\textrm{i}) = (a + c) + (b + d)\textrm{i}
$$

Subtracting complex numbers works in the same way: we just subtract the real parts and subtract the imaginary parts separately. For example,

$$
\begin{aligned}
(3 + 5\textrm{i}) - (2 - 3\textrm{i}) &= (3 + 5\textrm{i}) - (2 - 3\textrm{i}) \\
&= (3 - 2) + (5 - (-3))\textrm{i} \\
&= (3 - 2) + (5 + 3)\textrm{i} \\
&= 1 + 8\textrm{i}
\end{aligned}
$$

In general, we write

$$
(a + b\textrm{i}) - (c + d\textrm{i}) = (a - c) + (b - d)\textrm{i}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "3783edad-ba1d-564c-8e99-3ba74795716f" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2788 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "4ec81b99-be36-51f9-b8c9-9de86abfdb21" :step/math-academy-id :db/id 17592186054893} {:db/id 17592186055538 :step/content {:db/id 17592186055967 :tutorial/content "To add complex numbers, we just add the real parts and add the imaginary parts separately. For example,

$$
\begin{aligned}
(3 + 5\textrm{i}) + (2 - 3\textrm{i}) &= (3 + 5\textrm{i}) + (2 - 3\textrm{i}) \\
&= (3 + 2) + (5 + (-3))\textrm{i} \\
&= (3 + 2) + (5 - 3)\textrm{i} \\
&= 5 + 2\textrm{i}
\end{aligned}
$$

In general, we write

$$
(a + b\textrm{i}) + (c + d\textrm{i}) = (a + c) + (b + d)\textrm{i}
$$

Subtracting complex numbers works in the same way: we just subtract the real parts and subtract the imaginary parts separately. For example,

$$
\begin{aligned}
(3 + 5\textrm{i}) - (2 - 3\textrm{i}) &= (3 + 5\textrm{i}) - (2 - 3\textrm{i}) \\
&= (3 - 2) + (5 - (-3))\textrm{i} \\
&= (3 - 2) + (5 + 3)\textrm{i} \\
&= 1 + 8\textrm{i}
\end{aligned}
$$

In general, we write

$$
(a + b\textrm{i}) - (c + d\textrm{i}) = (a - c) + (b - d)\textrm{i}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "3783edad-ba1d-564c-8e99-3ba74795716f" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2788 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "4ec81b99-be36-51f9-b8c9-9de86abfdb21" :step/math-academy-id 14292 :step/next {:db/id 17592186055539}} {:db/id 17592186055967 :tutorial/content "To add complex numbers, we just add the real parts and add the imaginary parts separately. :tutorial/content "Let's consider the graph of the function $y=f(x)$ on the closed interval $[0,7]$ shown below.

![](images/39/39851b8fc5658ccfd92711eb9fe7a00a730300a3bf2e635911bdd51ea69de37a.png)

The **critical points** of $f(x)$ are the values of $x$ where $f'(x)=0$ or $f'(x)$ doesn't exist. Graphically, those are the values where the tangent to the graph is horizontal or where the tangent does not exist, respectively.

In the given graph, we can see that 

- at $x=2,$ the tangent to the graph is horizontal, so we have $f'(x)=0,$ while

- at $x=4,$ there is a sharp corner, so $f'(x)$ doesn't exist.

So, there are two critical points, and their $x$-coordinates are $x=2$ and $x=4.$ 

In particular, a critical point is called a **stationary point** if $f'(x)=0.$ So here, the points $x=2$ and $x=4$ are both critical points, but only the point at $x=2$ is a stationary point.

:step/math-academy-id 23042 :step/next {:db/id 17592186065159}} {:db/id 17592186065159 :step/content {:db/id 17592186065374 :tutorial/content "Some critical points are **local extrema**. There are two types of local extrema:

- A **local minimum** is the lowest point of a valley in a graph. Equivalently, $x=a$ is a local minimum if for $x$ values "close" to $x=a,$ we have $f(x) \geq f(a)$.

- A **local maximum** is the highest point of a peak in a graph. Equivalently, $x=a$ is a local maximum if for $x$ values "close" to $x=a,$ we have $f(x) \leq f(a)$.

![](images/d6/d6fbdf74b282bd5b8172fcc7927f84bbdfd050a717794f3b40c8e58b83d7b87e.png)

On the graph above, the critical point at $x=4$ is a local minimum since it is the lowest point of a valley. Likewise, the critical point at $x=6$ is a local maximum since it is the highest point of a peak. But the critical point at $x=2$ is not a local extremum since it is neither a peak nor a valley.

The **global extrema** of a function in an interval are given by the lowest or highest points of the function's graph in the whole interval.

- The lowest point is the **global minimum**, whereas

- the highest point is the **global maximum**.

Here, the global minimum is at $x=4$, and the global maximum is at $x=0.$

![](images/8a/8adb83da866dae1cd122b5271b2cb9036c72a389eaf1c48148888140bda576ac.png)

"Local" extrema are the lowest or highest points compared to points that are very close to them. On the other hand, "global" extrema are the lowest/highest points of the graph over its entire domain." :tutorial/id #uuid "05856315-caeb-577d-9dea-b5e5f8830820" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3898 :tutorial/title "Local and Global Extrema of a Function"} :step/id #uuid "b952eadc-3fe2-5be0-8961-f9af3dc6fcd5" :step/math-academy-id 23043 :step/next {:db/id 17592186064993}}] :activity/title "Global vs. Local Extrema and Critical Points" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186064409} {:db/id 17592186064992 :step/content {:db/id 17592186065347 :tutorial/content "Let's consider the graph of the function $y=f(x)$ on the closed interval $[0,7]$ shown below.

The **global extrema** of a function in an interval are given by the lowest or highest points of the function's graph in the whole interval.

- The lowest point is the **global minimum**, whereas

- the highest point is the **global maximum**.

Here, the global minimum is at $x=4$, and the global maximum is at $x=0.$

"Suppose that we have the two functions $u(x)=2x^3$ and $v(x)=x^2.$ How do we calculate the derivative of their product $(u(x) \cdot v(x))'?$

To do that, we can use the **product rule**, which states that the derivative of the product of two functions is given by the formula

$$
\left(u(x) \cdot  v(x)\right)' = u'(x) \cdot v(x) + u(x) \cdot v'(x).
$$

In our case, the derivatives of the two functions are given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}^{'}(x) & =(2{x}^{3})^{'}=6{x}^{2}, \\ {v}^{'}(x) & =({x}^{2})^{'}=2x.\end{aligned}
$$

If we plug all of this into the product rule formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{(u(x)\cdot v(x))}^{'} & =(6{x}^{2})({x}^{2})+(2{x}^{3})(2x) \\  & =6{x}^{4}+4{x}^{4} \\  & =10{x}^{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

This example was quite simple, and we could have solved it by calculating the product first and then taking the derivative. We can do it now to double check our result:

$$
\begin{aligned}{(u(x)\cdot v(x))}^{'} & =(2{x}^{3}\cdot {x}^{2})^{'} \\  & =(2{x}^{5})^{'} \\  & =10{x}^{4}\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

Sometimes, however, we cannot calculate the product algebraically, or it can be tedious to do it. In those cases, the product rule will turn out to be very useful!" :tutorial/id #uuid "958f67f2-8e00-5818-8af7-9f88561ef84c" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2622 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id For that, we can use the **quotient rule**. The quotient rule is a formula to calculate the derivative of the ratio of two functions like 

$$
f(x) = \dfrac {u(x)}{v(x)}.
$$

The quotient rule for differentiation states that the derivative of the function above is given by

$$
f'(x) = \dfrac {u'(x)\cdot v(x) - u(x) \cdot v'(x)} {[v(x)]^2}.
$$

For example, suppose that we have the function $f(x)$ given by

$$
f(x)= \dfrac{x}{x^2+1},
$$

and we want to find $f'(x).$ 

Here $u(x)=x$ and $v(x)=x^2+1.$  Their derivatives are given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}^{'}(x) & =(x)^{'}=1, \\ {v}^{'}(x) & =({x}^{2}+1)^{'}=2x.\end{aligned}
$$

If we plug them in the formula, we get:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{'}(x) & =\frac{{u}^{'}(x)\cdot v(x)-u(x)\cdot {v}^{'}(x)}{[v(x)]^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1\cdot ({x}^{2}+1)-x\cdot 2x}{({x}^{2}+1)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{{x}^{2}+1-2{x}^{2}}{({x}^{2}+1)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1-{x}^{2}}{({x}^{2}+1)^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "dd2362a7-73d2-577f-aa31-2150f8f6b63f" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2624 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "ed5427f5-4392-5166-a825-dd9dcb07cc3d" :step/math-academy-id For that, we can use the **quotient rule**. The quotient rule is a formula to calculate the derivative of the ratio of two functions like 

$$
f(x) = \dfrac {u(x)}{v(x)}.
$$

The quotient rule for differentiation states that the derivative of the function above is given by

$$
f'(x) = \dfrac {u'(x)\cdot v(x) - u(x) \cdot v'(x)} {[v(x)]^2}.
$$

For example, suppose that we have the function $f(x)$ given by

$$
f(x)= \dfrac{x}{x^2+1},
$$

and we want to find $f'(x).$ 

Here $u(x)=x$ and $v(x)=x^2+1.$  Their derivatives are given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}^{'}(x) & =(x)^{'}=1, \\ {v}^{'}(x) & =({x}^{2}+1)^{'}=2x.\end{aligned}
$$

If we plug them in the formula, we get:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{'}(x) & =\frac{{u}^{'}(x)\cdot v(x)-u(x)\cdot {v}^{'}(x)}{[v(x)]^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1\cdot ({x}^{2}+1)-x\cdot 2x}{({x}^{2}+1)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{{x}^{2}+1-2{x}^{2}}{({x}^{2}+1)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1-{x}^{2}}{({x}^{2}+1)^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "dd2362a7-73d2-577f-aa31-2150f8f6b63f" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2624 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "ed5427f5-4392-5166-a825-dd9dcb07cc3d" :step/math-academy-id 12332 :step/next {:db/id 17592186097431}} {:db/id 17592186097820 :tutorial/content "We know how to calculate the derivative of the product of two functions, but what if we have a quotient?

$$
y - y_1 = m (x - x_1), \hspace{1cm} m=-\dfrac{1}{f'(x_1)}.
$$

Here, $m=-\dfrac{1}{f'(x_1)}$ because the slope of the normal line is the negative reciprocal of the slope of the tangent line, and $f'(x_1)$ represents the slope of the tangent line to $y=f(x)$ at the point $(x_1,y_1).$

For example, suppose we want to compute the equation of the normal line to the curve $y=x^2$ at the point $A(1,1).$ This normal line is the dashed line shown below, which is perpendicular to the solid tangent line. 

![](images/31/31ba09ff14e5bd485794f283c5d6a5b087b6c21fdb9242af01b75ec8e8744e0d.png)

Since $y=x^2,$ we have $f(x)=x^2.$ We begin by calculating the derivative of $f(x)\mathbin{:}$

$$
f'(x) 		 = \dfrac {\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}(x^2)= 2x
$$

At $A(1,1),$ the slope of the tangent line is given by

$$
f'(1) 	= 2(1) = 2.
$$

However, we want the normal line, and the slope of the normal line is the negative reciprocal of the slope of the tangent line:

$$
m = -\dfrac{1}{f'(1)} = -\dfrac{1}{2}
$$

 

Finally, we work out the equation of the normal line using the point-slope form:

$$
\begin{aligned}y-1 & =-\frac{1}{2}(x-1) \\ y & =-\frac{x}{2}+\frac{1}{2}+1 \\ y & =-\frac{x}{2}+\frac{3}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the equation of the normal line is $y=-\dfrac x 2 + \dfrac 3 2.$ We could also write this in standard form as $x+2y=3.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "c50c999b-ac30-5116-acbd-795f13cc2b3d" Since $y=x^2,$ we have $f(x)=x^2.$ We begin by calculating the derivative of $f(x)\mathbin{:}$

$$
f'(x) 		 = \dfrac {\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}(x^2)= 2x
$$

At $A(1,1),$ the slope of the tangent line is given by

$$
f'(1) 	= 2(1) = 2.
$$

However, we want the normal line, and the slope of the normal line is the negative reciprocal of the slope of the tangent line:

$$
m = -\dfrac{1}{f'(1)} = -\dfrac{1}{2}
$$

 

Finally, we work out the equation of the normal line using the point-slope form:

$$
\begin{aligned}y-1 & =-\frac{1}{2}(x-1) \\ y & =-\frac{x}{2}+\frac{1}{2}+1 \\ y & =-\frac{x}{2}+\frac{3}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the equation of the normal line is $y=-\dfrac x 2 + \dfrac 3 2.$ We could also write this in standard form as $x+2y=3.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "c50c999b-ac30-5116-acbd-795f13cc2b3d" :tutorial/math-academy-id 359 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} {:db/id 17592186093328 :step/content {:db/id 17592186092384 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186091953 :question/id #uuid "4a734f55-ceac-587c-a831-fa8bed578a99" :question/math-academy-id "e-148"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "4a05f6c0-98ab-5197-922e-8e8dff1d4302" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186050473} {:db/id 17592186050711}] :knowledge-point/question-generator {:db/id 17592186480110} :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186092723} {:db/id 17592186092725} {:db/id 17592186233770} {:db/id 17592186233924} {:db/id 17592186233925} {:db/id 17592186233926} {:db/id 17592186234307} {:db/id 17592186238012} {:db/id 17592186238013} {:db/id 17592186238019} {:db/id 17592186317210} {:db/id 17592186329815} {:db/id 17592186338957}] :knowledge-point/title "Calculating the Slope of a Normal Line to a Curve at a Point"} :step/id #uuid "ee29e21c-ec79-5cef-8080-e39f4ded4176" :step/math-academy-id 668 :step/next {:db/id 17592186093087}} {:activity/expected-seconds 660.0 :activity/first-step {:db/id 17592186079227} :activity/id #uuid "c69d16f5-44d0-5069-b44e-d2caf86ea506" :activity/scope {:db/id 17592186049806 :topic/id #uuid "156024ea-0497-5260-b6dc-995afd569210" :topic/math-academy-id 638} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186079227 :step/content {:db/id 17592186079683 :tutorial/content "Consider the function $f(x)$ below:

$$

$$

$$

Now, the so-called **addition formula for sine** states that

$$

It is written as $f''(x).$

To calculate the second derivative of a function $f(x)$, we first need to calculate the first derivative $f'(x).$ After that, we calculate the derivative of $f'(x).$ So using prime $\left('\right)$ notation, we can define the second derivative of a function $f(x)$ as

$$
f''(x) = (f'(x))'.
$$

Let's try it out with the function $f(x) = 4x^2 + 3x.$ The first derivative is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{'}(x) & =(4{x}^{2}+3x)^{'} \\  & =4(2)x+3 \\  & =8x+3.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now calculate the derivative of $f'(x)$ to give us $f''(x).$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{''}(x) & =({f}^{'}(x))^{'} \\  & =(8x+3)^{'} \\  & =8+0 \\  & =8.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{'}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2{x}^{4}+3x) \\  & =2\cdot 4{x}^{4-1}+1\cdot 3{x}^{1-1} \\ \text{ } & =8{x}^{3}+3{x}^{0} \\  & =8{x}^{3}+3.\end{aligned}

$$

$$

Finally, computing the third derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{‴}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(24{x}^{2}) \\  & =24\cdot 2{x}^{2-1} \\ \text{ } & =48x.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

$$

$$

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{''}(x) & =({f}^{'}(x))^{'} \\  & =(8x+3)^{'} \\  & =8+0 \\  & =8.\end{aligned}

an invertible $n\times n$ matrix $A,$ we have

$$
|{A}^{-1}|=\frac{1}{|A|}.
$$

First, we find $|A|$ using a Laplace expansion across the $2$nd row:

$$
\begin{aligned}|A| & =|\begin{aligned}-5 & -3 & 4 \\ -2 & 1 & 2 \\ 1 & -4 & 6\end{aligned}| \\  & =-2(-1)^{2+1}|\begin{aligned}-3 & 4 \\ -4 & 6\end{aligned}|+1(-1)^{2+2}|\begin{aligned}-5 & 4 \\ 1 & 6\end{aligned}|+2(-1)^{2+3}|\begin{aligned}-5 & -3 \\ 1 & -4\end{aligned}| \\  & =2(-18+16)+(-30-4)-2(20+3) \\  & =-4-34-46 \\  & =-84\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we obtain 

$$
|{A}^{-1}|=\frac{1}{|A|}=-\frac{1}{84}.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186435770 :question/id #uuid "eee0d247-b841-57bb-b4de-7b3606da042f" :question/math-academy-id "q-42583" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "44f82cc2-edfd-5f43-b0c8-b4fb5bfe4f97" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{2}" :db/id 17592186435746} {:answer/id #uuid "48f7dc16-cbeb-5e5b-b98b-3d2a1113c52c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\frac{1}{4}" :db/id 17592186435747} {:answer/id #uuid "a7ea38b1-c61b-5047-b0ee-8b524e948890" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{81}" :db/id 17592186435755} {:answer/id #uuid "ca3a92c4-d4e6-5591-8bf1-5151ac26a42e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{27}" :db/id 17592186435759} {:answer/id #uuid "d6f0546b-c6ef-592b-ad4b-1acba6597c58" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\frac{1}{17}" :db/id 17592186435761}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186435747} :answer-field/id #uuid "b9759cd8-4862-5dd3-9edc-5966b55e2eb1" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186435765}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/problem "Find $|{A}^{-1}|,$ if $A=\begin{bmatrix}7 & 6 & -3 \\ 1 & 2 & -1 \\ 5 & -5 & 2\end{bmatrix}.$" :question/worked-solution "Given an invertible $n\times n$ matrix $A,$ we have

:question/problem "Given that 
$|\begin{aligned}a+2 & -2 & 2 \\ b+3 & 4 & 2 \\ c & 0 & 1\end{aligned}|=5,$
find 
$|\begin{aligned}a+1 & -2 & 2 \\ b & 4 & 2 \\ c & 0 & 1\end{aligned}|.$" :question/worked-solution "We "factor out" the given determinant from the determinant we would like to find:

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}a+1 & -2 & 2 \\ b & 4 & 2 \\ c & 0 & 1\end{aligned}| & =|\begin{aligned}(a+2)-1 & -2 & 2 \\ (b+3)-3 & 4 & 2 \\ c+0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}|\end{aligned}
$$

  

Now, using the linearity property of determinants and expanding the second determinant across the $3$rd row, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}(a+2)-1 & -2 & 2 \\ (b+3)-3 & 4 & 2 \\ c+0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}| & ={{|\begin{aligned}(a+2) & -2 & 2 \\ (b+3) & 4 & 2 \\ c & 0 & 1\end{aligned}|}_{⏟}}_{5}+|\begin{aligned}-1 & -2 & 2 \\ -3 & 4 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =5+1\cdot (-1)^{3+3}|\begin{aligned}-1 & -2 \\ -3 & 4\end{aligned}| \\  & =5+(-10) \\  & =-5.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186354639 :question/id #uuid "26f8d807-4854-5fae-88e0-bb503698def0" :question/math-academy-id "q-88301" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186119780 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "6e4dd07e-475b-5c89-883b-0e4adcf6a723" :knowledge-point/title "Calculating a Determinant Using the Linearity of the Determinant"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "356b3816-6db1-52b5-bb62-b3c3cf31be2b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "282" :db/id 17592186352065} {:answer/id #uuid "4961badc-1952-50cf-a3aa-c27c2154e001" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "447" :db/id 17592186352242} {:answer/id #uuid "7e93fedb-8a75-5259-a81d-4a24a5c3ba66" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "372" :db/id 17592186352678} {:answer/id #uuid "b7b4f3fb-84a7-5faa-a662-e6383aedf972" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "273" :db/id 17592186353139} {:answer/id #uuid "d43b6429-3ee0-5e37-bfcf-0795e21063ef" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "327" :db/id 17592186353406}] :answer-field/correct {:answer/id #uuid "b7b4f3fb-84a7-5faa-a662-e6383aedf972" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "273" :db/id 17592186353139} :answer-field/id #uuid "d31711c3-cb15-50d5-862f-d3265b1300b3" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186354174}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486 :db/ident :question.difficulty/hard} :question/problem "Find
$|\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & 6 \\ 91 & 92 & 93 \\ 90 & 92 & 93\end{aligned}|.$" :question/worked-solution "First, notice that the $2$nd row of our determinant is almost equal to the $3$rd row. So, we can rewrite the given determinant, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & 6 \\ 91 & 92 & 93 \\ 90 & 92 & 93\end{aligned}| & =|\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & 6 \\ 90+1 & 92+0 & 93+0 \\ 90 & 92 & 93\end{aligned}|\end{aligned}
$$

Next, using the linearity property of determinants, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & 6 \\ 90+1 & 92+0 & 93+0 \\ 90 & 92 & 93\end{aligned}| & =|\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & 6 \\ 90 & 92 & 93 \\ 90 & 92 & 93\end{aligned}|+|\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & 6 \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 90 & 92 & 93\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

The first determinant must be zero since it has two identical rows, while the second determinant can be expanded across the $2$nd row, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & 6 \\ 90 & 92 & 93 \\ 90 & 92 & 93\end{aligned}|+|\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & 6 \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 90 & 92 & 93\end{aligned}| & =0+1(-1)^{2+1}|\begin{aligned}3 & 6 \\ 92 & 93\end{aligned}| \\  & =-(3\cdot 93-6\cdot 92) \\  & =-(279-552) \\  & =273\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186354640 :question/id #uuid "da76c31c-efa0-5055-96f9-ec1ecc76273f" :question/math-academy-id "q-88304"} {:db/id 17592186420851 :question/id #uuid "80589b9c-bfb0-57bc-8e70-de307d877343" :question/math-academy-id "q-88306"} {:db/id 17592186420852 :question/id #uuid "8c3dc4f1-ad56-595b-a7eb-41a85271c7fe" :question/math-academy-id "q-130693"} {:db/id 17592186435767 :question/id #uuid "3797960f-4f46-583b-afe6-1bb724ee5f4b" :question/math-academy-id "q-130641" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "2fd88020-b9de-5670-bbb4-d000faac032e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "176" :db/id 17592186435744} {:answer/id #uuid "4e375b53-cb2c-56d7-a604-46a74124343b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "214" :db/id 17592186435749} {:answer/id #uuid "82e7b3e3-84d8-5737-a5f1-d3862a09a444" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "186" :db/id 17592186435753} {:answer/id #uuid "ac3611ee-496d-5cec-8534-0299f1c2f846" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "260" :db/id 17592186435756} {:answer/id #uuid "f62fda4e-f88c-56fa-9e53-1860b2a19543" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "244" :db/id 17592186435762}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186435756} :answer-field/id #uuid "0e7b949d-cbe6-5045-bf34-26b00edf4f82" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186435763}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/problem "Find
$|\begin{aligned}2 & 4 & -7 \\ 144 & 158 & 103 \\ 144 & 158 & 102\end{aligned}|=$" :question/worked-solution "First, notice that the $2$nd row of our determinant is almost equal to the $3$rd row. So, we can rewrite the given determinant, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}2 & 4 & -7 \\ 144 & 158 & 103 \\ 144 & 158 & 102\end{aligned}| & =|\begin{aligned}2 & 4 & -7 \\ 144+0 & 158+0 & 102+1 \\ 144 & 158 & 102\end{aligned}|\end{aligned}
$$

Next, using the linearity property of determinants, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}2 & 4 & -7 \\ 144+0 & 158+0 & 102+1 \\ 144 & 158 & 102\end{aligned}| & =|\begin{aligned}2 & 4 & -7 \\ 144 & 158 & 102 \\ 144 & 158 & 102\end{aligned}|+|\begin{aligned}2 & 4 & -7 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \\ 144 & 158 & 102\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

The first determinant must be zero since it has two identical rows, while the second determinant can be expanded across the $2$nd row, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}2 & 4 & -7 \\ 144 & 158 & 102 \\ 144 & 158 & 102\end{aligned}|+|\begin{aligned}2 & 4 & -7 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \\ 144 & 158 & 102\end{aligned}| & =0+1(-1)^{2+3}|\begin{aligned}2 & 4 \\ 144 & 158\end{aligned}| \\  & =-(2\cdot 158-4\cdot 144) \\  & =-(316-576) \\  & =260\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186435768 :question/id #uuid "788f9347-638e-5e07-bc97-727179291d72" :question/math-academy-id "q-130780" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "74feda84-0372-5ba8-a03f-6504fdd43cb8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-3" :db/id 17592186435751} {:answer/id #uuid "81e999d9-b74a-531e-b396-75bcda8940a5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-9" :db/id 17592186435752} {:answer/id #uuid "a5465cc4-707e-5513-9c9b-2c4ccb77d7a1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-12" :db/id 17592186435754} {:answer/id #uuid "aee93a59-f631-5538-b707-3dbdac3a5bb0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "15" :db/id 17592186435757} {:answer/id #uuid "c2c0bd69-0ae8-5c67-b00c-53d8d88f988d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "6" :db/id 17592186435758}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186435752} :answer-field/id #uuid "ea1881ff-14ad-5797-8c35-e1990ea0829e" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186435766}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "Given that

:topic/math-academy-id 1774} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186120630 :step/content {:db/id 17592186121022 :tutorial/content "In this topic, we will consider a few more properties of determinants. Let's start with the following important property. 

*The determinant of the product of two square matrices is equal to the product of the determinants.*

Symbolically, if ![](images/34/34058a2a5d1de088feed7d9825ba218394c9a8bb880b046be7b47307cdd37ce1.svg) and ![](images/25/256531b7f0ddb14dd11a59a3019a3361f1607d3fe16fa6d530a461344de8f39e.svg) are both square matrices, then

![](images/e5/e59b47ca5462a066093945e2698404e595a92e9e70a2b8c4f8b2f30df9c9fbf1.svg)

For instance, suppose that we want to find the determinant of the matrix ![](images/32/3207697e43e4f88223ad85c16964c3103a50c0c999a4ca14417695158d45526b.svg) that is defined as follows:
![](images/9a/9a705ea4bd482cdf83251288108b48ff5bc7354c9d51c1b710b9e734c8a32dea.svg)

To easily compute ![](images/da/dab9a65c1cba3cd9f271a1910b060e5428813107b3b54945776aab3839003d45.svg), we first compute the determinants of the two matrices and then multiply the results. Also, notice that both matrices in our product are triangular, so their determinants are given by the product of the diagonal entries:

![](images/fa/fa4214541c12b0a761fd7cb17f4efc2f6b4be2c1424094483a3c2f61ab63c0a0.svg)" :tutorial/id #uuid "5a8abcbc-c41d-5553-8b2e-daa7256d7d34" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3009 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "425217e0-d658-532e-a440-a3ddd4b953cd" :step/math-academy-id 16227 :step/next {:db/id 17592186120631}} {:db/id 17592186120631 :step/content {:db/id 17592186119778 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186119592 :question/id #uuid "c5560ec9-32d6-514d-92fa-fbd77500d943" :question/math-academy-id "e-4431"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "3b022adb-2663-550f-866d-3365bb2d78c9" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049159}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186120449} {:db/id 17592186120450} {:db/id 17592186265916} {:db/id 17592186265918} {:db/id 17592186265920} {:db/id 17592186265921} {:db/id 17592186354635} {:db/id 17592186420849} {:db/id 17592186420850} {:db/id 17592186420854} {:db/id 17592186484199} {:db/id 17592186484234}] :knowledge-point/title "Calculating the Determinant of a Product"} :step/id #uuid "b7196473-0bc4-579e-90dc-f9136aa28e30" :step/math-academy-id 16228 :step/next {:db/id 17592186120632}} {:db/id 17592186120632 :step/content {:db/id 17592186121023 :tutorial/content "Another useful property of determinants is that, for any invertible matrix $A,$ we have

$$
\det(A^{-1}) = \dfrac{1}{\det(A)}.
$$

To understand why the above property is true, remember that $A \cdot A^{-1} = I$ for any invertible matrix $A.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A\cdot {A}^{-1} & =I \\ det(A\cdot {A}^{-1}) & =det(I) \\ det(A)\cdot det({A}^{-1}) & =1 \\ det({A}^{-1}) & =\frac{1}{det(A)}.\end{aligned}
$$

$|\begin{aligned}2 & 4 & -7 \\ 144 & 158 & 103 \\ 144 & 158 & 102\end{aligned}|=$" :question/worked-solution "First, notice that the $2$nd row of our determinant is almost equal to the $3$rd row. So, we can rewrite the given determinant, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}2 & 4 & -7 \\ 144 & 158 & 103 \\ 144 & 158 & 102\end{aligned}| & =|\begin{aligned}2 & 4 & -7 \\ 144+0 & 158+0 & 102+1 \\ 144 & 158 & 102\end{aligned}|\end{aligned}
$$

Next, using the linearity property of determinants, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}2 & 4 & -7 \\ 144+0 & 158+0 & 102+1 \\ 144 & 158 & 102\end{aligned}| & =|\begin{aligned}2 & 4 & -7 \\ 144 & 158 & 102 \\ 144 & 158 & 102\end{aligned}|+|\begin{aligned}2 & 4 & -7 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \\ 144 & 158 & 102\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

The first determinant must be zero since it has two identical rows, while the second determinant can be expanded across the $2$nd row, as follows:

"Find $|{A}^{-1}|,$ if $A=\begin{bmatrix}-5 & -3 & 4 \\ -2 & 1 & 2 \\ 1 & -4 & 6\end{bmatrix}.$" :question/worked-solution "Given an invertible $n\times n$ matrix $A,$ we have

$$
|{A}^{-1}|=\frac{1}{|A|}.
$$

First, we find $|A|$ using a Laplace expansion across the $2$nd row:

$$
\begin{aligned}|A| & =|\begin{aligned}-5 & -3 & 4 \\ -2 & 1 & 2 \\ 1 & -4 & 6\end{aligned}| \\  & =-2(-1)^{2+1}|\begin{aligned}-3 & 4 \\ -4 & 6\end{aligned}|+1(-1)^{2+2}|\begin{aligned}-5 & 4 \\ 1 & 6\end{aligned}|+2(-1)^{2+3}|\begin{aligned}-5 & -3 \\ 1 & -4\end{aligned}| \\  & =2(-18+16)+(-30-4)-2(20+3) \\  & =-4-34-46 \\  & =-84\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we obtain 

$$
|{A}^{-1}|=\frac{1}{|A|}=-\frac{1}{84}.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "ab0d2d10-5ed3-5c47-8920-753336a27760" :step/next {:db/id 17592186435771}} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "44f82cc2-edfd-5f43-b0c8-b4fb5bfe4f97" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{2}" :db/id 17592186435746} {:answer/id #uuid "48f7dc16-cbeb-5e5b-b98b-3d2a1113c52c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\frac{1}{4}" :db/id 17592186435747} {:answer/id #uuid "a7ea38b1-c61b-5047-b0ee-8b524e948890" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{81}" :db/id 17592186435755} {:answer/id #uuid "ca3a92c4-d4e6-5591-8bf1-5151ac26a42e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{27}" :db/id 17592186435759} {:answer/id #uuid "d6f0546b-c6ef-592b-ad4b-1acba6597c58" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\frac{1}{17}" :db/id 17592186435761}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186435747} :answer-field/id #uuid "b9759cd8-4862-5dd3-9edc-5966b55e2eb1" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186435765} {:answer/id #uuid "44f82cc2-edfd-5f43-b0c8-b4fb5bfe4f97" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{2}" :db/id 17592186435746} {:answer/id #uuid "48f7dc16-cbeb-5e5b-b98b-3d2a1113c52c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\frac{1}{4}" :db/id 17592186435747} {:answer/id #uuid "a7ea38b1-c61b-5047-b0ee-8b524e948890" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{81}" :db/id 17592186435755} {:answer/id #uuid "ca3a92c4-d4e6-5591-8bf1-5151ac26a42e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{27}" :db/id 17592186435759} {:answer/id #uuid "d6f0546b-c6ef-592b-ad4b-1acba6597c58" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\frac{1}{17}" :db/id 17592186435761} {:db/id 17592186048866 :topic/difficulty 1.0831032664138704 :topic/encompasses [{:db/id 17592186429578 :encompassing/rationale "Initial Codex estimate from captured target-band crossing frequency. $$
\frac{(y-k)^{2}}{{a}^{2}}-\frac{(x-h)^{2}}{{b}^{2}}=1.
$$

To rewrite the equation of the hyperbola in the above form, we need to group $x$ and $y$ terms and complete the squares, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}-{x}^{2}+16{y}^{2}-32y-8x & =16 \\ 16{y}^{2}-32y-{x}^{2}-8x & =16 \\ 16[{y}^{2}-2y]-[{x}^{2}+8x] & =16 \\ 16[(y-1)^{2}-1]-[(x+4)^{2}-16] & =16 \\ 16(y-1)^{2}-16-(x+4)^{2}+16 & =16 \\ 16(y-1)^{2}-(x+4)^{2} & =16 \\ \frac{(y-1)^{2}}{1}-\frac{(x+4)^{2}}{16} & =1 \\ \frac{(y-1)^{2}}{1}-\frac{(x-(-4))^{2}}{16} & =1\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\frac{(y-k)^{2}}{{a}^{2}}-\frac{(x-h)^{2}}{{b}^{2}}=1.

$$
\frac{(y-0)^{2}}{5}-\frac{(x-(-7))^{2}}{6}=1

$$

$$
\int x^2 \,\textrm d x = \dfrac{x^{2+1}}{2+1} + C = \dfrac{x^3}{3}+C
$$

Let's check by differentiating:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{d}{dx}(\frac{x^{3}}{3} + C) &=  \\
\frac{d}{dx}(\frac{x^{3}}{3}) + \frac{d}{dx}(C) &=  \\
\frac{1}{3}\frac{d}{dx}(x^{3}) + 0 &=  \\
\frac{1}{3} \cdot 3x^{2} &=  \\
&= x^{2}✓
\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186503877} {:db/id 17592186064554 :question/id #uuid "9681ab06-ae34-5546-895c-3849a33f13b3" :question/math-academy-id "q-2005"} {:db/id 17592186064556 :question/id #uuid "a4162e45-b600-54a2-bad9-383dac48cede" :question/math-academy-id "q-2022"} {:db/id 17592186233174 :question/id #uuid "6e6c66f6-6133-59f6-a79d-0cbf1615accf" :question/math-academy-id "q-113665" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186064167 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "f2a4550c-7ed7-58aa-8928-23dd1cfd0cd7" :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Antiderivative of a Monomial"}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485 :db/ident :question.difficulty/easy} :question/problem "Calculate $\int {x}^{20}\,\text{d}x.$" :question/worked-solution "We apply the power rule with $n=20$, and we get

Antiderivative of a Radical Function"}] :question/problem "Find the antiderivative of $\sqrt x$." :question/worked-solution "We start by writing the square root as a rational power,

$$
\sqrt x= x^{1/2}
$$

So, we can apply the power rule with

$$
n=\dfrac{1}{2}
$$

and get

$$
\begin{aligned}
\int\sqrt{x}dx &= \intx^{1/2}dx \\
&= (x^{1/2 + 1})/((\frac{1}{2} + 1)) + C \\
&= (x^{3/2})/((\frac{3}{2})) + C \\
&= \frac{2x^{3/2}}{3} + C
\end{aligned}
$$

Again, let's check by differentiating:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{d}{dx}(\frac{2x^{3/2}}{3} + C) &=  \\
\frac{d}{dx}(\frac{2x^{3/2}}{3}) + \frac{d}{dx}(C) &=  \\
\frac{2}{3}\frac{d}{dx}(x^{3/2}) + 0 &=  \\
\frac{2}{3} \cdot \frac{3}{2}x^{3/2 - 1} &=  \\
&= x^{1/2}✓
\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186503917} {:db/id 17592186064557 :question/id #uuid "cb61c7fc-a0d3-5742-be73-cb3d6f6a29fa" :question/math-academy-id "q-2023"} {:db/id 17592186064713 :question/id #uuid "3174cae9-484e-5ca3-8e5c-3c9cddc86145" :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Antiderivative of a Reciprocal Function"}] :question/problem "Given that $f(x) = \dfrac 1 {x^3}$ and that $F'(x) = f(x)$, calculate $F(x)$." :question/worked-solution "Remember that integration is the opposite of differentiation. So, if

$$
F'(x) = f(x)
$$

then integrating both sides of this equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
F^{′}(x) &= f(x) \\
\intF^{′}(x)dx &= \intf(x)dx \\
F(x) &= \intf(x)dx
\end{aligned}
$$

Note that

$$
\dfrac 1 {x^3}= x^{-3}
$$

So, we can use the power rule with $n=-3$ and get

$$
\begin{aligned}
F(x) &= \intf(x)dx \\
&= \int\frac{1}{x^{3}}dx \\
&= \intx^{-3}dx \\
&= \frac{x^{-3 + 1}}{-3 + 1} + C \\
&=-\frac{x^{-2}}{2} + C \\
&=-\frac{1}{2x^{2}} + C
\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186502964} {:db/id 17592186064722 :question/id #uuid "35560944-ec26-532a-8ab4-c27135900127" :question/math-academy-id "q-29987"} {:db/id 17592186064723 :question/id #uuid "4f854a01-0859-5bcc-add9-c9a801f5da45" :question/math-academy-id "q-29989"} {:db/id 17592186233179 :question/id #uuid "25edeff2-faa4-50c4-bbfd-3291d7ac7694" :question/math-academy-id "q-113705"} {:db/id 17592186233751 :question/id #uuid "6a192223-274d-5d58-847a-c92d2faa98df" :question/math-academy-id "q-29633"} {:db/id 17592186233752 :question/id #uuid "8dcd24a2-ce5f-5ab6-8a92-814e8f1355a9" :question/math-academy-id "q-29662"} {:db/id 17592186234299 :question/id #uuid "44529618-fcf7-5581-8bd3-a0df68de242f" :question/math-academy-id "q-71100" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186064169 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "3174cae9-484e-5ca3-8e5c-3c9cddc86145" :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Antiderivative of a Reciprocal Function"}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485 :db/ident :question.difficulty/easy} :question/problem "Given that $f(x)={x}^{-1/7}$ and that ${F}^{'}(x)=f(x)$, calculate $F(x).$" :question/worked-solution "Remember that integration is the opposite of differentiation. So, if ${F}^{'}(x)=f(x),$ then integrating both sides of this equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{F}^{'}(x) & =f(x) \\ \int {F}^{'}(x)\,\text{d}x & =\int f(x)\,\text{d}x \\ F(x) & =\int f(x)\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

We can use the power rule with $n=-\frac{1}{7}$ and get

$$
\begin{aligned}F(x) & =\int f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int {x}^{-1/7}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{x}^{-1/7+1}}{(-\frac{1}{7}+1)}+C \\  & =\frac{{x}^{6/7}}{(\frac{6}{7})}+C \\  & =\frac{7}{6}{x}^{6/7}+C.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186502863 :question/id #uuid "054c92af-f6c0-5cb6-8c52-c81bf5740a21"} {:db/id 17592186502872 :question/id #uuid "1ea9e5d9-602f-5599-818f-aa6b87eda7f7"} {:db/id 17592186502876 :question/id #uuid "24409f16-92eb-5e3a-9a94-2612754d8d1a"} {:db/id 17592186502879 :question/id #uuid "2838d5a7-98fc-5b74-838a-12c9f0c1d487"} {:db/id 17592186502887 :question/id #uuid "35340db4-7b99-5255-81e2-d140281bf3c1"} {:db/id 17592186502891 :question/id #uuid "3a5e9787-8ef9-5e19-99e9-70e48a27adcf"} {:db/id 17592186502900 :question/id #uuid "40665566-8355-550d-acf0-8fd3e706266d"} {:db/id 17592186502914 :question/id #uuid "6ac48824-980d-5dff-8c73-e9a877cd9d8e"} {:db/id 17592186502920 :question/id #uuid "7466173d-cde9-509d-97b9-e88aaf8822fd"} {:db/id 17592186502921 :question/id #uuid "7db6e951-901a-5fa3-9344-ecedb4022de8"} {:db/id 17592186502927 :question/id #uuid "8c4c3de5-5797-5a42-a678-da4fa4e6e5be"} {:db/id 17592186502931 :question/id #uuid "99719f66-3778-50b5-89e7-75e1a56079c8"} {:db/id 17592186502938 :question/id #uuid "aa70fb16-17a5-5816-9e73-90243c9b4ed6"} {:db/id 17592186502948 :question/id #uuid "cc7d7a47-ab4b-5a3b-8ff4-ed432aa440ba"} {:db/id 17592186502954 :question/id #uuid "de2aa536-e15f-5af4-b511-e0e4c9d378a1"} {:db/id 17592186050057} {:activity/first-step {:db/id 17592186065001} :activity/id #uuid "b866a7ca-c501-50dd-8117-0d7904f47708" :activity/scope {:db/id 17592186049481 :topic/id #uuid "f8a6d16e-1a41-5d40-8c3d-467ebdcc3782" :topic/math-academy-id 308} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186065001 :step/content {:db/id 17592186065405 :tutorial/content "An **antiderivative** is the *opposite* of a derivative. For example:

- Using the power rule, we know that the *derivative* of $\color{blue}x^2$ is ${\color{red}2x}$.
- Going in the *opposite* direction, we say that an **antiderivative** of $\color{red}2x$ is ${\color{blue}x^2}$.

For any given function, there are infinitely many antiderivatives. For example:

- The derivative of $\color{blue}x^2$ is ${\color{red}2x}$, so an *antiderivative* of $\color{red}2x$ is ${\color{blue}x^2}$.
- The derivative of $\color{blue}x^2+1$ is ${\color{red}2x}$, so another *antiderivative* of $\color{red}2x$ is ${\color{blue}x^2+1}$.
- The derivative of $\color{blue}x^2+2$ is ${\color{red}2x}$, so another *antiderivative* of $\color{red}2x$ is ${\color{blue}x^2+2}$.
- ...

In general, all the antiderivatives of $\color{red}2x$ can be written in the form ${\color{blue}x^2+C}$, where $C$ is a constant.

To represent the antiderivative symbolically, we use a special symbol $\displaystyle \int$ called the **integral** symbol. So, using **integral notation**, we can write

$$
\int 2x \, \textrm d x = x^2 + C
$$

where $C$ represents an arbitrary constant and is called the **constant of integration**.

In words, $\displaystyle \int 2x \, \textrm d x$ is said as “the integral of $2x$ with respect to $x$” or “the antiderivative of $2x$.” Integrals like this are called **indefinite integrals**, and the function being **integrated** ($2x$ in this case) is called the **integrand**." :tutorial/id #uuid "a31b3485-463c-59da-8118-836cf7949efc" :tutorial/math-academy-id 691 :tutorial/title "Introduction"}
